What Republicans don’t know about Black voters’ resilience cost them

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1015 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sen.-elect Scott Colom speaks during a victory rally at Tougaloo College on Nov.
  • In a recent development, the campaign of Mississippi’s Sen.-elect Scott Colom was rightfully praised for its clever and brutal ads.
  • However, it was fitting that the Democrat’s closing message traded the edge for a solemn reminder of who and what brought him so far on his journey to his election as Mississippi’s first Black U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sen.-elect Scott Colom speaks during a victory rally at Tougaloo College on Nov. 11. (Brandon Bell/Getty Images).

In a recent development, the campaign of Mississippi’s Sen.-elect Scott Colom was rightfully praised for its clever and brutal ads. The “pick another protein” spot will forever be stuck in the brains of a huge swath of Americans, especially Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith. She underestimated Colom and his team, and will soon be an ex-senator.

However, it was fitting that the Democrat’s closing message traded the edge for a solemn reminder of who and what brought him so far on his journey to his election as Mississippi’s first Black U.S. senator since Reconstruction.

The ad delivered an all-American lesson about history, born of bravery and sacrifice.

Filmed at the Jackson, Miss., home of slain civil rights leader Medgar Evers, the ad featured Colom recounting the story of Evers, a World War II veteran who survived Normandy, only to be shot in the back by a racist assassin, resentful that a Black man dared to exercise his rights as a citizen in the country he fought for.

Industry observers note that “He was killed for helping Mississippians vote,” Colom mentioned. “On Tuesday, use your vote and honor everyone who died for that right.”.

In a state where voting is still racially polarized, it was clear that Colom would not win over a majority of white voters; he won an estimated 25 percent, better than Democrats in recent elections and cutting into Trump’s margins, but certainly not a path to victory.

Black voters in Mississippi made the difference, as they often have. With their allies in the cause of justice, they heeded the call. They showed up despite the state’s stringent and often confusing voting restrictions, purges of the voting rolls engineered by Republican Secretary of State Michael Watson (who used unverified data from a credit bureau), and the U.S. Supreme Court Louisiana v. Callais decision that led to a wave of Southern states breaking up Black-majority districts.

When the Mississippi purges resulted in “affidavit ballots” that required verification to count, as The Washington Post reported, young Black women tracked down those voters, one by one, to do everything they could to ensure voters’ efforts were not in vain.

Black voters mattered in states all over the country, but especially in the South, where low turnout has plagued Democrats, particularly in midterm elections.

Keisha Lance Bottoms was elected the first Black female governor in the country in Georgia, where Democrats won up and down the ballot. Newly elected senators Annie Andrews in South Carolina and James Talarico of Texas campaigned for and earned support from Black voters with proposals that rose above platitudes. And don’t sleep on North Carolina, where voters flipped seats the GOP tried to gerrymander into a hardened majority. The sight of hundreds of students from HBCU NC A&T State University, denied a campus early voting site, marching to the polls, must have made the ancestors smile.

In Florida and Louisiana, where Democrats had little financial support and lost their statewide races, Black voters brought them tantalizingly close to victory and energized for the contests to come.

According to recent reports, I still don’t expect Republicans to give up the election shenanigans, done in the name of “election integrity” and color blindness but in reality designed to demoralize as much as suppress. Why try to win over a diverse electorate with an inclusive, policy-driven message when manipulating Black-majority districts can still work?

According to recent reports, the number of Black U.S. House members in the next session of Congress will fall, offset by a few Democrats who survived in redrawn districts, including Shomari Figures of Alabama and Don Davis of North Carolina.

But you can’t redistrict a state, and you can’t skip town halls and expect tradition, support for the Confederacy and an “R” after your name to forever save you — the Hyde-Smith playbook.

Recent findings suggest that "I blocked Scott Colom from being a federal judge, and you blocked him from being U.S. senator," she bragged, too soon, on election night.

Maybe she should have emphasized affordability, saving rural hospitals and serving all Mississippians, as Colom did.

What did GOP officials in those Southern red states think they would accomplish by focusing on their base and ignoring everyone else in states they were supposed to be serving?

Did they not pay attention in history class, or maybe they attended one of those post-integration private schools where an unedited version of America’s past might not have been on the lesson blueprint?

Did they believe that voters who remembered Evers, Fannie Lou Hamer, Vernon Dahmer and countless others would shrug and say “you win” when legislatures and elections officials quickly and cynically pounced to quiet their voices?

That would be disrespectful to all the people who worked for, sometimes died for rights they knew they may never enjoy, yet had a belief in America and the rightness of their cause.

Scott Colom and the Evers family remembered. He was emotional in his reaction, in an MS NOW interview, when asked about the statement from Reena Evers-Everette, daughter of Medgar and Myrlie Evers. “Their courage helped make this moment possible,” she said.

It has been revealed that colum agreed: “I absolutely stand on their shoulders. And from the bottom of my heart, I’m going to do everything I can to make them proud.”.

Post-election, he has been very gracious, saying that he intends to serve all Mississippians, including the woman whom I suspect would hit a different note if the election had turned in her favor.

In a recent development, I have no doubt Scott Colom means it. He knows who paid the price to get him this far.

She is host of the CQ Roll Call “Equal Time with Mary C. Curtis” podcast. Follow her on X @mcurtisnc3.

Latest Update: On Location: Dig Stars Amy Poehler and Geraldine Viswanathan on Italian Gelato, Go-Karting—and Tailgating

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1384 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • On Location peels back the curtain on some of your favorite films, television demonstrates, and more.
  • According to recent reports, amy Poehler had never been to Greece, but she was immediately entranced by Kate Myers’s novel Excavations about four women coming together for an archaeological dig in Athens.
  • “The way in which Greek people mingle with real antiquities every day, walking past very important structures, is archaeology in process,” the Saturday Night Live alum tells Traveler.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On Location peels back the curtain on some of your favorite films, television demonstrates, and more. This time, we take a look at Dig.

According to recent reports, amy Poehler had never been to Greece, but she was immediately entranced by Kate Myers’s novel Excavations about four women coming together for an archaeological dig in Athens. So she took her first trip there to set the scene for her 10-part Peacock comedy series Dig, which drops November 23.

“The way in which Greek people mingle with real antiquities every day, walking past very important structures, is archaeology in process,” the Saturday Night Live alum tells Traveler. “The old and the new are constantly bumping up against each other. It was very cool to be there and really helped remind us of the theme of the show that the past is just around the corner and you can't hide from it.”.

It has been revealed that each of the characters comes to the dig site at different stage of their life, with Poehler as an archaeologist stuck as second fiddle to beloved Neville (Hugh Laurie). But it’s her bond with fellow diggers, heartbroken free spirit Dylan (Geraldine Viswanathan), young and flustered Patty (Fina Strazza), and refined but ready to rebel Clare (Antonia Thomas) that provides the backbone of the series—a coming of age story for every age.

Despite being set purely in Greece, Poehler indicates they quickly found that “Puglia wine country, Greece, and Los Angeles can kind of double for each other, which is weird." So the team made southeastern Italy their home base, checking in at Rocco Forte's Masseria Torre Maizza, where they indulged in seafood (“We got overwhelmed by how good the food was!”) and bought tons of pottery wherever they traveled, a side effect of talking about it on the show so much.

Industry observers note that off-set, they found high-speed fun, thanks to the keen ears of Laurie. “We could hear the roar of go-karts from our hotel, so he went around on a motorbike—he's so cool—and found this place,” Viswanathan indicates of Circuit Kart Evolution in Fasano. Poehler jumps in: “The crew and most of the cast raced, but a couple of outsider Europeans who snuck in ended up winning because they had the real lead foot!”.

Amy Poehler's 10-part Peacock series films all across the Mediterranean.

Sources indicate that as for where a second season could take them, the cast will only drop hints. Viswanathan indicates it will be “a little spicier," while Poehler adds “it would be more passionate and fiery." But one thing's for sure, they are ready to start digging again soon. "We have some ideas for where to go and what kind of stuff we could dig up,” Poehler says. “Archeological digs are in a lot of different countries, so we could go all over!”.

According to recent reports, with her executive producer hat on, Poehler really honed in on the details of Greek culture during her time in Athens, in order to capture that same essence on screen. “I’m a Latest Yorker, so Athens is a really cool, vibrant, interesting city, but it does have a lot more graffiti than we expected,” she admits, adding that “some of it is really beautiful.” That meant they had to add that grittiness to some of their recreated sets in Italy and California. Another unique aspect: “the light in Greece is so specific and beautiful,” she notes of the natural rays. The best part? “We got to wrap and then go have the best salad you’d ever had in your life—I’m still thinking about it.” Her favorite was a meal at Barbounaki, where “the guy basically said trust me and came back with a whole fish and cut it at the table—it was so good.”.

The fifth-century BCE Temple of Poseidon serves as an epic ancient backdrop in Dig.

Sources indicate that just over an hour’s drive southeast of Athens stands the remains of the Doric-style Temple of Poseidon, dating back to the mid-fifth century BCE, where Poehler and Laurie filmed. “Talk about set decoration—you’re standing in front of something so amazing,” she states of the ruins at the end of Cape Sounion overlooking the Aegean Sea. The sacred place is even mentioned in Homer’s Odyssey, so needless to say, it’s also a busy tourist attraction. “We had to get there at the crack of dawn before the tours,” Poehler says, noting that the landmark’s staff was standing behind them counting down the minutes they had left. “That’s tough when you’re doing an emotional scene and you know someone wants to get you out of there.” But eventually they did have to open to the public as the cameras kept rolling. “It was funny to be pretending to have this conversation when there’s an American tourist behind you in the shot eating a bag of jelly beans.”.

Sources indicate that the port town of Monopoli provided the rich seaside vibe to double as Greece. Viswanathan states the initial montage where viewers are introduced to her character Dylan when she wakes up on a bench and asks for directions to the dig site was all in town, “which was so dreamy.” Poehler particularly loved the shopping scenes in its old town, including one with Laurie, shot at the hat shop Castrignano dal 1923 (sharp-eyed viewers will see it retains its Italian signage despite being set in Greece). “We wanted a place that Neville would go to pick out his hat for the year, and of course because it’s Italy, there was a beautiful old hat store in the middle of Monopoli and we used some of their hats.”.

At Polignano a Mare, Poehler and co-creator Michael Schur kept open a local gelato stand for the public to enjoy free scoops.

According to recent reports, known for its dramatic scenery and crescent beaches, Polignano a Mare is best remembered to the duo for its most famous treat. “Gelato, so much gelato—Amy let the whole town eat gelato,” Viswanathan revealed. Indeed, after filming at a stand in town, Poehler and co-creator Michael Schur kept it open for the public to enjoy free scoops too. “Then Mike reminded me that I have not paid my half,” she admits. Despite being lactose intolerant, Viswanathan has a sweet spot for hazelnut, while Poehler is all about stracciatella, a refined form of chocolate chip. “I have to say, as an American, chocolate chip is very hard to find—it’s being replaced by mint chip,” to which her co-star replies, “ That’s so not right.”.

In a recent development, the crew also headed inland to the hilltop town of Carovigno with a medieval fortress and a compact city center, which provided the bones for their set. “The locals were very interested in the fact that a production came in and shut down their town square and changed all of the store signs to Greek,” Poehler states. Viswanathan adds: “They were like, these Americans are confused—and lost!” But to get there, they also had to navigate the distinctly Italian way of driving. “It was intense—they come up really close and tailgate in a real way,” Poehler mentioned. “You’ve got to get out of the way!”.

Some of the Mediterranean scenery was recreated on a Universal Studios backlot in California.

Recent findings suggest that back on the Universal Studios backlot, set designer Dan Bishop—who’s worked on Mad Men and Parks and Recreation—recreated the Greek settings and dig site. “He and his team went over to Greece and got a bunch of local beer and signs, so when we were shooting in Los Angeles, it was really fun to be around all the stuff that felt authentic, from the colors and flowers to the buildings—it’s really key to get a feel of that.” But there was one twist that was distinctly Hollywood. “At times we could hear the Fast and Furious: [Hollywood Drift] roller coaster while we were shooting,” Poehler said of the theme park ride that opened in September, after they filmed. “We were hearing them do test runs—it’s open now, which is really exciting,” Viswanathan indicates. While she hadn't been on it yet, she commented, “the night is young.” As for Poehler, she's most happy with her feet firmly on the ground.

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (721 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cntraveler ↗ Open Full Page

The Best Shopping in Athens for Crafts, Old and Fresh

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (721 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Resplendent, timeless Athens is no stranger to feats of invention and imagination.
  • The Acropolis rises over Monastiraki Square and Tzistarakis Mosque.
  • It has been revealed that following a stint in Paris designing for Jean Paul Gaultier and Kenzo over 25 years ago, Lito Karakostanoglou set up her jewelry brand, Lito, in Kolonaki.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Resplendent, timeless Athens is no stranger to feats of invention and imagination. From the hand-carved marble stelae and temple friezes of the stately Acropolis to painted terra-cotta vessels unearthed throughout Attica, this is a city with millennia's worth of artistic output. You'll see this legacy on full display today in the museums and galleries that protect its artifacts. But, crucially, a upcoming wave of makers are sculpting ceramics, weaving baskets, and vigorously curating heirlooms for the contemporary eye. There is plenty to discover in the historic center—at Monastiraki's sprawling outdoor market and ceramics studios, and Syntagma's perfumeries—though that's only the start. Athens may be among the world's oldest cities, but in bustling flea markets and quiet showrooms, its many creatives are paving the path forward.

The Acropolis rises over Monastiraki Square and Tzistarakis Mosque.

It has been revealed that following a stint in Paris designing for Jean Paul Gaultier and Kenzo over 25 years ago, Lito Karakostanoglou set up her jewelry brand, Lito, in Kolonaki. Treat the boutique and its nature-inspired offerings as a cabinet of curiosities. The showroom upstairs is your go-to for one-off pieces. Meanwhile, renowned family jeweler Lalaounis, on Voukourestiou Street, contains glittering collections that take cues from Nubian and Hellenistic art. Harder to find, but easier on the purse, is Neso Studio, in a prewar residential building on Praxitelous. Gold, gold-plated, and silver pieces are handmade there using wax casting techniques. It's best to check ahead for opening times.

Former managing director of label Yiorgos Eleftheriades, Yiorgos Mo turned his knack for collecting into Mo Vintage Athens in 2020. At his tiny shop in arty Koukaki, nab designer pieces from the 1970s to '90s—keep an eye out for Mugler rarities. A 20-minute walk north will take you to L'On, focusing on '80s and '90s garb; think Armani bodysuits and denim sprinkled amid garments from lesser-known Greek labels. Among Psirri's graffiti-sprayed shutters a few blocks over, shop custom-designed Mantility silk scarves and Homatino ceramics on display at Monument Hotel Athens. Nearby, hat workshop Savapile, led by Lisa Sarigiannidou, is the only remaining straw-hat maker in Greece still sewing Italian braid with traditional millinery techniques.

Sheep’s wool kilim and handloomed carpets are draped on a wall of Anthologist.

In eclectic Monastiraki, Mon Coin Studio—which features works from some 300 Greek ceramists—is equally varied. Its collaborative efforts culminate in three annual group demonstrates, one of which is always dedicated to a region rich with a ceramics past such as Sifnos, Lesbos, or Crete. Head north to Vathi for blown-glass amphorae and handloomed throws at Anthologist; it's likely founder Andria Mitsakos will offer you tea and dates as you peruse. South of the Acropolis, shop at Ere Athens, where you can tuck into a cappuccino and banana bread (a perk of going to a store that's run by a pastry chef) while browsing locally made pottery neatly laid atop wood cabinets. Popular picks include paint-splattered cake stands by potter Nicola Fasano and painterly vases from Naked Summers.

Founded by brothers Giorgos and Apostolis Korres, The Naxos Apothecary near Syntagma Square creates tinctures and creams inspired by the Med. Scientific vessels and cloaked candles decorate the space, populated by staff wearing navy lab coats reminiscent of an old-school pharmacy. Leave no display case unexplored, then head upstairs for the herbal tea bar and an outpost of label Ancient Greek Sandals. Just as curated is perfume boutique and florist Phāon in Kolonaki, owned by art director and set designer duo Alexandros Kalogiros and Dimitra Louana Marlanti. Here, find soaps and scents from Astier de Villatte and Ormaie Paris, as well as golden candlesticks by Vasiliki and ceramic lotus flowers courtesy of Despina Charitonidi. Gnocchi the Jack Russell gives everyone a warm welcome.

Hyper Hypo’s selection of books.

Noting a lack of art and design bookshops in the city, graphic designer Stathis Mitropoulos and former fashion editor Andreas Kokkino opened their own. Hyper Hypo, meaning “above and below,” offers literature on photography, interior design, local culture, and more. Dimitris Papaioannou's Sketches From Life, drawn over three summers in Anafi, and Eleanor Lines's illustrated Doors of Kypseli stand out against the Aegean blue walls, while a pair of neon-lit eyes glow above the counter. Plus, Hyper Hypo's seasonal event programming and rare book pop-ups make a visit all the more memorable.

Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., speaks during a news conference at the Capitol last summer. Few details have emerged so far about the government’s search of her home earlier this fall. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

A judge mentioned he will order the release of some information about the federal investigation into Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., which included a search of her Washington house last month.

Recent findings suggest that judge James Boasberg for the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia made the statement Tuesday during a hearing brought by news organizations and an advocacy group seeking details about the search. Boasberg ordered the government to provide him by Friday what could be disclosed in the case. He pointed to how investigators are handling the “speech or debate” clause immunity that Omar has as a sitting member of Congress.

“This is purely legal questions, interesting questions, about the privilege, the extent of the privilege and how it would apply,” Boasberg said.

The Constitution includes an immunity for members of Congress for the “speech or debate” they engage in as part of their jobs.

Boasberg also directed the government to propose redactions to the as-yet secret docket. While he said next week’s expected disclosures would not include the 67-page document that investigators provided to justify the search, he left the door open to unsealing that down the road if the government closes the case or brings charges.

Justice Department attorney Alessandra Serano argued against broad disclosures, calling it “very rare that a precharging, pre-indictment unsealing would happen.”.

The high-profile nature of the investigation leaked into the courtroom Tuesday, as Boasberg cited statements by President Donald Trump and others about the investigation into Omar.

“You have had administration officials, prominent ones, talking about the purpose of the investigation,” Boasberg noted.

Administration officials have accused Omar of committing immigration crimes for years, and Trump noted last month the DOJ was looking into Omar “strongly.” Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said on a recent podcast that investigators had served multiple search warrants and were investigating possible immigration fraud tied to when Omar entered the United States as a child.

Separately, Boasberg noted he may problem rulings in the coming weeks unsealing portions of other court cases tied to the investigation, including one brought by Omar herself earlier this month seeking the return of the items seized in the search.

Recent findings suggest that the administration executed the search warrant in October, just a few weeks before the midterm elections. The timing of the search drew accusations of political bias from Democrats who claimed that the administration brought the case to sway the midterm elections.

For years Trump has said he wanted criminal charges to be brought against his political foes, including Omar and others in Congress.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

American Airlines is making another change to its senior leadership team, with Chief Operating Officer David Seymour set to retire at the end of the year.

In a recent development, seymour will step down on Dec. 31 and remain with the Fort Worth, Texas-based carrier in an advisory capacity through the first quarter of 2027, CEO Robert Isom confirmed Friday.

In a recent development, seymour has served as American’s chief operating officer since 2020. He joined the airline in 1999 and held various leadership positions overseeing technical operations, crew scheduling, and flight operations.

“He’s the guy you want in the room when the stakes are high,” Isom wrote in a letter to employees.

Industry observers note that jonCarlo “JC” Gulbranson, American’s current senior vice president of operations, will succeed Seymour on Jan. 1. He will report directly to Isom and assume oversight of the carrier’s technical operations, safety, and regulatory compliance teams.

It has been revealed that gulbranson began his airline career at Northwest Airlines in 2000 before joining US Airways in 2008. He helped oversee the integration of flight operations systems following the merger with American.

Recent findings suggest that american will also move its corporate security team under its government affairs division. A upcoming reporting structure for the airline’s regional operations will be announced in December.

“For nearly three decades, jet fuel hasn’t just been in my veins. It’s been part of my DNA. To this day, I wake up excited to get to work — which is just about all you can ask for in a job,” Seymour wrote in a LinkedIn post.

The changes follow a broader management reshuffle revealed in August as the carrier works to narrow its profitability gap with competitors Delta and United.

  • Recent findings suggest that my first Thanksgiving was a lavish 12-person dinner in Connecticut in 2014.
  • Take it from an immigrant: this holiday is full of weird contradictions.
  • It has been revealed that as we approach the last Thursday of November, with money very much on our minds, the below well-traveled parents share their hard-won wisdom on pulling off affordable family travel—including how to find treasure in New York City’s Chinatown without paying an arm and a leg, seek out free entertainment in the streets of Oaxaca, and embrace the joys of accessible public transportation in Europe.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that my first Thanksgiving was a lavish 12-person dinner in Connecticut in 2014. I had moved to the US in March of that year and had planned on working from home until a friend generously invited me to go spend the day with her family; an act of unguarded openness that I’ve realized is one of the many things that differentiates Americans from Brits. As soon as we got off the train in Cambridge, Massachusetts, I realized that even though my friend lived in a nasty, overcrowded apartment in Brooklyn, she came from a family that had immense wealth. After dinner, as I helped wash plates in the kitchen, my friend’s mum asked her why she wouldn’t just move into the lovely building they had bought for her. She turned beet red and handed me another dirty plate without looking at me.

Take it from an immigrant: this holiday is full of weird contradictions. Of course, there’s the annual reminder of colonization which requires a careful forgetting of the people who have been colonized. And then there’s the financial aspect of it. At first blush, it seems like the least capitalist holiday of the year—there isn’t the expense of Christmas or Hanukkah gift-giving or the extravagance of Halloween candy. Yet the holiday also marks the start of one of the year's busiest travel seasons when families are taking great expense to reunite, vacation, and explore outside of their every day lives.

It has been revealed that as we approach the last Thursday of November, with money very much on our minds, the below well-traveled parents share their hard-won wisdom on pulling off affordable family travel—including how to find treasure in New York City’s Chinatown without paying an arm and a leg, seek out free entertainment in the streets of Oaxaca, and embrace the joys of accessible public transportation in Europe. All of these stories say something about the wealth of the person writing it, whether or not they wanted to reveal that information. I’m obsessed with getting to the truth about someone’s class (it’s why I wrote my book on the subject), and so these family dispatches, which serve as equal parts advice and confession, are a treat I’ll come back to when I’m not busy washing a rich family’s plates. —Mona Chalabi, Pulitzer Prize-winning writer and illustrator.

Keep reading for the tips and tricks of affordable family travel, road-tested by the experts and illustrated by Mona Chalabi.

I know the secret to parenting and I’m willing to share it: snacks. Snacks are everything—they’re an activity, a mood changer, and a window into culture for kids. Hit a local farmers market on your first day or if you’re somewhere truly out of their comfort zone even a local convenience store—like 7-Eleven in Tokyo—for something that can feel both familiar and novel. If your hotel room has a refrigerator you can store any pre-cut fruit that you buy, or opt for items that don’t require refrigeration like apples, bananas, and clementines. Bring a lightweight backpack, refill each morning, and watch the hangry meltdowns (mostly) vanish. —Dana Kravis, global executive director, CNT video.

Recent findings suggest that last December in London, we stayed in a quaint Airbnb in Primrose Hill and explored different neighborhoods on foot. When our kids, then eight and three, got tired, we hopped on a double-decker bus and headed upstairs, hoping for front seats. Suddenly, getting home became an amusement park ride: Christmas lights, bustling streets, panoramic views. The kids loved it; as a photographer, I loved the vantage point. London caps daily bus fares when you use the same card or phone, and children under 11 ride free. We’ve done this in Singapore, too. Our rule: skip the sightseeing tour (or Uber) and make public transportation part of the family adventure. —Tanveer Badal, photographer.

Breakfast is where family vacations are made, or broken. My moody teenagers can’t be pried out of bed no matter what city they wake up in, so instead of wringing my uncaffeinated hands and hoping to get us all on the same schedule, I just bring my own breakfast, coffee included. Whether in Paris, Rome, or a tent, you will find me hand-grinding my coffee beans, brewing a pour-over, and snacking on a pastry left over from the previous day while I peruse headlines. Avoiding the time and expense of a sit-down breakfast, and indulging in a bit of morning self-care, means we can focus on the adventures and meals we are actually going to remember. —Chris Morocco, food director of Bon Appétit and Epicurious.

My parents and I meet in Aruba every winter for a family vacation that’s warm and relaxing when everyone else is cold and miserable. It’s a classic only child/parents trip where we spend most of our time eating lunch talking about where we’re going to eat dinner. We spend our days mostly just reading parallel to each other. I’ve never been an e-reader user, so I have to bring several physical books to read to get me through the week. The key is that my mom and I have some shared taste in books, so when we finish our own we can swap and save ourselves buying extra books (or lugging even heavier luggage through the airport). —Alison Leiby, comedian and writer.

Finding creative ways to entertain wiggly one-year-olds with limited attention spans can be daunting, but it turns out all you need is a good window. From London to California, staying in rooms on low floors with windows overlooking lots of activity below has resulted in seemingly endless engagement—waving at commuters striding by or golfers strolling a few feet away? Bonus points if the room has curtains with electronic controls—that guarantees an extra hour of ooohs and aaahs, at least. —Sarah Khan, contributing editor.

I have a thing for seeing “The World’s Biggest or Oldest,” and so here we were at Missouri’s Oldest Wooden Suspension Bridge. “Don’t tell your mom,” I noted to my kids, because any bridge that was built from wood during the Civil War should be treated with caution—and, also, all good dad stories start that way. We started up the van, piled everyone in, and began the adventure. The wood cracked and echoed as we drove over the river. It sounded like a popping spinal cord. We swayed, and for a moment, I actually questioned myself. I should have just taken them to the park. Thankfully, I can now confidently say that Missouri’s oldest wooden suspension bridge can hold the weight of a mini-van. —Shannon Carpenter, humorist.

It has been revealed that new York is an expensive city and the best way to keep it cheap is to throw petty cash at it. Instead of buying tickets to an overpriced kid’s experience, I give my children a few twenty dollar bills and take them to Chinatown for a shopping spree. They love the atrocious arcade, and there are fake Labubus, squishy dumplings, a plastic “jade” green dragon that my son now keeps on his bedside, and a 'gold' necklace my daughter thinks is treasure. —Stephanie Danler, author.

According to recent reports, as a seasoned travel writer, I know that any hotel that’s gotten media coverage is often pushing $1,000/night. My trick for affordable family lodging is loading up Google maps, figuring out which area we’re going to stay in, and picking a cheerful place with good reviews in the $250 range. It’s almost never one you’ve heard of, but they’re always clean and cheerful, usually family-owned, and we always leave with substantial hugs and promises to keep in touch. That doesn’t happen at the Georges V. My kids (12 and 8) loved a converted windmill in Rome, a townhouse two blocks from the Rijksmuseum and—most recently—an orange grove near Siracusa where they spent so much time chasing the owner’s cats they even forgot Wi-Fi existed. A steal at any price! —Priyanka Mattoo, filmmaker and author.

People tell you about a million things you “need” before your baby is born, but there's one that has come in the most handy, and I've had a true love/hate relationship with it since day one: A travel car seat. After a ton of research—some may say over-research—we bought a Maxi Cosi Romi. It's rated high for safety, but it's also easy to strap into a car and also an airplane. We always bring it on the airplane, and that's where the headache comes in. While the Maxi Cosi Romi is considered lightweight, it's also big and bulky, and the only way to get it through the airport and onto the plane is by wearing it in a special backpack. I'm pretty sure that I'm one of the most annoying people in any airport as I'm walking through it since I can't really see if I'm bumping into people in the TSA line or getting to the gate. The thing is that, after I considered the numbers, it's actually a really wise investment because most rental car places charge anywhere from $10 to $15 a day to rent a car seat, so we've already started saving money because of it. Now, that's about a hundred or more dollars we're not spending when we go out of town and bring the Maxi. It's wildly annoying and inconvenient, and I look like I'm wearing a jetpack as I'm walking through the airport, but it's worth it. —Jason Diamond, 'Figuring' family columnist at The Cut.

I️ live in Brooklyn where people leave really good stuff out on the street. Once I️ found one of those giant extra storage containers you put on top of your car. I️ haven't found the time to figure out how to put it on top of the car; it's been taking up valuable space in my home for over a year. The other day, I️ found another one that looked even fancier. I️ dragged it home. One day, ideally before our car gets too old to work anymore, I️ will figure this out, then get rid of the extra one somehow (do I️ need to call 311?). After that, my husband, our two kids, our dog, our parakeets and I️ will pack up everything we could possibly need to rent a house somewhere for a week or two. I️ have my eye on Block Island or Martha's Vineyard. —Liana Finck, cartoonist and author.

From bustling markets to neighborhood festivals, I've learned that some of the best family entertainment happens in the streets. In Oaxaca, my four-year-old was mesmerized by calendas, raucous community processions with brass bands, towering puppets called monos de calenda, and rag-covered revelers known as tiliches. Paradegoers tossed my kid candy, fireworks exploded overhead, and the party raged late into the night. We didn't pay a peso. Before booking pricey family activities, research local festivals, celebrations, and public performances. Sometimes the most exciting show in town is happening right on the sidewalk. —Ashlea Halpern, contributing editor.

According to recent reports, on our last family vacation to Rajasthan, a passionfruit lassi from our five-star hotel nearly ruined the trip. We’re talking emergency roadside bathroom stops and several days of Zofran. We’ve been taking our kids—Vijay, Vik, and Meera—to Rajasthan since they were babies; they’re teenagers now. And we’ve learned one unexpected lesson: the sickest we’ve ever been in India was after eating at our five-star hotel. More than once.

So we’ve adopted a newly introduced philosophy: pack the right medicine and embrace street food. In Jaipur, Vineet Sharma, founder of Jaipur Walks, led us on a street food tour around the bustling market, introducing us to piping-hot pyaaz kachori and creamy, saffron-rich kulfi. His advice? Choose clean stalls with high turnover, and favor food cooked fresh and served hot over raw offerings. At busy stalls, food is often prepared continuously and served straight from the heat—sometimes a more reassuring bet than a meal at a luxury hotel or high-end restaurant. And if your stomach’s going to revolt, at least make the meal memorable. —Christine Chitnis, author and photographer.

It has been revealed that this may not be the most popular piece of advice, and I doubt it'll be the most obvious: take your kids overseas during school time. Hear me out: the longer you can stretch your child's travels beyond the limited school holidays when ticket prices always soar, the better for your wallet. Of course, every parent needs to set their own boundary on what and how much school their kind can miss in the name of travel but I feel, especially at a young age, the benefits of the trip outweigh the additional days in the classroom. As I am writing this, I am preparing to leave tomorrow with my first grader for Italy for a week. We are cooking up plans to take our two kids on a long haul trip to the southern hemisphere that'll cut into a week of school. I have heard from more than one expert that Disney especially, should be done when your kids are young, and outside normal school holidays if you want to get great value. I don't do it often but I do balance the guilt with rules—we have to read every day, and do exercises from a homework packet to keep on top of the basics. One day, and soon, I know I won't want to do this much more. But for now, I'm taking every chance to do so. —Erin Florio, global features director.

#123685. Zinke PAC gave to family foundation he was investigated for

Zinke PAC gave to family foundation he was investigated for

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1224 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ryan Zinke, R-Mont., leaves a meeting of the House Republican Conference at the Capitol Hill Club on July 15, 2025.
  • Ryan Zinke gave $200,000 in campaign cash to a family foundation headed by his wife that was once at the center of a federal investigation and an ethics scandal that led him to resign as Interior secretary in 2019.
  • The gift, which has not previously been reported, was made on Aug.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Rep. Ryan Zinke, R-Mont., leaves a meeting of the House Republican Conference at the Capitol Hill Club on July 15, 2025. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

Outgoing Montana GOP Rep. Ryan Zinke gave $200,000 in campaign cash to a family foundation headed by his wife that was once at the center of a federal investigation and an ethics scandal that led him to resign as Interior secretary in 2019.

The gift, which has not previously been reported, was made on Aug. 31 from Zinke’s leadership political action committee to the nonprofit Great Northern Veterans Peace Foundation, campaign finance records show. The donation is more than the foundation has reported receiving in any year since it was founded nearly two decades ago.

Zinke’s wife, son, and sister right now serve on its board of directors, according to the foundation’s annual filing with the state of Montana.

Industry observers note that in a brief interview, Zinke denied that any portion of the money transferred to the foundation will directly benefit him or any of his family members who sit on the board of directors. “No, no, never," he stated when asked if any family members will draw a salary from the gift.

The money will instead go to building a storage barn and kid’s sledding park on the property controlled by the foundation, Zinke mentioned.

None of the records indicate Zinke violated the law or directly benefited from the gift to his foundation.

“While it's not uncommon for a politician to transfer leftover money from a political war chest to charity, it is pretty rare for a politician to transfer leftover political funds to a charity that they or a relative controls,” stated Michael Beckel, director of money in politics reform at Issue One, a bipartisan group that seeks to reduce influence of money in politics.

Instead, outgoing members typically transfer remaining campaign cash to local party committees or candidates, Beckel added.

Ethics experts say Zinke’s move highlights ongoing concerns over the broad latitude campaign finance law gives leadership PACs in how they spend money.

“I definitely think it is something to be concerned about,” said Stuart McPhail, director of campaign finance litigation at Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, a nonprofit watchdog.

“Leadership PACs are really nothing more than personal slush funds under today's rules,” he mentioned, noting that unlike regular campaign committees, member leadership PACs are not prohibited from donating to charities or organizations that could directly benefit the member or relative.

Zinke, a former Navy SEAL who commanded special forces during the Iraq War, converted his traditional campaign committee to a leadership PAC — Commander Zinke Leadership Fund — in March 2026, shortly after announcing he would not run for reelection. It last reported having $1.4 million cash on hand in October of this year.

It marks the second time one of Zinke’s political committees made a payment to the organization. In 2019, the committee Zinke ran during his earlier years in Congress — he served one term in the House before being tapped as Trump’s first-term Interior secretary — gave over $11,000 to the foundation before winding down operations.

The Great Northern Veterans Peace Foundation was founded by Zinke and his wife in 2007 in his hometown of Whitefish, Mont., with plans to provide winter recreational activities for children. Its latest tax filing reports revenue of $15,000 and roughly equal expenses in 2024 for snow plowing and park maintenance.

Zinke’s dealings with the organization were the subject of an ongoing inspector general investigation when he resigned as Interior secretary in January 2019.

Investigators ultimately did not find that Zinke violated conflict-of-interest laws, but they concluded that he failed to comply with federal ethics obligations and “misused his official position in violation of federal regulations.” The Justice Department declined to prosecute Zinke.

Industry observers note that zinke stepped down from the foundation in 2017, shortly after his Senate confirmation. But investigators found that he continued to represent the organization in negotiations with the developers of a commercial project adjacent to the foundation’s land and lied to an ethics agent about his involvement in the project.

The project’s investors included David Lesar, then-chairman of oil services organization Halliburton.

Another Zinke-tied leadership PAC has previously raised eyebrows in Washington.

Supporting Electing American Leaders PAC — known as SEAL PAC — where Zinke serves as chairman, has been marred by accusations that it funneled money to political consultants instead of candidates. A 2022 CQ Roll Call analysis found that 87 percent of the PAC’s spending went to operating expenses.

The PAC also made recurring monthly payments to a company registered to Zinke’s son, Wolfgang Zinke, and based at a Zinke family-owned home in Whitefish.

SEAL PAC’s executive director, Rob Catron, maintained that the payments constitute a consulting fee to Wolfgang Zinke for management of the PAC website, among other tasks. “He earns every penny of it,” Catron mentioned.

Since May 2022, the PAC has given roughly $270,000 to Wolfgang Zinke’s company, FG Solutions, for mailing and printing, records show — more than any individual candidate or committee supported by the PAC. The company also received $5,000 from a related super PAC, SEAL PAC USA, which can solicit unlimited contributions for independent expenditures but can’t donate directly to candidates.

Montana corporate records show Wolfgang Zinke founded FG Solutions – which notes it provides services including “personal assistant and any lawful purpose” – just 10 days before it received its first payment from the PAC in 2022.

Catron defended how the PAC spends money on veterans running for the House, arguing that it takes money to raise money.

“We raise a lion’s share of our funding through national direct mail fundraising, which is very expensive to do,” he remarked, citing the PAC’s use of a national text message fundraising campaign as a major expense.

In a recent development, SEAL PAC raised about $9.6 million this election cycle, distributing about $1.1 million to GOP lawmakers and candidates, according to Federal Election Commission filings. Most of the committee's funds went to operating expenses, including over $3 million paid to Direct Support Services, a Washington-based vendor, for direct mail postage.

Zinke’s not the only lawmaker to face scrutiny over how they spent surplus campaign cash in recent years.

It has been revealed that in 2023, Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., set off alarm bells for transferring $200,000 from his campaign committee to The Sanders Institute, a nonprofit founded by his wife and stepson, following a $350,000 donation from his 2020 presidential campaign coffers.

The organization briefly shut down during Sanders’ presidential run in 2019 to avoid the appearance of impropriety.

Sanders’ stepson, David Driscoll — a former executive at Nike and snowboard manufacturer Burton — is listed on the think tank’s website as its executive director, drawing a six-figure annual salary according to tax filings.

It’s unusual, though not unheard of, for campaign committees to pay family members of the candidate for bona fide work.

“If [Wolfgang Zinke] is actually performing this work, he’s qualified to do it, and this is his typical market rate for this kind of contract, then it would be permissible, even if this was a campaign account,” McPhail noted about SEAL PAC's payments.

But the payments could present a legal “gray area” over whether personal-use restrictions apply to certain PACs, according to McPhail.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that editor’s Note: AirlineGeeks is proud to present our ‘Livery of the Week’ series. Every Friday, a team member will share an airline livery, which can be from the past, present, or even a special scheme. Some airline liveries are works of art. The complexity associated with painting around critical flight components and the added weight requires outside-the-box thinking from designers. The average airliner can cost upwards of $200,000 to repaint, creating a separate aircraft repainting industry as a result.

Have an idea for a livery that we should highlight? Drop us a line.

Iberia’s standard livery combines a predominantly white fuselage with a red-and-yellow tail inspired by the colors of Spain’s national flag. Introduced in 2013, the design marked the carrier’s first major rebranding in more than three decades.

According to recent reports, the airline unveiled its new corporate identity on October 15, 2013, as part of a broader restructuring effort. The redesign replaced the familiar red, orange, and yellow stripes that had appeared on Iberia aircraft since the late 1970s.

It has been revealed that the most prominent change came on the vertical stabilizer. Iberia introduced a sweeping red-and-yellow design that extends from the tail onto the rear fuselage. A white diagonal section separates the two colors, giving the aircraft a different appearance from the geometric logo used on the previous livery.

The fuselage also received a substantial update. Large red “IBERIA” titles replaced the smaller lettering used on earlier aircraft, while the horizontal stripes running along the windows were eliminated. The result was a predominantly white aircraft with most of its color concentrated toward the tail.

Iberia’s new branding retained the red and yellow of the Spanish flag but removed the royal crown from its main corporate logo. The crown had been part of the airline’s previous identity and remained represented separately on aircraft near their registration markings.

The redesign followed Iberia’s 2011 merger with British Airways under International Airlines Group. At the time, the Spanish carrier was undergoing a significant restructuring that included changes to its fleet, route network, and passenger experience.

Industry observers note that the first aircraft to receive the updated livery was an Airbus A330-300 named *Juan Carlos I*, which was presented in November 2013. The newly introduced appearance was subsequently introduced across the airline’s fleet as aircraft underwent scheduled repainting.

Iberia’s earlier livery had been introduced in 1977 and featured a stylized red-and-yellow “IB” logo on the tail. Although the design received minor updates over the years, its basic appearance remained recognizable on aircraft ranging from Boeing 727s and 747s to Airbus A320s and A340s.

The current scheme has since appeared on several generations of Iberia aircraft, including Airbus A320-family jets, A330s and A350s. It also appears on the airline’s Airbus A321XLR fleet, which entered service in 2024 as Iberia became the launch operator of the long-range narrowbody.

It has been revealed that iberia has occasionally introduced special liveries celebrating milestones in its history, including retro designs commemorating the airline’s earlier aircraft. Its standard scheme, however, has remained largely unchanged since the 2013 rebranding.

Now hiring: Staff to power Democrats’ probes

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that ranking member Jamie Raskin, D-Md., arrives at the Rayburn Building for a House Judiciary Committee hearing in February.
  • Democrats in Congress have promised to hit the ground running with sprawling oversight investigations in the new year, making the most of their coming majority.
  • Industry observers note that that means staffing up major committees.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that ranking member Jamie Raskin, D-Md., arrives at the Rayburn Building for a House Judiciary Committee hearing in February. He will be a key player in leading oversight efforts next year — and so will Democratic staff. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

Democrats in Congress have promised to hit the ground running with sprawling oversight investigations in the new year, making the most of their coming majority.

Industry observers note that that means staffing up major committees. And for the dozens of attorneys and other aides preparing to take on a belligerent Trump administration that has cast Democratic oversight as potentially criminal, the job will come with extra scrutiny.

In a recent development, arya Hariharan, former chief oversight counsel to Sen. Richard J. Durbin on the Senate Judiciary Committee and now a partner at Holland & Knight, said the pressure will be on from day one.

“Are you prepared to not sleep very much and know that every single thing you do is going to be scrutinized, every footnote, every comma?” Hariharan said.

Still, the way Hariharan sees it, serving on the Hill is worth it. “I hope they all fall in love with it because it’s a lovely place to work,” she notes of staffers headed there for the first time.

Sources indicate that the work done by attorneys and other staff in oversight probes can swiftly become part of constitutional law. When Trump adviser Peter Navarro defied a subpoena from Democrats investigating the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol, it touched off debates about executive privilege and contempt of Congress. Probes of Hunter Biden led to similar court fights.

Sources indicate that some questions have gone all the way up to the Supreme Court, like in Trump v. Mazars, when the House fought to access Trump’s business records during his first administration in furtherance of toughening up government ethics laws.

It has been revealed that there’s every indication that pressure will continue in the fresh Congress. James Melendres, a partner at Snell & Wilmer, remarked Democrats are poised for aggressive oversight efforts, even if they know it could be tough to make headway against litigation resistant administration officials.

Industry observers note that “Democrats are going to have less than two years to show results. I think they are going to move really fast,” Melendres remarked.

Democrats will likely soon start to send out preservation letters to private companies, institutions and others they intend to probe in the fresh year, if they haven’t already, Melendres stated.

“There may be significant pushback from the administration, from agencies and individual government officials who receive requests. I think third-party, nongovernment agencies and individuals are going to be high on the list for these committees,” he said.

Sources indicate that in addition to the hiring that happens over the next few weeks, House Democrats will have major decisions to make about chamber and committee rules for the newly introduced Congress, including who will hold subpoena authority. And off-Hill observers will be watching closely.

“For companies, for individuals and their counsel, mapping all of that is going to be a major part of the job between now and early January,” Melendres stated.

Lawmakers need to nail down funding levels for congressional committees and staff — the amount of money involved can make a significant difference in how big investigations get. Major committees, and major investigations, take a large amount of staff and expertise to get going.

It has been revealed that for instance, the special House panel that investigated the Jan. 6 attack on the Capitol spent about $14 million in less than 18 months, including for dozens of staffers.

Standing committees, such as Oversight and Judiciary, take a good chunk of change, too. In 2025 the House spent $12.9 million on the House Oversight and Government Reform panel, and $13.1 million on the House Judiciary Committee.

Those expenditures mean dozens of staff working long hours to review documents, send letters, send subpoenas and conduct interviews. Judiciary ranking member Jamie Raskin, D-Md., who is expected to serve as chair next year, said he wouldn’t get into specifics yet about how many resources the newly introduced Congress may devote to oversight efforts.

“But we are talking about the most corrupt administration in the history of the United States, and this is an overwhelming and daunting task that faces us,” Raskin said.

The Trump administration itself has already signaled it intends to push back forcefully on congressional oversight efforts.

Earlier this month, President Donald Trump described Democrats’ vows to investigate his administration as “extortion at the highest level” and called for the Justice Department to “look into this criminal act, immediately!”.

Days later, the White House counsel sent a letter saying that subpoena threats from House Oversight ranking member Robert Garcia, D-Calif., and others “may cross the line into blatant criminality.”.

According to recent reports, U.S. Attorney Aaron Reitz for the Southern District of Texas followed up with letters of his own to Sens. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn.; Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass.; and Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., urging them to preserve documents tied to their promised oversight.

“The American people are entitled to freely associate without their elected officials terrorizing them with aggressive, harassing government action,” Reitz’s letter to Warren stated.

Members of the incoming majority have signaled they intend to defend themselves and their probes, and Blumenthal said he won’t be deterred by the letter.

“There’s no way that I’m going to be intimidated or bullied. It would be laughable and ludicrous, but it is a clear abuse and misuse of prosecutorial powers and weaponization by the Department of Justice,” said Blumenthal, who serves as the top Democrat on the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations.

As for Raskin, he called the White House counsel letter and other missives “absurd on its face.”.

“I’m sure they would love to get into a whole series of letters and counter-letters and litigation. They’re trying to distract everybody from the fact that they just lost the worst landslide electoral repudiation in at least a half century in America, and so they’re going to pick a fight,” Raskin told reporters.

Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., the likely incoming speaker, told reporters last week that he intended oversight efforts in his chamber to be led by Raskin and Garcia.

Industry observers note that “We haven’t ruled anything in. We haven’t ruled anything out. We’re going to follow the facts. We’re going to apply the law. We’re going to be guided by the Constitution, and we’re going to let the chips fall where they may,” Jeffries stated.

Democrats have already publicly listed a handful of job postings for oversight staff and counsel, ranging from the Science to Armed Services to Judiciary panels, set to start early next year.

According to recent reports, beyond those hires, House Democrats will have to make one major pick they haven’t yet confirmed — the House counsel. The position, first created in the 1970s, is hired by the majority and advocates for the chamber in court. That attorney, along with a group of bipartisan House leaders controlled by the majority, will steer the chamber’s legal strategy.

According to recent reports, in prior Democratic Congresses, that office has been active in court; Doug Letter frequently argued on behalf of the Democratic House majority seeking to enforce subpoenas on behalf of congressional committees. The position is held by Matthew Berry in the current Republican-controlled House.

“I mean, I think a lot of people are interested in that job,” Raskin remarked.

Latino voters moved sharply away from Republicans this year, and a record number of Latino Democratic candidates were elected.

But California Rep. Linda T. Sánchez has a warning for her fellow Democrats.

“Latino voters gave Democrats a two-year lease, but it expires in 2028 unless the party changes its playbook for good,” noted Sánchez, who leads the campaign arm of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus.

Failure to address rising costs and push back against President Donald Trump’s immigration agenda could once again scramble the political calculus and spark another realignment in two years, said House Democratic Caucus Chair Pete Aguilar of California.

“While Latinos shifted towards Democrats and … gave us this mandate as a party, Democrats must continue to earn their trust, not just every two years, but every single day,’’ he noted.

Leaders of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus joined newly elected Latino members on Tuesday for a news conference to celebrate the recent wins and the role the group played in securing the House majority for Democrats. The caucus will boast 55 members in the next Congress, its largest roster ever, according to Sánchez.

BOLD PAC, the caucus’ campaign arm, invested heavily in Latino candidates this year, including in primaries.

Industry observers note that california Rep. Salud Carbajal noted that BOLD PAC raised more than $18.5 million this cycle, which helped candidates leverage outside money.

Working-class majority-Latino districts in South Texas, Arizona and California were among the areas that provided Democrats with their biggest wins. Democrats capitalized on voter dissatisfaction over rising costs, the very issue that helped Trump and the GOP make significant gains among Hispanic voters just two years earlier.

But the wins weren’t limited to districts with sizable Latino populations.

Rep.-elect Denise Powell, who flipped a swing seat in Nebraska, credited BOLD PAC for playing a key role in her win.

“Yes, there are Latinos in Omaha, and those Latinos actually helped decide this race,’’ she said. “BOLD believed in me as a candidate, but they also believed in our community.”.

Rep.-elect Bobby Pulido, who came to politics after a successful career as a Latin Grammy-winning Tejano singer, flipped a redrawn South Texas border district that Trump would have carried by 18 points in 2024.

“A lot of people feel like they don't belong to either party. But there's one thing about Latinos is we belong to each other,’’ Pulido said. “It's very hard to be a Latino right now in this country. … I expect to see us united, more united than ever, because it's a tough time right now.”.

Several of the winning candidates deployed novel strategies to reach voters. Pulido famously began performing at quinceañeras after his Republican opponent dismissed him as a performer.

Colorado Rep.-elect Manny Rutinel, who flipped a battleground district north of Denver, attended World Cup and Broncos watch parties. “If people don't hear our message, then it doesn't matter,’’ he noted.

The candidates “met those voters where they were,’’ Sánchez said. “They went into those communities and interacted in a very real and meaningful way. That's something I think that strategists or consultants don't always get. It's not just about pumping out lots of television commercials.”.

Amid those successes for Latino Democrats, Florida, home to one of the largest Latino electorates in the country, was a different story. Republicans held all three majority-Latino districts in the Sunshine State, though former news anchor Eliott Rodriguez, the son of Cuban immigrants, came within half a percentage point of unseating GOP Rep. María Elvira Salazar in a district that backed Trump by 15 points in 2024.

BOLD PAC did have a victory to celebrate in Florida, with Rep. Darren Soto, the deputy chair of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus, narrowly prevailing in a district that Republicans redrew as one that no longer had a Latino majority.

“The redistricting wars ended up failing because of the investment by BOLD PAC,’’ Soto said.

A mother indicates Delta Air Lines separated her from her two-year-old daughter, then told her to ask other passengers to switch seats. She says she had purchased Comfort+ and originally selected seats together. If her account is accurate, this was a problem for Delta to resolve before boarding, not something to leave a parent negotiating in the aisle.

In a recent development, in a Reddit post, a passenger describes trying to resolve separate seat assignments on a flight from Orlando (MCO) to Atlanta (ATL). She was traveling with her husband, their 2½-year-old daughter, and their one-year-old son.

She indicates she was directed to the gate for assistance, but received this response:.

This remains her account and we don’t have a way to verify the booking history or the exchange with the gate staff. She also does not clearly state how the family ultimately sat onboard.

It has been revealed that I have traveled extensively with my children, including when they were very young. There is a considerable difference between wanting the entire family together and needing a two-year-old beside a parent.

It is unreasonable to ask an airline to rearrange a cabin so that every adult in a traveling party can sit together. Heidi and I can sit apart. One parent can sit with one child while the other sits elsewhere with the other child. We have done that many times.

Sources indicate that but a toddler needs an adult who can help with the seatbelt, food, and everything else that comes with flying at that age. The stranger assigned to the adjacent seat cannot reasonably become the person expected to provide that help.

I see no excuse for the Delta agent. Once an agent knows a toddler has been assigned a seat away from both parents, someone needs to take responsibility for finding a workable arrangement and it should be someone in a position of authority…like the gate agent.

I am also sympathetic to passengers who pre-select a seat and then find themselves pressured to move.

It has been revealed that A parent should not board, occupy someone else’s seat, and announce that the family needs to sit together and a passenger should not be shamed for declining an aisle-to-middle swap. There may be very good reasons that person selected that particular seat, and those reasons are not necessarily anyone else’s business.

That is precisely why the airline should handle this.

According to recent reports, an agent can review the seat map, identify possible swaps, and ask for volunteers. If necessary, the airline can offer an incentive rather than expect a stranger to absorb the inconvenience for free. There may also be a solution involving a different cabin, provided the family agrees and any fare difference is addressed.

The ultimate solution to situations like these does not have to preserve every preference the family had when booking. It does need to put a young child beside a responsible adult.

The published Delta family seating policy states:.

“Delta strives to seat family members together upon request.”.

It directs customers who cannot obtain seats together online or through the app to contact reservations to review the available options. That wording is less reassuring than a guarantee. Even so, I would expect the assistance to amount to more than telling a parent to start asking around once onboard.

Recent findings suggest that parents should understand fare restrictions and select seats when possible, but a two-year-old’s need to sit beside a parent does not disappear because the family purchased a cheaper ticket and it becomes legally dicey to not sell basic economy tickets to young children. However, in this case it was not a basic economy ticket but a Comfort+ seat.

Sources indicate that selecting seats months in advance does not mean you can stop checking them. Whenever I receive a schedule change, I review the flights and seat assignments and check again often in the week leading up to travel. Be sure to take a screenshot of your original seat assignments if they were not reflected on your ticket confirmation.

According to recent reports, if a young child becomes separated from a parent, contact the airline promptly and explain the child’s age. If reservations cannot resolve it, arrive early and ask an airport agent…don’t agree to negotiate onboard…it’s unreasonable, even for Frontier Airlines.

This is called “gardening” your reservation.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On Location peels back the curtain on some of your favorite films, television shows, and more. This time, we take a look at Fjord.

It has been revealed that following in the footsteps of Anatomy of a Fall and Sentimental Value, Cristian Mungiu’s fresh film Fjord continues a recent trend of complex, critically acclaimed family dramas set against a gorgeous—if appropriately chilly—European backdrop. The Romanian New Wave director won his second Palme d’Or at this year’s Cannes Film Festival for the Norway-set film, which is also his first shot outside of his home country and Romania’s official selection for the best international feature category at the 2027 Oscars.

Loosely based on a real court case, Fjord follows a devout evangelical Romanian man named Mihai (Sebastian Stan) and his Norwegian wife Lisbet (Renate Reinsve) who move to a remote fjord village in Norway with their five children. Their conservative lifestyle soon puts them at odds with their progressive neighbors, and they find themselves in a custody battle after child abuse allegations surface, setting up a complicated debate between two opposing cultures and worldviews.

Cristian Mungiu’s latest film is based on a real-life court case.

The film was shot over 36 days in spring 2025 in Western Norway’s Hjørundfjorden. The dramatic and mostly tourist-free fjord near the city of Ålesund cuts through the Sunnmøre Alps, with peaks rising up to 5,600 feet directly from the water.

For the family home, location scouts selected a tiny village called Stenes, comprising just a few rustic buildings scattered on the shores of the fjord’s Norangsfjorden arm. Nearby, they shot church scenes at a simple wooden structure in the town of Øye with school scenes taking place in Sæbø and courthouse scenes being filmed in the “significant city” of Ålesund.

As the title of the film suggests, the fjord is more than just a mere setting—it’s a poetic space suffused with symbolic meaning for Mungiu. “I was attracted by this idea of a very secluded community where people can’t avoid finally talking to one another,” Mungiu notes. “The fjord evokes for me this need for solidarity among people when confronted with extreme coldness and severe weather.”.

Mungiu sought to balance the epic scale of the fjord setting with the legal drama of the film.

In a recent development, while audiences might expect the grandeur of a fjord to humble the people who live within it, in this movie, Mungiu instead uses the geographical formation to highlight their folly. “Normally, in front of nature’s force, people should become conscious of their fragility,” Mungiu notes, “but too often their huge egos make them forget how mortal and insignificant they are, and they end up investing all their energy into imposing their point of view on others.”.

The landscape worked particularly well within the context of Mungiu’s unique visual storytelling style: He conceives of each scene as a single shot, without cuts or close-ups, letting his characters move through expansive frames. As he describes it, “Every shot needs to be perfectly balanced in terms of light, interpretation, choreography, rhythm.” For this project, he imagined scenes that would call to mind the winter landscapes of Flemish Renaissance master Pieter Bruegel the Elder, who painted small human figures dwarfed by snowy scenery. The wide shots, Mungiu says, “allow the majestic nature to feel a bit intimidating and menacing.”.

The winter landscapes in the film were inspired by the work of Flemish Renaissance painter Pieter Bruegel the Elder.

Sources indicate that when it came time to select the perfect fjord, Mungiu was purely pragmatic. “I imagine scenes quite in detail when I write the screenplay and while scouting,” he explains. “I try to find locations as close as possible to what I’ve imagined.” He drew a “very precise sketch” for his location scout of what he was looking for: two neighboring houses at the end of a fjord, “with mountains and forests behind, quiet deep water in front, and a narrow road connecting them to the rest of the world—all this ideally covered in snow during wintertime.”.

His production team found a spot that looked just as he envisioned in Stenes, deep down the fjord and away from the coast, to maximize the potential for more snow. Then the hardest part started: convincing the homeowners to rent their properties out for the shoot.

In a recent development, “Once we started our scouting, we felt that we were visiting a form of paradise,” he says. “The light always comes from an angle, the air is pure, the colors are strong, the calm of the ocean is threatening, the snow on the peaks looks menacing.” Everything in the area, he continues, “is clean, organized, precise, logical, and functional.” Mungiu jokes, “For an OCD person like me, it was the perfect place.”.

According to recent reports, of course, the wildness of the fjord came with its own set of challenges, from avalanche warnings to a lack of consistent snow cover (they trucked in powder from the mountains). But Mungiu and his team tried to use these issues to their artistic advantage. On the first day of shooting, for instance, a major storm forced them to move production inside and shoot an emotionally complex scene. Inspired by the dramatic gusts, they hung an enormous Norwegian flag just outside the window to thrash and snap in the gale, “adding a visual element to the inner feelings of Lisbet in a very delicate moment for her as a character.”.

Recent findings suggest that the primary gateway town for the fjord is Ålesund, a coastal city known for its abundant Art Nouveau architecture. While it’s only about 20 miles from Stenes as the crow flies, the journey takes about two hours of scenic driving and ferry crossings to get to the spots where the movie was shot.

Sebastian Stan as Mihai Gheorghiu, the devout evangelical main character who relocates his family to the titular Norwegian fjord.

If you want to see the fjord for yourself, an ideal lodging option is the lovely Hotel Union Øye, which opened early for the season to host the cast. Now a member of Relais & Châteaux, the gingerbread-like hotel debuted in 1891 and over the decades has hosted the likes of Henrik Ibsen, Arthur Conan Doyle, and Edvard Grieg, who composed music on the piano in the salon.

Recent findings suggest that it’s also possible to visit Hjørundfjorden on one of Norway’s most iconic journeys: a sailing with Hurtigruten, which is part pleasure cruise line, part local passenger ferry, and part cargo vessel for remote communities. In 2027, the line’s Coastal Express route, which hugs the coast from Bergen in the south to Kirkenes in the north, will visit Hjørundfjorden in May and September, while the Svalbard Line will make a stop at Sæbø in the fjord from May through September. (In the film’s Ålesund-set courtroom scenes, you can even see the ferry looming outside the windows.).

Havila Voyages, a family-run Hurtigruten competitor, also stops in Hjørundfjorden seasonally from September 1 to October 31; optional excursions include a scenic drive through the surrounding countryside and mountain valleys; an e-bike tour through the narrow Norangsdalen valley along the “Queen’s Route” (so named because it was supposedly visited by seven queens); or a guided hike to a mountain dairy farm, followed by a snack of a svele (crepe).

And if you can’t make it to Norway, Mungiu is presenting an exhibition of his photographs from scouting trips and the film’s production called Fjord. The Pictures at New York’s Romanian Cultural Institute in New York (through November 30). His images, all shot on a phone, depict the landscapes, people, architecture, and even weather that helped shape the film’s visual language.

Breaking: Airline Elite Status So Close, Yet So Far: The Drawback To Being A Free Agent

💡 Key Takeaways

  • It has been revealed that I fly United quite a bit and if I’m being honest, the experience is usually excellent…I seek out the A321neo, as Starlink has shifted from a nice bonus to requirement.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I boast often about being a free agent when it comes to both hotels and airlines…I’m done chasing elite status (at least top-tier elite status) because the cost/benefit analysis no longer works for me. But there are some days I wonder….

It has been revealed that I fly United quite a bit and if I’m being honest, the experience is usually excellent…I seek out the A321neo, as Starlink has shifted from a nice bonus to requirement. But it’s not just that. The food has improved and service has been great..flight attendants appear happy (they have a contract after all) and the operation has also been good: my personal on-time arrival rate with United is over 90% while it hovers at around 50% for American.

And sometimes after another great United flight, like my journey back to California over the weekend, I do wonder if I  am better served just getting back on the hamster wheel and putting most of my eggs in the United basket. This flight was from Chicago to Los Angeles and I just missed the upgrade to first class as a Gold…had I been Platinum, I would have scored an upgrade.

According to recent reports, I’m close…not that I’m projected to spend $5K in the last month of the year on United airfare…but it is conceivably within reach. And in the next month I’m flying Aer Lingus, American, Delta, JetBlue, KLM, and United….maybe even more.

And having Premier Platinum status would certainly help with some upgrades and I’d put the PlusPoints to use….

But then I pinch myself and think I’m actually only 2/3 there with 1/12 of the year left…and to spend all that money on United instead of flying the carriers and routings and times that work best for me (mostly in premium cabins…) just doesn’t make sense.

So I return to reality and think, no, the status just isn’t worth it and if I really need the premium cabin seat, I’ll pay for it. And the irony is that the majority of my flights this year have been in premium cabins and to reach top-tier status you have to essentially buy premium cabin fares anyway or else you will never spend enough. So what’s the point? Free baggage? Extra legroom seats for the family? I don’t find that worthwhile.

So I guess the bottom line is that by splitting my loyalty this year I’ll make Gold on American and Gold on United (nothing on Alaska, Delta, or JetBlue, though I have flown them all) whereas I could have rather easily made Platinum on United had I been a bit more loyal to a product that I do genuinely like.

But no. I still think I’m making the correct choice for my circumstances.

And yet it’s the allure of frequent flyer elite status is still somewhat enchanting….

American Grows Maintenance Footprint in Miami
