    An American Eagle pilot asked air traffic control about an unexplained traffic advisory near Baltimore and received an answer that probably was not what he was expecting: there had been “alien sightings” in the area. The exchange makes for entertaining listening, though the actual report is considerably less dramatic.

    A recording circulating online captures an unusual conversation reportedly involving American Eagle flight 5432 from Washington National (DCA) to Philadelphia (PHL) on November 21, 2026.

    According to International Business Times, PSA Airlines operated the flight with a Bombardier CRJ-900, using the callsign Blue Streak 5432. Near Baltimore, the pilot asked about a traffic advisory without an identification tag. The controller explained that the flight had already passed the only other known traffic nearby.

    Then came the unexpected observation:.

    “I mean, we have had alien sightings out there, so…”.

    The controller went on to describe an earlier report from another pilot about something zigzagging ahead of an aircraft near Martin State Airport, without a corresponding radar target.

    The American Eagle pilot took the comment in good humor, suggesting it would make an interesting story to tell his family.

    Sources indicate that A pilot reporting strange lights near Baltimore got an unexpected response from ATC, who casually mentioned there had been alien sightings in the area. The pilot joked that he’d have quite the story to tell his family. 👽✈️#ATC #Aviation #Aliens pic.twitter.com/rtalRieUwH.

    — Flightdrama (@flightdrama) November 21, 2026.

    Before you start booking a window seat from BWI specifically to look for visitors from another planet, the American Eagle crew was asking about a traffic advisory… these pilots did not actually see an unidentified object outside their aircraft.

    The zigzagging object was part of the controller’s recollection of a different pilot’s report: there’s quite a leap from an unexplained alert and a controller’s remark to an extraterrestrial encounter.

    Yet after so much grim aviation news lately, I enjoyed this one.

    Pilots and controllers have serious responsibilities, but there is room for a little personality on the frequency when circumstances permit. It is often the testy verbal exchanges between pilots and air traffic controllers that make headlines, but a passing remark like this also gives us a glimpse of the human beings doing the work.

    Industry observers note that an American Eagle pilot’s question about a traffic advisory prompted an unexpected reference to earlier alien sightings near Baltimore. While there was no alien spacecraft sighting, it is an entertaining radio exchange and a rather good story.

    Mary Peltola unseats Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (782 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Mary Peltola speaks during her election night party in Anchorage on Nov.
    • Mary Peltola has defeated Republican Sen.
    • In a recent development, the Associated Press called the race for Peltola around 10:19 p.m.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Former Alaska Rep. Mary Peltola speaks during her election night party in Anchorage on Nov. 3. (Charly Triballeau/ AFP via Getty Images).

    Former Rep. Mary Peltola has defeated Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska, giving Senate Democrats their ninth pickup of the midterm elections and bringing their caucus’s total seats in the next Congress to 56.

    In a recent development, the Associated Press called the race for Peltola around 10:19 p.m. Eastern time on Tuesday, a full two weeks after Election Day. The latest tranche of ballots counted put the former congresswoman past the 50-percent threshold to win the election outright without Alaska’s ranked choice voting system kicking in.

    With her victory, Peltola, who is Yup’ik, becomes one of the first Native American women elected to the Senate, along with fellow Democrat Peggy Flanagan, who won the open seat in Minnesota this month.

    “As a lifelong Alaskan who has dedicated my life to serving our state, there is no greater honor than having Alaskans’ support in our fight to take on corporate greed, lower costs, and put Alaska first.,” Peltola mentioned in a statement after the race was called.

    It has been revealed that the Alaska race was the final Senate contest to be called in a midterm election that saw Democrats win commanding majorities in both chambers of Congress. Besides Alaska, Democrats also flipped Senate seats in North Carolina, Maine, Ohio, Texas, Iowa, Kansas, South Carolina and Mississippi.

    It has been revealed that peltola, a former state legislator, made history in 2022 when she became the first Alaska Native elected to Congress, winning a special election for the state’s at-large district. She comfortably won the general election that fall but was narrowly unseated in 2024 by Republican Nick Begich.

    She entered the Senate contest in January, positioning herself as an independent-minded Democrat and invoking the legacies of two well-liked Alaska Republicans, the late Sen. Ted Stevens and the late Rep. Don Young, whom she succeeded in the House.

    She campaigned on the slogan “fish, family, freedom” and played up her moderate views and deep roots in the state.

    Sources indicate that but the race was marked by allegations of political gamesmanship. In addition to the incumbent Sullivan, a retired colonel in the U.S. Marine Corps Reserves, the Senate ballot also included a retired teacher named Dan J. Sullivan. The New York Times reported late last month that operatives aligned with Peltola’s campaign were involved in the effort to recruit the second Dan Sullivan in an attempt to confuse voters.

    Peltola has noted she had no connection to the scheme.

    Recent findings suggest that prior to Election Day, the Trump administration filed a lawsuit seeking to delay certification of the result if Sen. Sullivan were to lose. The lawsuit was tossed earlier this month by a federal judge.

    Industry observers note that trump also suggested that all votes cast for Dan J. Sullivan should be added to the incumbent’s total. “If you add them up, Dan Sullivan wins,” the president told reporters Monday. But as of Tuesday evening when the race was called, Peltola had more votes than both Sullivans combined.

    It has been revealed that the Alaska race was initially viewed as a long shot for Democrats. The Last Frontier has elected a Democratic senator just once in the past 50 years – in 2008, when Mark Begich ousted Stevens. Begich, the Democratic uncle of the current Republican congressman, served a single term before he was ousted by Sullivan in 2014.

    But anger in Alaska over the rising cost of food and fuel — already among the highest in the nation — provided Democrats with an opening.

    "56 seats was an unimaginable result even just a few months ago," Senate Democratic leader Charles E. Schumer said in a statement Tuesday night. "But I knew if we concentrated on getting the best candidates, and if we focused like a laser on the costs, corruption, and chaos that Donald Trump has wrought throughout America, we would have shot.".

    In other Alaska races, Democrats flipped the governor’s mansion, with former state Rep. Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins winning an open-seat race to become the first Democrat elected governor of the state since Tony Knowles won a second term in 1998.

    It has been revealed that the race for the state’s at-large House district will be decided by ranked choice voting, with tabulations expected to take place Wednesday. Begich, the GOP incumbent, was leading Tuesday with 47.5 percent of the vote and is expected to prevail over independent Bill Hill, who had the backing of national Democrats and trailed with 42 percent. Another Democrat and a Libertarian combined for the remainder of the vote.

Shoppers can take 25% off sitewide (the one major exclusion: the Series 3 collection), which nets out to as much as $186 per item. This sale runs through 11:59 PM PST on December 1, or the date on which supplies run out, so you've got a little time to decide. You can also shop in stores if you prefer and score the same discount. Not sure what to get? If I were in the market for a new carry-on, I'd go with the Bigger Carry-On—in fact, I recently took it with me on a five-day trip. During the sale, it's $221 instead of $295.

    It has been revealed that buying luggage for the whole family? If you spend $750 or more, you'll get 10% off the entire order. If you are shopping for multiple pieces, know that you can save even more by bundling items. There are a whole bunch of options that can help cut down on any holiday decision fatigue—the best-selling Jetsetter bundle saves you $255, with sets like the Work From Anywhere bundle or the Best Selling bundle saving you $124. There's also a build your own bundle option for those looking with specific items in mind.

    Whichever route you go, you can rest easy knowing each piece is crafted for travelers who value both form and function: hard-shell suitcases that glide seamlessly through terminals, compact carry-ons with convenient compartments, and travel bags that make packing feel like an art.

    For even steeper Black Friday discounts, head to Away's Last Chance sale page. As the name suggests, these items aren't coming back, so if there's something you like, don't dillydally (but also keep in mind that you won't be able to return it). There are a ton of fun pieces for kids in there, including a few items from the Toy Story collaboration. The Featherlight Weekender is marked down 30%, bringing its price tag down to $103, as is the ultra-chic Pet Carrier ($159, down from $228). The Softside Compact Carry-On is another great find, especially for business travelers or anyone looking to shift their personal item from a tote or backpack to a roller ($123, down from $205). One more item to call out, especially for those with football games or stadium concerts on their calendar—the clear Stadium Bag, which is 30% off in cherry red or island pink trim ($52, down from $75).

    Recent findings suggest that away is making travel more accessible for those who give back to their communities with a 10% discount for veterans, active military members, medical personnel, teachers, and students. Whether you're a student preparing for a semester abroad or a teacher gearing up for a well-deserved getaway, this offer makes premium luggage more affordable. Simply verify your status through ID.me, and you’re all set to enjoy stylish, durable travel essentials at a discounted price. For more details, visit Away’s Hero Discounts.

    Sharing your love of travel has its perks with Away’s $40 off referral offer. When you introduce a friend to the brand, they’ll receive $40 off their first purchase of $125 or more—and once their order is complete, you’ll get $40 off your next one, too. The best part? You can earn up to $200 in rewards by referring as many as five friends. To claim the offer, your friend simply uses your referral link to visit Away’s Get Rewarded page, where a unique code appears to apply at checkout. The discount is valid on suitcases and bags only, making it an ideal way to refresh your own travel setup while helping someone else discover the quality and design that make Away a go-to for savvy travelers.

    It has been revealed that away proves that great design and thoughtful functionality don’t have to come at a steep price. The brand’s lineup of best-selling luggage under $300 includes sleek staples like The Carry-On ($275) and The Bigger Carry-On ($295)—lightweight, durable pieces that glide effortlessly through terminals and tuck neatly into overhead bins. You can explore more travel-ready finds in Away’s Under $300 collection.

    In a recent development, for families, Away’s Family Travel collection makes group trips easier with space-maximizing suitcases, kids’ luggage, diaper bags, crossbody bags, and even pet carriers. Larger pieces like The Medium Flex and The Trunk offer extra capacity and deep compartments, perfect for storing everyone’s essentials in one place.

    According to recent reports, A great way to save on luggage that's latest to you and help reduce waste? Away Reclaimed, the brand's hub for secondhand luggage. Many pieces go for up to $100 less than their original retail value, and each item is graded on a scale of ‘Good’ to ‘Great’ to ‘Excellent’, based on how many cosmetic flaws are present. Per Away, every item is in “travel-ready condition,” and the “surfaces and interiors are cleaned and refreshed.” As you can imagine, inventory comes and goes fairly quickly. If you have something specific in mind, know that you can select the “Notify Me” button on any item page to receive an email notification when the size and color you're looking for becomes available.

    Sources indicate that away’s appeal goes beyond its minimalist design—it’s the thoughtful details that make the brand a trusted travel companion. Orders over $100 ship free, and if something isn’t quite right, you can return or exchange unused items within 100 days, either online or at one of Away’s 17 stores. Every suitcase is backed by a lifetime warranty, covering functional repairs so your luggage lasts trip after trip.

    According to recent reports, there’s purpose behind the polish, too: With sustainability in mind, Away incorporates more recycled materials into its luggage and ships everything in 100% recyclable packaging. And with Shop Pay, you can choose interest-free installments to make investing in quality gear a little easier.

    If your Away promo code isn't working at checkout, don't panic—there are a few simple things you can do. First, double check that the code is spelled correctly with no extra spaces or typos. If that doesn't work, take a look at the exact details of the promo code to make sure it's still active and hasn't expired already. Keep in mind that some discount codes have a minimum spend requirement, so you'll want to be sure you've hit any necessary criteria for the deal. If everything looks right and your Away promo code still isn't working, clear your browser's cache and give the page a refresh. Shoppers can also contact Away's customer service for help.

    #123635. The 40 Best Resorts in the Caribbean: 2026 Readers’ Choice Awards

    📅 21 Dec 2018 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2368 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cntraveler ↗ Open Full Page

    The 40 Best Resorts in the Caribbean: 2026 Readers’ Choice Awards

    📅 21 Dec 2018 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2368 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

    ⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that trends come and go, but here at Condé Nast Traveler, one thing never changes: your insatiable appetite for seeing the world.
    • View this gallery as a list of the top resorts in the Caribbean with scores here.
    • Recent findings suggest that anse Chastanet is a retreat for active travelers who enjoy its unique open-air luxury, whether enjoying a romantic honeymoon, scuba diving in the Soufriere Marine Management Area, or just exploring eco-paradise.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that trends come and go, but here at Condé Nast Traveler, one thing never changes: your insatiable appetite for seeing the world. This year, our readers cast an almighty 798,867 votes in our 39th Readers’ Choice Awards to tell us about the planet’s best travel experiences: You fell hard for palace hotels in Morocco, cruised down the Amazon, and got swept up in Fresh York City’s exhilarating energy. Now, read on to find out where your favorites fall among the winners—and get inspired for where to go next, whether it's to a top-rated hotel or resort, or centered around a worthy cruise, spa, or island. These are the best resorts in the world as voted by you, our readers.

    View this gallery as a list of the top resorts in the Caribbean with scores here.

    Recent findings suggest that anse Chastanet is a retreat for active travelers who enjoy its unique open-air luxury, whether enjoying a romantic honeymoon, scuba diving in the Soufriere Marine Management Area, or just exploring eco-paradise. The 600-acre, 51-accommodation property has two soft sand beaches, four restaurants, three bars, and enough options—from jungle biking on the property’s trails, to snorkeling with a marine biologist, to playing pickleball, to a chocolate-focused treatment menu at Kai Belté Spa —to keep guests as active or relaxed as they prefer. The resort can also arrange unforgettable romantic experiences like an ultra-luxe private sunset catamaran sailing or a Private Castaway Beach Dinner. Many of the rooms feature either open-air louvered walls or true open-air walls, with each room individually designed and carefully angled with privacy in mind. Many rooms feature stunning views of the Caribbean, the Pitons, or both. The gorgeous property is located on a steep hillside with many stairs, uneven pathways, and no elevators, so access may be a challenge for people with limited mobility.

    Check Availability at Booking.com.

    Recent findings suggest that the namesake hillside resort set above Toiny Bay gives “wild” an unexpected new meaning when it comes to sceney St. Barts. On the shrubby southeastern point of the island, this unfussy haven is where an in-the-know social set head to find serenity. The star amenity here is the private beach, accessible via a three-minute Defender ride down switchbacking roads. Le Toiny’s stretch of soft sand is considered the sole private hotel beach on all of St. Barts. Plus, some of the oldest traditional English-style cottages on the island, dating back to the 1700s, can be found beside the beach club (one is at the moment used as treatment areas for the spa). The suites and villas were redesigned in 2024 to create airy living spaces that draw your eye outward to the leafy open-air surroundings and azure water views just beyond your private pool deck.

    Check Availability at Booking.com.

    In a recent development, grand Cayman may be famous for its SCUBA diving and offshore banking, but with several daily non-stops from Latest York and Boston, it’s increasingly drawing families to its powdery, placid western Caribbean beaches. On the island’s Seven Mile Beach—one of the loveliest stretches of sand in the world—you'll find the 266-room Kimpton Seafire Resort & Spa, with a boutique atmosphere that manages to be both child-friendly (two pools, a kids club) and hip (colorful, contemporary design, and a lobby scene replete with pool table, library, and daily happy hour). The food is also strong: Hit beachside Coccoloba for fish tacos and ceviches; Ave, the resort's primary restaurant, for epic breakfast buffets (including house-made cronuts); and the sceney Avecita for progressive Spanish fare like white anchovy toast and prawn tartare, served up alongside craft cocktails at the chef’s counter. You can always snorkel and parasail right off the hotel’s beach, but you’re also just a short ride from Stingray City (where you can stand on a sandbar and touch giant rays as they swim by), world-class gardens (look for the endangered blue iguana), golf, and roadside jerk chicken. Hit Rum Point to toast the sunset—or maybe you'll prefer doing that from your own private balcony.

    It has been revealed that this romantic all-suite beachfront retreat north of the sprawling all-inclusives of Punta Cana is a diamond literally in the rough—the last two miles of the approach road are so bone rattling that it may be worth ponying up more than $250 for the ten-minute helicopter transfer from the airport in Punta Cana. But behind the resort’s unmarked security gate, Zoëtry is breathtaking. The open-air lobby has a soaring peaked thatch roof, and the 51rooms, divided between two-story thatched buildings and freestanding villas, are arranged around two snaking pools and are no more than a one-minute walk from the beach. With classic clean lines, they are dramatic by virtue of their size (the smallest is 775 square feet) and simple comforts—wicker ceilings, dark hardwood floors and furniture, white-on-white beds, immense bathrooms with black slate showers and deep soaking tubs. The resort’s restaurants draw culinary inspiration from traditional Dominican fare and international flavors, with an emphasis on using locally grown and organic ingredients.

    Sources indicate that for toes-in-the-sand luxury with impeccable service, foodie-approved eateries, Caribbean-cool rooms, and views that will have all your friends and family seeing green, La Samanna can’t be beat. Set along the white sands of Baie Longue, known for being one of the most beautiful beaches in all of St. Martin, guests are never far from the startlingly turquoise waters, and La Samanna offers plenty of ways to get out on the water, including complimentary kayaks, paddleboards, snorkeling gear, and more. With three main restaurants—one of which changes in concept between lunch and dinner—plus a fabulous daily breakfast and top-notch room service, there’s really no reason to leave for meals. The star of the show is L’Oursin, the upscale French restaurant just off the lobby, where each table comes with a view of the sailboat-spotted sea. If you can, splurge on one of the property's eight independent villas—the double-level mansions have everything a group could need to vacation more than comfortably.

    Check Availability at Booking.com.

    It has been revealed that the "secret" part of Secret Bay's name is no accident—the resort's 10 gorgeous villas give new meaning to the word hideaway. Touches vary from villa to villa, but all have interiors and floors made of Guyanese Greenheart, bedroom furniture made of Dominican red cedar, open decks, private pools, and 180-degree views over the mountain peaks of Dominica and the Caribbean Sea. Though we doubt you'll get tired of living your own castaway fantasies (albeit with much nicer accommodations), Secret Bay's concierge is available to help craft personalized itineraries: think rainforest hikes with a famed naturalist, or a sunset sail along the island's western coast.

    Check Availability at Booking.com.

    Anguilla is a small-but-mighty island packed with a handful of luxury properties, dining options, and a whole bunch of outstanding beaches. Barnes Bay and Meads Bay surround the property on both sides, with waters that are occasionally rough but known to be swimmable at other times of the year. Regardless of the conditions, white beach chairs line the sand in pristine formation each morning, and three large pool areas—two kid-friendly, and one adults-only—provide plenty of swimming options when the ocean is unavailable. The property stretches across the shore, which means each room provides a unique view of some combination of the wide property’s beachfront, ocean, palm trees, or garden areas. In the ocean-view one-bedroom suite, we overlooked the modernist pool deck as well as the distant ocean, with a plunge pool on the balcony and ample outdoor space for afternoon lounging. The bathroom was equipped with two sinks, a large tub, and a marble walk-in shower.

    Check Availability at Booking.com.

    All rooms at this Sandals Resort are in stone buildings on a two-mile-long beach in a 500-acre wilderness preserve on the island's south coast. The resort is arranged as three European villages—Dutch, French, and Italian (including a Venetian piazza)—and the architecture includes lots of marble columns and vaulted ceilings. "Buildings are spread out, but it still feels like an intimate retreat." Rooms differ according to village: French rooms have mahogany four-poster beds and Caribbean decor, while Italian rooms are heavy on marble. The plantation-style Eleanor's, complete with a waterwheel and a stone fireplace, serves contemporary Caribbean cuisine.

    Check Availability at Booking.com.

    According to recent reports, though the Buccaneer, on the U.S. Virgin Island of St. Croix, has been proudly run by the Armstrong family for over 70 years—it's the longest-running resort in the Caribbean—its history dates even further back to the property's earliest construction by a Knight of Malta in 1653. Since then, it's been a private home; a sugar mill; a cotton estate, then a cattle estate; and now, an incredibly warm, family-friendly resort that's more like a country club. You have access to an 18-hole golf course, eight tennis courts, three beaches (whether you prefer kayaking and snorkeling or lounging in peace and quiet), a full water sports center, and none of the pretense. Arrive for lunch at the Grotto in your bathing suit, and please don't sleep through the terrific breakfast buffet. The Buccanneer knows how to put out a spread. Once you're done moving about for the day, settle into the deluxe oceanfront room—the resort's most popular—and lie on your bed beneath the 16-foot-high wood ceilings, watching the waves lap the beach out your picture window.

    Industry observers note that the tiny volcanic island of Grenada is both an unexpected and obvious choice for Six Senses’ foray into the Caribbean. Compared to significant-hitting neighbors like St. Lucia and Antigua, it has been overlooked by travelers to the region. But this means that it remains largely uncrowded and retains a more rustic version of tourism. Six Senses has done well to anchor itself to that. Here, your welcome ritual begins with a sensory spice “tour;” its 56 suites and 15 villas are stylish but designed to sit unobtrusively on the landscape; and its curated excursions—from rainforest hikes to Rastafarian farm visits—spotlight the best of Grenada’s natural bounty. In classic Six Senses style, wellness is a key protagonist, and you can seek out everything from aerial yoga to sleep therapy, as well as treatments like the Caribbean Cleansing Ritual that nod to the surroundings. It’s very tempting to stay put, heading to the spa or sipping rum cocktails poolside, but you’d do well to pair off with one of the property’s community hosts and head out: to spice-laden markets in its photogenic capital or for a bit of beachside limin’ (defined locally as “kicking with friends”), a beloved national pastime.

    Check Availability at Booking.com.

    Sources indicate that the old adage of getting what you pay for rings true here, and while it may be a splurge, it will be an unforgettable stay. The rooms are quiet, the beds are comfortable, and in my opinion, this is the best stretch of beach on the island. If you’re looking for luxury—and budget isn’t an issue—the Ritz is the top of the line. Guests who stay in the 320 spacious and chic rooms can expect to be spoiled. Servers cruise around the shore on Segway scooters, effortlessly balancing trays of tropical cocktails. The concierge can secure reservations for you at sold-out restaurants, set up offsite tours, and suggest itineraries for any kind of traveler. The 15,000-square-foot spa at the Ritz is one of the largest and best on the island, and the property's on-site restaurants are simply divine. The vibe is upscale without being stuffy, with guests in the elevators side by side wearing pool towels and Prada.

    Check Availability at Booking.com.

    Sources indicate that A relatively latest addition to St. Barts' luxury hotel scene, Le Barthélemy is a sophisticated winner that keeps with the island's low-rise sensibility. Set between a lagoon and Grand Cul-de-Sac beach along the island's northeastern shore, the hotel is an education in understated elegance. Rooms are spare and enormous, with lots of wood and one or two pops of bright color—some even have small, rectangular plunge pools for mini-laps. The food at  Amis St. Barth is unabashedly modern French, with attention paid to proper portions in the tropics: in other words, not too much. Water sports enthusiasts have an expanse of calm shallow waters for kayaking, kite-surfing, and snorkeling—a flotilla of a dozen sea turtles that survived the storms of 2017 remain in residence and are easily visible.

    Check Availability at Booking.com.

    Industry observers note that those who knew and loved Le Carl Gustaf the first time around will have even more reason to fall for it now that the Barriere group has taken over. The hotelier organization—known for reviving particularly beloved but withering properties—has made sure to keep the spirit of Le Carl chic and easy. The raw wood and petite terraces still make it feel like the beach house of a fabulous French friend, yet the hotel’s reimagined approach to the environment gives it a 21st-century edge. Paris design firm Gilles and Boissier gussied up the 21 rooms with creams, stone, and linen, as well as a profusion of palms separating various spaces with a curtain of greenery. Suites have been reconfigured to catch sea breezes, providing natural air conditioning. And a fleet of electric bikes brings guests down the hill upon which the hotel stands like a lookout, over the town and coastline, to nearby Shell Beach, the perfect place for a picnic prepared by the hotel’s staff that feels, appropriately simple and chic—much like Le Carl itself.

    Check Availability at Booking.com.

    Romance is taken to a whole other level at this adults-only St. Lucia resort. With 36 plunge pool suites, butler service, and a personalized bar with only the top-shelf, this enclave was made for couples to relax and reconnect. While there's no shortage of places to lounge or splash around in on property, the resort also offers an array of excursions to explore the gorgeous corner of the Caribbean St. Lucia lays claim to. From rainforest nature walks with a fully packed picnic basket to adrenaline-pumping ATV tours, Serenity at Coconut Bay knows there's many ways to take in all the gorgeous scenery.

    American Airlines is joining in the “Cyber Week” shopping holiday with the planned release of a branded jacket made from reclaimed leather from the carrier’s old aircraft, including the McDonnell Douglas MD-80.

    The special, limited-edition MA-1 flight jackets are made by Alpha Industries and come with an American patch celebrating the carrier’s 100th anniversary.

    It has been revealed that the airline plans to make 10 jackets available for purchase each day from Nov. 30 through Dec. 4, at the price of 200,000 AAdvantage miles each.

    It has been revealed that alpha Industries remarked it received 650 seats from American for the project. Each jacket requires 10 to 12 seats to make, depending on the quality of the material.

    American is also advertising its other branded merchandise ahead of the holidays, including suitcases and limited-edition pickleball paddles made in collaboration with Volair.

    From Nov. 27 through Dec. 2, AAdvantage members can save up to 50% when purchasing 500,000 or more miles.

    #123632. My Favorite Villa: A Storybook Trullo in Puglia With Six Bedrooms, a Private Chef, and Olive Grove Views

    My Favorite Villa: A Storybook Trullo in Puglia With Six Bedrooms, a Private Chef, and Olive Grove Views

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1086 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • My best friend and I had an entire six-bedroom estate in Puglia, Italy, to ourselves for three nights in early November.
    • Recent findings suggest that I'd been looking forward to sleeping in a trullo, one of the traditional dry-stone houses with conical roofs that dot this part of southern Italy.
    • Trullo delle Dame is one of the newest additions to Mandarin Oriental's Exceptional Homes collection, and for someone who loves the privacy of a villa but also appreciates the little comforts of a hotel stay, I found it to be a lovely combination: A property manager greeted us on arrival, the bathrooms were stocked with Mandarin Oriental amenities, and there was daily housekeeping and turndown.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    My best friend and I had an entire six-bedroom estate in Puglia, Italy, to ourselves for three nights in early November. We could have invited another 10 people, but there was something rather wonderful about having all that space for just the two of us. The region's whitewashed streets had emptied of their summer crowds, and the countryside around our home away from home was quiet enough that we felt no particular urgency to go anywhere.

    Recent findings suggest that I'd been looking forward to sleeping in a trullo, one of the traditional dry-stone houses with conical roofs that dot this part of southern Italy. At Trullo delle Dame, my bedroom sat directly beneath one of those cones, and every night, I fell asleep looking up at the curved stone ceiling. It felt like a storybook hideaway reimagined by someone with a very good eye for design. The soaking tub in my room didn't hurt either.

    Check Availability at Mandarin Oriental.

    Trullo delle Dame is one of the newest additions to Mandarin Oriental's Exceptional Homes collection, and for someone who loves the privacy of a villa but also appreciates the little comforts of a hotel stay, I found it to be a lovely combination: A property manager greeted us on arrival, the bathrooms were stocked with Mandarin Oriental amenities, and there was daily housekeeping and turndown. It was all the service of a hotel, with the space and character of a traditional Puglian home.

    The original stone walls and domed ceilings have been preserved throughout the restored trulli, with sleek off-white furniture, stone walls, and traditional glazed ceramic or terra-cotta ornaments called pumi strewn about. The six bedrooms, including five en suite bedrooms and a primary suite, are spread out across the property. While I was there with my friend, I kept thinking about how well the house would work for a multigenerational family trip. There's enough space for everyone to retreat to their own rooms, and plenty of reasons to come back together over a chef-prepared meal, a card game in the seating area overlooking the countryside, or a dip in the saltwater infinity pool.

    It has been revealed that my favorite spot in the estate was the outdoor kitchen—specifically at the enormous round dining table, complete with a giant lazy Susan. One afternoon, we made orecchiette there, shaping the little ears of pasta by hand, flour up to our wrists, before sitting down to eat what we'd made. I could picture a dozen people around that table on a summer evening, passing plates of pasta and pouring each other another glass of wine (which the Mandarin Oriental team will stock the fridge with upon request).

    Throughout the stay, our days fell into an easy routine. We'd walk through the olive groves in the mornings, read on the couch in the afternoons, and spend a few hours on the loungers by the pool. The water was unheated, so we were content to stay poolside in November. But I imagine it's where everyone ends up in July.

    As tempting as it was to stay put, there was too much good food and wine in the surrounding countryside to spend all three days at the house. We drove the three miles into Cisternino for a meal at Taverna della Torre, and I'm still thinking about the gnocchi with white truffles. Another afternoon took us to Giovanni Aiello, an independent winery near Putignano, where we got to help make some of the bottle labels. The cellar is beautiful, and you can even have your tasting inside an old wine barrel. With the towns of Martina Franca and Ostuni also within easy driving distance, we could have happily spent a few more days eating our way around Puglia.

    Some little bites, courtesy of the private chef.

    Breakfast is always an elaborate spread.

    According to recent reports, of course, we hardly needed to leave the house to eat well. Each morning, our private chef laid out a breakfast spread of fresh yogurt, meats and cheeses, pies, pancakes, juices, and fruit, along with freshly brewed cappuccinos. There was enough food to feed considerably more than two people, though we did our best. In the evenings, he prepared multicourse dinners using local, seasonal produce. Of everything he made, my favorite was a fava bean purée with roasted peppers.

    According to recent reports, as two busy working moms, we rapidly got used to the luxury of not having to think about what anyone would eat. Waking up to a breakfast feast and a creamy coffee, knowing someone else would deal with the dishes, was perhaps the hardest thing to give up at the end of the trip. (My family may need to lower their breakfast expectations for the foreseeable future.) And while we thoroughly enjoyed our few days off from mom duties, I could see how having a chef would make a family vacation feel much more like a vacation for the parents too. No grocery runs, no figuring out what to cook for 12 people, and no kitchen to clean up afterward.

    The writer participating in a pasta-making class in the outdoor kitchen.

    The fruits of their labor: lots of orecchiette!

    It has been revealed that if we came back with our kids, I'd happily sign them up for a pizza-making session while we snuck off for a massage in the olive groves, all activities the brand offers to guests. The trees, which produce the estate's own olive oil, also make a rather lovely setting for a yoga class, which can also be arranged during the warmer months.

    Sources indicate that A few things worth knowing before booking: The private chef, food, and drinks are charged separately from the villa rental. You'll also want a car to explore the neighboring towns, although the concierge can arrange transfers. And if you're coming in November, as we did, check restaurant opening hours before heading out, since some places shorten their hours after the summer season. The unheated pool is also worth keeping in mind if you're traveling with children outside the warmer months.

    It has been revealed that on the morning we left, our chef packed us meat-and-cheese sandwiches for the road. After three days of elaborate breakfasts and multicourse dinners, those sandwiches somehow ranked among my favorite things he'd made. As we drove away, I thought about how I'd happily come back with a houseful of friends and family in summer—but I'd want the same bedroom under the cone.

    #123630. A Real-Life Santa’s Workshop: How Macy’s Parade Studio Works All Year to Prep for Thanksgiving Day Magic

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2362 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cntraveler ↗ Open Full Page

    A Real-Life Santa’s Workshop: How Macy’s Parade Studio Works All Year to Prep for Thanksgiving Day Magic

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2362 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

    ⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that santa’s workshop just might be inside a rather plain red-and-black brick building in northern Fresh Jersey.
    • In a recent development, this year, the festivities are grander than ever, as the team has toiled for two years in preparation for a major milestone: the parade’s 100th edition.
    • A snapshot of the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade from 1940.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that santa’s workshop just might be inside a rather plain red-and-black brick building in northern Fresh Jersey. Sitting about 10 miles northwest of Midtown Manhattan in Moonachie’s industrial park district, the 72,000-square-foot warehouse is home to Macy’s Parade Studio, where 60 designers, carpenters, welders, seamstresses, and other artisans chip away year-round to prepare for one morning a year: the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade.

    In a recent development, this year, the festivities are grander than ever, as the team has toiled for two years in preparation for a major milestone: the parade’s 100th edition. Instead of the normal 50 to 60 inflatables, there will be nearly 100. The usual 500 upcoming costumes will be upped to 1,000, while more than 11,000 volunteers will be a part of the milestone event.

    A snapshot of the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade from 1940.

    It has been revealed that it’s a massive endeavor for a tradition that started as a two-block-long procession of Central Park Zoo animals, a handful of bands, and Santa, all traveling six miles from Harlem to the department store’s flagship in Herald Square at 34th and Broadway in 1924 (it was suspended for three years during World War II from 1942 to 1944). The parade led to the unveiling of Macy’s window displays with puppets by marionette artist Tony Sarg to kick off the holiday—and retail—season.

    Recent findings suggest that “It started as a bunch of Macy's immigrant coworkers coming together to create a party like they had in their home countries,” Brendan Kennedy, director of creative production, tells me during a visit in late September. But soon, the animals were deemed to be “too scary” for children. Three years later, the balloons debuted, the work of Sarg, who he calls “one of the godfathers of puppetry” and “our Walt Disney.” His genius idea: flip marionettes upside down to become high-flying balloons on strings, creating the iconic tradition we know today.

    Taking a peek at the concept art hanging inside the Macy's workshop.

    Recent findings suggest that wandering through the facility is like making your way through a pop culture fun house. A pair of Minions hang from the rafters, mingling with Pokémon’s Pikachu and Goofy, who is stuck in a wreath. A Planter’s Peanut Ferris wheel spins in the center, while models of the parade’s own famous characters, Tom Turkey, Blue Hippopotamus, and the fishy pair Rainbow and Greybow Trout, sit out to dry in front of shelves lined with paint buckets of every hue.

    “This is like our own Hollywood lot,” Kennedy says. Indeed, there’s the distinct feel of a soundstage paired with the wildest arts and crafts studio you've ever seen, all together feeling like something out of Willy Wonka’s dreams. Before making its home here in 2011, the Parade Studio was located inside the old Tootsie Roll factory in Hoboken, New Jersey, for decades.

    Sources indicate that despite the holiday joy bursting from every seam, parade preparation is serious business. Every single element is handcrafted and hand-painted. "Generally it all starts with a napkin sketch,” Kennedy explains of the initial rough drawing. “It goes into full modeling in 3-D, and then engineering, where we have to figure out how to get this thing into the real world.”.

    But year after year, like the true elves of the holiday season they are, they pull it off—testing every float and balloon for any and every possible weather condition—so that on Thanksgiving morning, the 3.5 million lining the Manhattan route as well as the nearly 35 million watching the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade at home (airing on NBC and Peacock from 8:30 a.m. to noon) can just sit back and revel in the delights of the season.

    “What makes the parade so special is that it is an event that has been produced by colleagues since it began in 1924, and it continues to be Macy Studios colleagues' gift to Fresh York City and gift to people who are tuning in around the country to watch on television,” Macy’s director of production operations Kathleen Wright tells Traveler.

    Below, we peek behind the scenes of the Macy’s Parade Studio as the team prepares for the 100th parade, and how they strategy to honor the traditions of the last century.

    Some of the 3-D printed models that serve as the blueprints for the parade's iconic floats.

    Recent findings suggest that the larger-than-life magic of the parade starts on the smallest scale. In the Studio’s 3-D print room, nearly a dozen machines hum away, creating miniature models—the first step in conceiving how to build each float. But that’s not the only tool used. Recently, engineers and sculptors have turned to augmented reality goggles, not just to picture the elements, but even wearing them while sculpting to make sure they get details right in a 3-D space.

    The day I visit, the team is problem-solving on the new Purina Dog Chow Salute to Service Dogs float, which features three oversized dog puppets.

    An array of the painted models inside the studio.

    In a recent development, “When floats come to life through some sort of animation is when it’s at its peak,” Kennedy claims. While animatronics could provide the movements, they would lack the human touch. “With a puppet, I can look directly at you, give you a little show, and then pan to the next person. You get a lot more energy and excitement. There’s a long history of puppetry in the parade, so we made a concerted effort to include it.”.

    Recent findings suggest that the team works through solutions for the best way to have a puppeteer lie below the float bed, controlling the motions from below while positioned with body pillows that still allow them to see the parade-goers through a scrim. They consider using delivery truck slats to increase the height of the float so the puppeteer can remain comfortable and still operate the puppet.

    Mr. Peanut is the historic parade's oldest character.

    Recent findings suggest that in another section, another fresh float is going for a test spin. Planters’ Mr. Peanut Power Plant will celebrate the parade’s oldest character, with peanut-shaped confetti erupting through his top hat, as well as a rotating Ferris wheel showcasing his evolution from 1916, starting with the napkin sketch created by a 13-year-old boy from Virginia.

    Also on the floor is a puppet of the original character Mr. Inspector, a stern-looking comic book character with a top hat and magnifying glass, who first appeared as a balloon in the 1929 parade. This version of the character was taken out of the archives and freshened up in order to be part of Macy’s own Tony Sarg’s Amazing Marionettes float.

    It has been revealed that “Everything has to be refurbished,” Kennedy notes. “These are New York City streets—it’s not like a perfect Narnia land. So they hit a bump, we have to work through it, or if it rains, we have to check for water damage.”.

    While the methods are precise, the methodology is all about creativity and resourcefulness. Case in point: While working on the Wednesday Addams float in 2024, Tim Burton himself asked for more decay and rot. So a sculptor modified his glue gun to spray spider webs around the entire float. “It’s a good example of how anything can become a tool,” he says of making fiction come to life.

    But there are some strict restrictions. Floats have to fold up to the size of a standard city bus in order to fit through the Lincoln Tunnel into Manhattan. The massive convoy travels in two nights before Thanksgiving. Once settled, the team reassembles every piece, some using cranes, as every float gets its final touches before the big day.

    Peeking inside the planning of the parade's Mickey Mouse float.

    Next, we step into the Balloon Studio, where again, everything starts with a 3-D model. After it’s approved, a larger form “white model,” roughly a few feet long, is generated (clay models were used in the past) and used to hand-draw lines that determine the shapes and sizes of each piece of balloon fabric that needs to be cut and how they’ll be melded together, much like sewing with a dress pattern.

    Dangling from beams above is a display of white models of the past, with the monotone versions of Super Mario, Buzz Lightyear, Snoopy, and the Pillsbury Doughboy, among others. But today the focus is on the freshly-completed Sorcerer’s Apprentice Mickey Mouse, hanging from a little stand to mimic levitation. I count no less than nine pieces of fabric sketched out in pencil just for the nose—and about 18 for the front side of each ear.

    Artisans stitch together all the massive textiles that go onto the floats.

    In a recent development, at the next station, we see a pair of artisans doing seemingly mundane work stitching large swaths of fabric together with sewing machines. To a trained eye, though, the scene is actually chock full of proprietary Macy’s secrets. While rubber was used in the past, today the balloons are made of off-white secret material the makeup of which is closely guarded. The material is heat-sealed together using these Macy’s-designed machines with wheels that heat up to 410 degrees Fahrenheit. Then the material is painted using a formula that’s also—you guessed it—proprietary.

    The secrets all come together as the completed balloons are first inflated indoors to make sure that the paint looks good and to check how it behaves with air. Some are inspected in the Studio while others that require more space are pumped up from the floor since it would float at the nearby Prudential Center. The balloons are inflated at various stages to ensure the air is filling up as intended.

    The big test came on November 7, when they hosted the annual Balloonfest at MetLife Stadium to see how the balloons behave in outdoor conditions, as well as give city agencies the chance to approve everything.

    According to recent reports, once that’s checked off, the night before the parade is the Balloon Inflation (which is open to the public; stay tuned for details here), when each character is blown up on the streets of the Upper West Side and prepped for its own turkey trot through Midtown. “They really are flying pieces of art,” Kennedy says.

    A shimmering Christmas tree costume.

    A dress from the costume operations studio.

    Sources indicate that while the floats and balloons may get the headlines, there would be no parade without the nearly 11,000 volunteers who help make the day happen, which is now 2.5-miles from the Upper West Side to Herald Square—and they all have to be dressed for the occasion. This year at least 1,500 more costumes are needed, but that doesn't intimidate costume director and associate producer Kimberly Montgomery, who’s been doing this for 27 years. “It’s gone so fast because it’s just been so darn fun,” she states of her tenure.

    Costumes follow after the design of the float, with the larger backdrop serving as the source of wardrobe inspiration.

    Recent findings suggest that every costume always begins in the same place. “We start with the design of the float and then riff off of that to tell a story with live people,” she explains. Just then, she catches a glimpse of a new design of a float with street signs and immediately starts brainstorming: “Maybe people on bikes will give it some texture and energy.” After all, she sees the floats as roving stages. "They're like mini Broadway reveals.”.

    Recent findings suggest that when the very first 1924 parade arrived at Macy’s, it was met by employees dressed as clowns—and this year there will be 1,000 clowns throughout the parade, just a portion of the costume packets that she’s been working all year to assemble. And it's not just with what they'll wear. The late November weather is a major consideration as well. Costume kits also include ear and hand warmers, “the first two areas to get cold,” she claims. Most costumes are also made loose enough so that the paraders can layer up underneath.

    There are roughly 3,500 costumes produced for the balloon handler brigade.

    Balloon handlers get a different treatment. “Their costumes are a lot simpler because they have to pay attention to what they're doing,” she claims. In fact, some balloons, like Buzz Lightyear, Sorcerer’s Mickey, and the Minion have nearly 100 people handling them. In total, about 3,500 of the costumes are for balloon handlers. “It’s serious business, so they get a coverall and a tabard that’s color coded with a picture of the character they’re holding.” She points out Toad the mushroom for Mario and an alien planet for Buzz Lightyear. And for the Minions, the team even has little cowboy hats.

    In a recent development, of course there are odes to the past in the costumes too. Some historic costumes have been pulled out of the archives, like an intricate Broadway-quality Mother Goose dress. Others have been given fresh interpretations, like the original character Harold, who debuted in 1945 as a clown, but had stints as a baseball player (as he was seen in Miracle on 34th Street), fireman, and policeman. For this centennial, there will be 100 Harolds—25 of each iteration—as inflatable costumes (balloons aren’t the only ones that are blown up here!).

    Prepping for the big day begin bright and early at 4:30 a.m.

    With all this prep, dressing thousands of people then operates like clockwork, as they arrive around 4:30 a.m. at ballrooms around town in their street clothes and exit transformed. For 2.5 hours, shuttles transport them all to the parade start line.

    According to recent reports, after all the pomp and circumstances are over, Montgomery turns to a new phase of the process: Laundry. “All of this goes in giant piles of whites, darks, and colors. We’ve got to get it laundered and put back in size order.”.

    And once everything is back in order, they start again on the following year’s parade. “No matter what holiday it is, we always have our finger on the pulse of Thanksgiving,” Wright states.

    Britt bill would launch national office to combat financial fraud

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (500 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that britt has made fighting elder financial abuse a priority.
    • In a recent development, A bill introduced by Sen.
    • In a recent development, the draft bill would establish a National Office for Scam and Fraud Prevention in the White House that would coordinate federal, state and private sector efforts.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that britt has made fighting elder financial abuse a priority. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    In a recent development, A bill introduced by Sen. Katie Britt on Wednesday aims to combat a rising diversity of financial fraud by unifying the U.S. effort to fight it.

    In a recent development, the draft bill would establish a National Office for Scam and Fraud Prevention in the White House that would coordinate federal, state and private sector efforts. It is aimed at ensuring that federal agencies, law enforcement, financial institutions, telecommunications and technology companies and other groups work together, according to an overview from Britt.

    The upcoming office would promote intelligence sharing across the public and private sectors, coordinate consumer education efforts and improve assistance for victims.

    Britt, R-Ala., said the effort is needed because fraudsters operate nimbly utilizing social media while taking advantage of fragmented or disorganized responses from individual companies and government agencies.

    “This effort is about bringing everyone to the table and making sure our response keeps pace with the criminals who are exploiting upcoming technologies and gaps between sectors,” she stated in a statement. “When we work together to identify threats earlier and share information more effectively, we can better protect American families and businesses.”.

    The office would develop a “lexicon of fraud” so that terms for different kinds of scams are standardized between various federal law enforcement agencies to promote a “whole-of-government response,” a Britt aide remarked.

    The office also would work to broaden the approach to combating fraud beyond just having financial institutions reimburse victims. It would tap telecommunications and technology companies to address fraud at its source, such as rip-offs that start as text messages, social media posts or online advertisements.

    Sources indicate that britt has made fighting elder financial abuse a priority. She is the sponsor of a bill that would allow state, local and tribal law enforcement agencies to use federal grant funding to investigate financial fraud, particularly scams targeted at the elderly.

    The measure highlights the prevalence of "pig butchering," a common technique where a predator cultivates a personal relationship with a victim over many months to extract the most cash.

    Recent findings suggest that the House passed its version of the bill in September with overwhelming bipartisan support. The House sponsor is Rep. Zach Nunn, R-Iowa.

    Senior financial abuse also was the focus of a bill the House passed in an overwhelming 414-2 vote in June. The legislation, sponsored by Rep. Ann Wagner, R-Mo., would codify Securities and Exchange Commission guidance that permits mutual funds and their agents to postpone the sale of securities if there is a reasonable belief that financial exploitation of someone who is elderly or disabled is occurring.

    It's not clear whether the Senate will take action on these bills or Britt's by the end of the year.

    “If it doesn’t get through in the lame duck, it will continue to be a priority in the 120th [Congress],” the Britt aide stated.

    #123628. Tech Report: How We Pulled It Off: A Pakistani Wedding Under the Mudéjar Arches of Seville

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2472 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cntraveler ↗ Open Full Page

    Tech Report: How We Pulled It Off: A Pakistani Wedding Under the Mudéjar Arches of Seville

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2472 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

    ⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that an incredible love story deserves an incredible wedding.
    • According to recent reports, “She got into college and was moving out of state, and it felt like this might be the last chance that I would possibly have to be with this girl,” Awaez remembered.
    • Falaknaz Chranya and Awaez Jiwani met on a middle-school field trip.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that an incredible love story deserves an incredible wedding. Growing up in the Atlanta suburbs, Falaknaz Chranya and Awaez Jiwani met on a field trip in middle school, then became best friends as teenagers. It was toward the end of high school that their connection turned romantic.

    According to recent reports, “She got into college and was moving out of state, and it felt like this might be the last chance that I would possibly have to be with this girl,” Awaez remembered. “We decided to see where things would take us.”.

    Falaknaz Chranya and Awaez Jiwani met on a middle-school field trip.

    The two grew up in the Atlanta area and got together toward the end of high school.

    The relationship took them into their twenties through to a proposal in July 2023: an elaborate scavenger hunt that Awaez staged around Chicago, where they lived briefly before turning to Atlanta. When plotting their wedding, they were sure they wanted something just as detailed and thoughtful, and immediately landed on a destination celebration. “We knew we didn’t want to have it in Atlanta, because we didn’t feel like we would be able to give our guests the kind of intentional experience we really wanted to,” says Falaknaz.

    Ahead, the couple explains how and why they chose to hold a Seville destination wedding in August 2025 for 160 guests, and discusses the (many!) venues they booked for their various events, the fun guest surprise they plotted, and loads of other sangria-soaked details.

    Hotel Alfonso XIII is an elegant, historic property commissioned by and named for the Spanish king.

    The property and Sevilla in general are known for the Mudéjar-style architecture of Southern Spain.

    Industry observers note that falaknaz and Awaez were open to getting married anywhere, a wonderful but intimidating prospect. They scoured Pinterest and spoke to planners across the US. “We looked into Chicago, we looked into California, and at one point we looked into a cabin wedding in Montana,” the bride claims. “None of those really felt right until I came across some of the venues in Seville, Spain.”.

    Her major moment of connection was seeing the Hotel Alfonso XIII, an elegant, historic property commissioned by and named for a king of Spain, who aimed to host esteemed international guests there. The scale and vibe of Seville itself—smaller than other European cities, but with an incredible history, stunning architecture, and loads to do—appealed as well. The couple reached out to several planners and booked a trip to visit the Alfonso and several other venues.

    It has been revealed that in person, the property was just as incredible as they’d hoped. “Hotel Alfonso was honestly a non-negotiable for me once we stayed there that very first trip,” claims Awaez. “We were exposed to all the different ways we could utilize the hotel and make the most of it.”.

    And given the hotel’s 150 rooms, the majority of their guest list could stay there, and did. “One of the major things we wanted from the wedding was everyone to be together. We loved the idea of it being almost a resort, where you’re constantly bumping into people from the wedding,” says Falaknaz.

    The couple chose event-planning firm Bodas del Sur because it had worked on South Asian weddings before.

    As they tried to narrow down the location for their wedding, the couple had a few dismaying calls with potential event firms. “We met with a lot of planners, and they had a lot of stipulations right off the bat. They weren't really open to hearing what we wanted out of our wedding,” Falaknaz says. They ultimately opted to work with Bodas del Sur, a Seville-based firm that specializes in destination weddings across Andalusia and gave them utter confidence in their ideas. “From our very first conversation, they just seemed like they were going to make what we wanted happen,” the bride continues. “Whatever we said, they ran with it, like, ‘Okay, these are all the ways we can make it happen.’ That was the most reassuring thing: that we felt heard.”.

    In addition to their vast experience with Seville venues and vendors, Bodas del Sur had also worked on South Asian weddings in the past, indicates the bride, “so it gave us a lot of confidence that they knew what they were doing.”.

    A 15th century palace, Casa de Pilatos, played host to the night of dancing and performances known in Packistani-Muslim weddings as the sangeet.

    A key aspect of the typical South Asian wedding is that it involves several events, and for the couple’s own Muslim-Pakistani celebration, they figured out rapidly that not all of them made sense for the Hotel Alfonso XIII. Though Falaknaz began to panic at the realization—“Of course I was like, all hope is lost, we have to go back to the drawing board”—the Bodas team took them to see more spaces, which cemented Seville for them as a whole.

    Industry observers note that “The first venue they took us to was Casa de Pilatos. We both walked in and were like, ‘Oh my gosh, this is it. We can’t possibly give this up,’” Falaknaz says. “And the more places they took us to, the more we fell in love with Seville.” The biggest draw for the couple was the city’s rich Islamic heritage—it was under Muslim rule for over 500 years—and the corresponding architectural features, such as the arches, pillars, and intricate tiles, a fusion with Christian motifs known as Mudéjar style.

    A 15th century palace, Casa de Pilatos, played host to the night of dancing and performances known in Packistani-Muslim weddings as the sangeet.

    The mehendi, in which the bride is decorated with henna, was a daytime celebration held at Casa Guardiola, a 19th century formerly private home known for its iconic Sevillian architecture.

    “That blend was something we just weren’t finding elsewhere,” says Falaknaz. “That’s truly where we felt like we could give our guests the kind of experience we wanted—that would make them feel connected to something that was more than just a wedding.”.

    The couple held four major events over three days. The mehendi, in which the bride is decorated with henna, was a daytime celebration held at Casa Guardiola, a 19th-century formerly private home commissioned by a nobleman that stands as an apex of Sevillian Romantic architecture. The pithi, another daytime party during which the couple is decorated with turmeric paste to represent a pre-wedding cleansing as well as the golden joy to come, was staged at Hotel Alfonso XIII. The night of dancing and performances, also known as the sangeet, happened at Casa de Pilatos, while the slightly more Western-style wedding reception and its after-party were at Hacienda La Soledad, an estate constructed in 1542 as the center of an olive grove.

    The Sevilla celebration of 160 people felt “tiny” compared to the Atlanta nuptials the couple held for their legal ceremony.

    The one ceremony the couple didn’t have on site in Spain? The actual wedding itself. Their Nikkah, the Islamic wedding rites, was held at an Ismaili Jamatkhana at home in Atlanta, in an effort to include the much larger guest list of everyone notable to their families, about 600 people in all. That contributed to the relatively tiny group of 160 in Seville feeling much more intimate—“Well, intimate was still about 160, but intimate for us,” says Falaknaz.

    Industry observers note that “We felt connected to doing that in a place where we both grew up. We were able to do it in our mosque at home, the one we grew up going to and where all of our friends and parents’ community is. It was really special to have that be a part of the storyline, that we’ll share hopefully when we have kids,” indicates Falaknaz. “It was nice to be able to share that with everyone that wouldn't be able to make it to Spain.”.

    The wedding reception had the simplest decor, in ivory and gold, with tablescapes of singular, slender cala lilies and pearl chandeliers.

    Given the spectacular aesthetics of their chosen venues, the couple decided to bring in very little outside decor, and keep what they did bring in complementary. “The intention was to find places that spoke for themselves,” states Awaez. “We wouldn’t have to dedicate so much time to constructing the decor, versus the place standing on its own.”.

    In a recent development, for their first two events, they matched the color schemes to the major activities, with the pithi blanketed in shades of turmeric (from fluffy roses to mirrored pillows), and the mehendi outfitted in reddish browns and burnt orange. To create the feeling of intimacy and home at the latter, tables and other furniture were kept low, and wide cushions lay on a floor covered in overlapping rugs to encourage lounging.

    Their sangeet was a night filled with dance performances, channeling a peacock theme to echo the jewel-toned florals and vivid garden colors.

    Their sangeet, the night filled with dance performances, fittingly received a peacock theme, which carried from the feathers embroidered on Falaknaz’s gold gown by Taali to the signage to a jewel-toned palette for the florals. “We pulled colors that we felt would balance the venue, with these beautiful blues in the tiling and obviously the greens in the gardens,” says Falaknaz, who changed into a glittering indigo lehenga by Seema Gujral for her own performance.

    Sources indicate that the wedding reception had the simplest decor, in ivory and gold, with tablescapes of singular, slender calla lilies and pearl chandeliers, with architectural floral sculptures set around a fountain. Their planners were the key minds behind the creative vibe of the wedding, along with a local florist, La Galería by Jesús Fuertes.

    Transportation to the sangeet was by horse-drawn carriage, and the couple's photography sessions included a ride around Seville's iconic Plaza de España.

    Recent findings suggest that while the schedule (and culture) of the wedding events was very expected, the couple kept guests on their toes when it came to transportation to the sangeet: They were taken by horse-drawn carriages to Casa de Palatos. “They were so surprised to see a whole bunch of carriages waiting outside for us. It was such a cool moment,” notes Awaez. The rides took a scenic route through the Plaza de España before reaching the venue. “We knew that our guests probably weren't going to be able to have a lot of downtime between the events to explore the city,” says Falaknaz of the bonus tour.

    Falaknaz wore a glittering lehenga by Seema Gujral.

    While much of dinner was Desi dishes, the couple also served the most Spanish of dishes—paella.

    A key part of Awaez and Falaknaz’s three planning trips to Seville involved considering the caterers that their planners suggested. “We were genuinely concerned about how the food was going to taste, especially out in Spain in comparison to our typical Indian-Pakistani restaurants here in the U.S.,” notes Awaez. “We tested and tried a lot of those options that they shared with us, and found several of our own, and ultimately the two that we landed on were fantastic.” They worked with the staff of the Indian restaurant Taj Mahal Sevilla to cater their sangeet, and Ágape 360 Catering y Eventos for their mehendi and reception.

    Sources indicate that the gastronomic director of Ágape 360, Manuel de Pablo Deco, is Spanish but was excited to learn and adapt to the couple’s cultural needs: For a few crucial dishes, among them Desi-style karahi paneer and a nihari beef stew, the couple’s mothers actually found YouTube videos demonstrating the technique for cooking the recipes. “We sent those videos over to Manu, and he studied them to a T. He really learned to cook Indian food from scratch,” notes the grateful bride.

    According to recent reports, after days of distinctly Pakistani events, the couple’s wedding reception was an unabashed celebration of the local culture. Tinto de verano, a popular summery version of sangria, was served at the cocktail hour, while passed hors d’oeuvres included tapas bites like torta de potatas, Moorish-spiced meat skewers, and chicken croquettes. A troupe of flamenco dancers performed; the couple had seen the group dance at a taverna their planners had recommended on their first planning trip to Seville. While much of their dinner was Desi dishes, they also served the most Spanish of dishes—paella, in both seafood and vegetarian styles—followed by flan for dessert.

    To create the feeling of intimacy, tables and florals were kept low.

    A step and repeat served as a photo op for guests to snap their own shots.

    It has been revealed that to maximize their booking and the guest experience alike, Falaknaz and Awaez utilized each possible room or space within their venues. For the sangeet, they took family and couple portraits in the gardens of the Casa de Pilatos, moved to the central, most ornate courtyard for dinner and speeches, held performances in the soaring “courtyard of the halt,” and then moved to an entirely inner room for the after-party, given the local ordinance in the city center that required outdoor spaces to quiet down after 11:00 pm.

    Industry observers note that in order to keep the energy high for that final transition, they enlisted the help of their bridal party, who performed the final dance act of the night. “Almost flash mob style, we ran off the stage and through the crowd and into the indoor space,” indicates Falaknaz. The same crowd-pleasing song that’d been playing outside was already being piped indoors— “Dholi Taro Dhol Baaje,” from the beloved Bollywood movie Hum Dil De Chuke Sanam—so the group of 100+ party-goers was enticed to stay a little longer. Or a lot longer: The party continued back at the hotel’s basement, stretching until 3:00 am.

    The couple invited friends to join them after the wedding for a trip to La Tomatina in Valencia.

    The end of the trip afforded more one-on-one time with guests than the busy wedding weekend.

    Sources indicate that wedding events took place Friday through Monday, and most guests left on Tuesday, though plenty decided to extend their trip on either end. The newlyweds themselves decided to attend La Tomatina festival in Valencia, in which festival-goers eat but also pelt each other with tomatoes—otherwise known as the biggest food fight in the world. They threw out an invitation for any interested guests to join them, and more than 30 wound up attending.

    Recent findings suggest that “It was really special to be able to decompress after the wedding with so many of our friends, and actually have more quality time with them than we did at the wedding,” indicates Falaknaz. And it turned out to be a suitably colorful ending for an unforgettable wedding celebration.
