    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The no annual fee Chase Freedom Unlimited® is one of Chase’s most compelling cards for everyday spending, especially if you’re willing to put in the effort to maximize value.
    • In a recent development, I don’t want to bury the lede — if you collect Chase Ultimate Rewards points and use any personal Chase card other than the Chase Freedom Unlimited for your everyday spending, you’re not doing it right.
    • This post is my in-depth Chase Freedom Unlimited review, so let’s take a look at all the details of the card, starting with the very basics.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The no annual fee Chase Freedom Unlimited® is one of Chase’s most compelling cards for everyday spending, especially if you’re willing to put in the effort to maximize value. The card offers 3% cash back (or 3x points) on dining, 1.5% cash back (or 1.5x points) on everyday spending, and there are ways to get significantly more value than that.

    In a recent development, I don’t want to bury the lede — if you collect Chase Ultimate Rewards points and use any personal Chase card other than the Chase Freedom Unlimited for your everyday spending, you’re not doing it right. The catch is that there’s a learning curve to using this card — for some people this will just be a good card, while for other people this will be an amazing card.

    This post is my in-depth Chase Freedom Unlimited review, so let’s take a look at all the details of the card, starting with the very basics.

    Link: Learn more about the Chase Freedom Unlimited®.

    Before I get into my detailed Chase Freedom Unlimited review, let me summarize some of the basics:.

    Here are my thoughts on the main Chase Freedom Unlimited pros and cons:.

    Recent findings suggest that the Chase Freedom Unlimited is part of Chase’s “Freedom” card portfolio, and is an excellent complement to any of Chase’s cards earning Ultimate Rewards points. Before diving into all those details, let’s look at the Freedom Unlimited’s welcome bonus, eligibility, and fees, since those are obviously major factors people consider when applying for cards.

    The Chase Freedom Unlimited at the moment has a welcome bonus whereby you can earn $200 cash back (20,000 points) after spending $500 within the first three months.

    On the surface, points can be redeemed for one cent each, but you can potentially get a lot more value than that, as these points can be converted into Ultimate Rewards points. Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I value those at 1.7 cents each.

    It’s worth mentioning that the Chase Freedom Unlimited comes with an introductory APR offer that breaks down into two parts: purchases and balance transfers. Enjoy 0% Intro APR for 15 months from account opening on purchases, then a variable APR of 18.49% - 27.99%.

    For balance transfers: Enjoy 0% Intro APR for 15 months from account opening on balance transfers, then a variable APR of 18.49% - 27.99%.

    Sources indicate that these intro APR periods can be useful, but just make sure you pay off your entire balance before the offer ends. Otherwise, you’ll be stuck paying a high interest rate, which defeats the purpose.

    Industry observers note that eligibility for the Chase Freedom Unlimited is unrelated to eligibility for any other Chase cards, so you could earn the bonus on this card and the Freedom Flex Card, etc. The Chase Freedom Unlimited is not available to those who at the moment have the card, or those who have received a new cardmember bonus on the card in the past 24 months.

    Chase’s general credit card application rules, such as 5/24, generally apply, though that rule isn’t necessarily consistently enforced anymore.

    There’s not a published credit score you need to get approved for the Freedom Unlimited, though I’d hope to have a score in the good to excellent range, ideally 700+ points. However, people with lower scores have been approved, and people with higher scores have been rejected.

    It has been revealed that the Chase Freedom Unlimited has no annual fee, which is unbeatable. You can also add authorized consumers to the card for no fee, so you can accrue rewards for their spending as well as your own. Obviously that’s a major upside of the card.

    While the Chase Freedom Unlimited is a fantastic card for purchases within the United States, it does have 3% foreign transaction fees, so I don’t recommend using this card abroad.

    If you’re looking for a great card with no foreign transaction fees, consider the Chase Sapphire Preferred® Card (learn more) or Chase Sapphire Reserve® Card (learn more).

    The Chase Freedom Unlimited has an awesome rewards structure, which not only includes an excellent return on everyday spending, but also includes some valuable bonus categories.

    Before we get into this, note that in each case the percentage cash back can be converted into Ultimate Rewards points, at a rate of one cent per point. I’ll talk more below about how that’s possible, but that’s really how you maximize value with the card.

    Industry observers note that the Chase Freedom Unlimited offers 5% cash back on travel purchased through Chase Travel℠ (or potentially 5x Ultimate Rewards points). Purchases made outside the Chase travel portal will earn 1.5% cash back (or 1.5 Ultimate Rewards points per dollar).

    In a recent development, the Chase Freedom Unlimited offers 3% cash back on dining, including takeout and delivery (or potentially 3x Ultimate Rewards points). This is great for a no annual fee card, as this essentially makes this one of the best credit cards for dining spending.

    Recent findings suggest that the Chase Freedom Unlimited offers 3% cash back at drugstores (or potentially 3x Ultimate Rewards points). This is an awesome bonus, since drugstores isn’t a category where you otherwise see many cards offering bonuses.

    The Chase Freedom Unlimited offers 1.5% cash back on everyday spending (or potentially 1.5x Ultimate Rewards points). The 1.5% cash back return isn’t that exciting, given that other cards offer 2% cash back. What is valuable, however, is the ability to earn 1.5x Ultimate Rewards points per dollar spent, as there’s no better Chase card for everyday spending.

    Personally I value Chase points at 1.7 cents each, so to me the card offers the equivalent of a 2.55% return on everyday spending.

    The Chase Freedom Unlimited offers 1.5% cash back on everyday purchases, and 3-5% cash back in select bonus categories. On the surface, those rewards are really straightforward, as you can redeem the cash back for statement credits, a direct deposit in an eligible Chase account, for gift cards, or for travel booked through Chase Travel. You can even redeem your cash back toward Amazon purchases, though at the rate of 0.8 cents per point (so please don’t redeem that way!!).

    However, if you’re looking to earn travel rewards, you can get a significantly better return on spending than that.

    Industry observers note that while the Chase Freedom Unlimited is a cash back card, in reality the card earns Ultimate Rewards points. You earn 1.5x points per dollar spent, and then ordinarily each point can be redeemed for one cent cash back. That’s how Chase arrives at the valuation of 1.5% cash back with the card.

    It has been revealed that however, if you have the Chase Freedom Unlimited in conjunction with another card that earns “premium” Ultimate Rewards points, then you can do significantly better. These cards include the following:.

    Recent findings suggest that with one of those cards, suddenly your points are much more valuable. Transferring points between cards is easy and can be done online. You can learn more about that process in this post.

    Personally, the way I like to redeem Ultimate Rewards points is to transfer them to airline and hotel partners, which include the following:.

    It has been revealed that this can be the best way to redeem points toward premium travel experiences. If you want to redeem for first or business class travel or stay at luxury hotels, this option is for you.

    It has been revealed that one thing worth noting is that Chase recently devalued the transfer ratio to World of Hyatt to 4:3 for the Chase Sapphire Preferred and Ink Business Preferred. You’ll need the Chase Sapphire Reserve or Sapphire Reserve for Business to get the full 1:1 transfer rate with Hyatt. No matter which of these cards you have, points transfer to all other partners at a 1:1 ratio.

    While my favorite way to redeem Ultimate Rewards points is through the transfer partners, there are also ways to redeem Chase points at an advantageous rate toward travel purchased through Chase Travel℠:.

    That increases the value of your points by up to 100% right there.

    Sources indicate that for a no annual fee card, the Chase Freedom Unlimited offers a solid selection of benefits and purchase protection, which cardmembers will certainly appreciate. Let’s cover those, though let me of course remind everyone to always check the guide to benefits for the latest terms & conditions associated with these perks.

    With the Chase Freedom Unlimited, you can extend the time period of your United States manufacturer’s warranty by an additional year on eligible warranties of three years or less. If you’re making an expensive purchase, this could save you a huge amount.

    According to recent reports, with the Chase Freedom Unlimited, you’re covered for fresh purchases for 120 days against damage or theft of up to $500 per item, and up to $50,000 per account. Again, this makes the card an excellent option for everyday spending, given how much money purchase protection can save you.

    In a recent development, the Chase Freedom Unlimited will reimburse cardmembers up to $1,500 per covered traveler and $6,000 per trip on prepaid fares that can’t be cancelled if your trip is canceled or cut short by sickness or another covered reason. More premium cards have more travel protections and higher limits, but this is pretty nice for a no annual fee cash back card.

    In a recent development, with Chase Credit Journey, you get unlimited access to your credit score and more. This is free for Chase customers, including those who have the Chase Freedom Unlimited.

    It has been revealed that one of the great features of Chase cards is access to Chase Offers, which provides savings on purchases with all kinds of retailers. This program has saved me a significant amount of money, and having the Chase Freedom Unlimited gives you access to that.

    With the Chase Freedom Unlimited, you get six months of complimentary DashPass membership. Note that when you take advantage of this, you’ll be auto-enrolled in a paid DoorDash plan after six months, at the rate of $9.99 per month. So you’ll want to be sure you cancel before the complimentary plan expires, assuming you don’t value it.

    DoorDash DashPass gets you $0 delivery fees and lower service fees on eligible orders through both the DoorDash and Caviar delivery platforms. You get up to $10 off non-restaurant DoorDash orders each quarter, up to $40 a year. This perk is currently valid for enrollment through December 31, 2027.

    The Chase Freedom Unlimited qualifies for 2% cash back on Lyft purchases made through the app — a 0.5% bonus on top of the card’s standard earning rate. This promotion runs through September 30, 2027.

    The Chase Freedom Unlimited is one of the all around best cards for everyday spending. It’s a credit card that I have, and it’s one that I think is worth holding onto.

    If you’re in the Chase Ultimate Rewards ecosystem and put everyday spending on cards in the portfolio, then picking up the Chase Freedom Unlimited is a must. However, the key is to have the card in conjunction with a card earning premium Ultimate Rewards points — the Chase Sapphire Preferred, Chase Sapphire Reserve, Ink Business Preferred, or Sapphire Reserve for Business — so that you’re really maximizing your rewards.

    I’d also like to look a bit more closely at the best strategy to take with the Chase Freedom Unlimited.

    I can’t emphasize enough that having the Chase Freedom Unlimited in conjunction with either the Sapphire Preferred or Sapphire Reserve is probably the best card combo you can have. That’s because not only can you combine the benefits of the two cards, but this greatly increases the value you get from your Freedom Unlimited points.

    For example, if you have the Sapphire Reserve and Freedom Unlimited:.

    There are presently two Chase Freedom products you can apply for — the Chase Freedom Unlimited and Chase Freedom Flex® Credit Card (learn more). Both cards have no annual fees, so what are the major differences between the cards?

    The cards otherwise have overlapping bonus categories, like offering 3x points on dining and drugstores, etc. Personally I think both cards are worth having. If I could just have one, though, I’d probably choose the Freedom Unlimited, since it’s better for everyday spending.

    Chase has two “Unlimited” cards — the Chase Freedom Unlimited and the Ink Business Unlimited® Credit Card (learn more). These cards are very similar — both have no annual fee, and both offer 1.5x points (the Ink Unlimited on business purchases). So, what’s the difference?

    Industry observers note that other than those differences, the two cards are very similar. I have both of these cards (yes, I have a lot of Chase credit cards).

    The Citi Double Cash® Card (learn more) is probably the closest competitor to the Chase Freedom Unlimited, regardless of whether you’re looking to earn points or cash back.

    According to recent reports, the Citi Double Cash also has no annual fee and offers 1% cash back when you make a purchase, and 1% cash back after you pay for that purchase in the form of ThankYou points. So you’ll earn 2.0 cents back on the dollar, rather than 1.5. Furthermore, in conjunction with a card like the Citi Strata Premier® Card (learn more) or Citi Strata Elite® Card (learn more), you can move points at the best possible ratio to travel partners.

    Since I value Citi ThankYou and Chase Ultimate Rewards points roughly equally, this could also be an attractive card for everyday spending.

    The reason some people may still prefer the Freedom Unlimited is because of the Chase Ultimate Rewards ecosystem. On top of that, the Freedom Unlimited has bonus categories, which the Citi Double Cash doesn’t have.

    The Capital One VentureOne Rewards Credit Card (learn more) is another competitor to the Chase Freedom Unlimited, and it has a few pros and cons. The Capital One VentureOne has no annual fee and no foreign transaction fees, and offers a minimum of 1.25x miles per dollar spent.

    Those miles can either be redeemed for one cent each toward a travel purchase, or they can be moved to Capital One’s airline and hotel transfer partners.

    Industry observers note that the downside of the VentureOne is that the rewards structure isn’t as lucrative, on the surface. The upside, though, is the lack of foreign transaction fees, and the ability to directly transfer points to airline and hotel partners, even without having another card.

    So which card is better depends on whether you’re looking for a “one size fits all” no annual fee card, or want to use it as part of a larger strategy.

    The Chase Freedom Unlimited is a key card to maximizing your overall Chase Ultimate Rewards strategy, in conjunction with the Sapphire Preferred or Sapphire Reserve.

    According to recent reports, the Chase Freedom Unlimited has no annual fee, and offers a minimum of 1.5x points per dollar spent.     FAA Projects Busiest Thanksgiving Travel Week in 16 Years

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (280 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Airlinegeeks

    ⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • More than 417,000 flights will operate in the U.S.
    • If accurate, that figure would translate to the busiest Thanksgiving travel period in 16 years.
    • Tuesday is expected to be the single busiest day of the interval, with more than 52,000 flights.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    More than 417,000 flights will operate in the U.S. this week and early next week as Americans travel ahead of and after Thanksgiving, according to the FAA.

    If accurate, that figure would translate to the busiest Thanksgiving travel period in 16 years.

    Tuesday is expected to be the single busiest day of the interval, with more than 52,000 flights.

    Air traffic will dip only slightly on Wednesday (49,831 flights) and nearly halve on Thanksgiving Day (27,619 flights) itself, the FAA said, with a rebound following Friday to Tuesday, Dec. 1. There will be over 50,000 flights per day on the Sunday, Monday, and Tuesday after Thanksgiving.

    Perhaps aiming to assuage concerns from the public after a turbulent couple of weeks, transportation officials said they are prioritizing traveler safety and taking “unprecedented action” to limit flight delays and cancellations.

    Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy noted that the Trump administration has assembled a “tiger team” of experts to prevent another mass ground stop.

    “Our air traffic controllers and safety professionals are working around the clock to keep Americans moving during what is expected to be the busiest Thanksgiving travel week in 16 years,” FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said in a statement. “The growing demand for air travel makes it more important than ever to continue modernizing our air traffic control system and build a national airspace system for the 21st century.”.

    According to recent reports, the FAA is also advising travelers to get to the airport early and check with their airline for updates if bad weather seems likely to impact their trip. The agency noted the high likelihood of thunderstorms in the Southeast, Mid-Atlantic, and Northeast this week.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., holds a news conference in the Capitol on Nov.
    • Saying that “Medicare for All” is no longer “a radical idea,” Sen.
    • Industry observers note that democrats could bring it about through the filibuster-proof budget reconciliation process, the Vermont independent and avowed democratic socialist told reporters.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., holds a news conference in the Capitol on Nov. 10. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

    Saying that “Medicare for All” is no longer “a radical idea,” Sen. Bernie Sanders stated Wednesday that he would prioritize passing the universal health care proposal if he assumes the chairmanship of the Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee next year as expected.

    Industry observers note that democrats could bring it about through the filibuster-proof budget reconciliation process, the Vermont independent and avowed democratic socialist told reporters. And the idea could be buoyed by an influx of progressive lawmakers elected in the midterms.

    Sanders noted Medicare for All is gaining support from voters across the country who are looking to overhaul the American health care system as costs have soared. Democrats on the committee will move the legislation “as aggressively as we can, as rapidly as we can,” he said.

    Industry observers note that his version, introduced in April and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, would implement the universal health care system over four years. In the first year, the the age of Medicare eligibility would drop to 55 from 65, while coverage would expand to include dental, hearing and vision care. The bill would also provide coverage for eligible children during the first year.

    The age of eligibility would fall another 10 years in each of the following years until the fourth year, when coverage would be extended to all Americans.

    Recent findings suggest that “If there has ever been a time in the modern history of our country . . . to address the crises facing working families, this is that time,” Sanders said, noting that Democrats will have a 56-44 majority when the 120th Congress begins in January, the largest margin for either party in 16 years.

    Sen. Tammy Baldwin, D-Wis., along with nine other Senate Democrats, last week offered an alternative Medicare expansion plan, which would lower the eligibility to those ages 50 and up.

    Sources indicate that while who will be leading Senate Democrats is still an open question — Chris Van Hollen of Maryland is challenging Charles E. Schumer of New York, who has been the top Senate Democrat since 2017 — Sanders mentioned he is confident the Medicare for All bill will get to the Senate floor, “no matter who the [Senate majority] leader is.” Sanders previously expressed opposition to Schumer leading the conference.

    Asked about efforts to extend the Affordable Care Act enhanced subsidies, Sanders responded he’s “all in.” However, he added “the American people and elected officials understand the current health care system is broken.”.

    Subsidies that help enrollees pay for health care premiums on the ACA exchanges were expanded during the COVID-19 pandemic, but these enhanced credits expired at the end of last year, raising costs for many who relied on them to help defray costs.

    House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, nominated on Wednesday to be speaker next year, previously outlined broader health care priorities such as extending the ACA tax credits and reversing Medicaid cuts enacted in Republicans' reconciliation package last year. When asked Tuesday how far Democrats want to lower the Medicare eligibility age, Jeffries responded, “that’s all part of an ongoing conversation.”.

    Recent findings suggest that in addition to expanding Medicare coverage, Sanders reiterated his push to lower prescription drug prices. The Vermont lawmaker previously introduced legislation aimed at reducing the cost of brand name prescription drugs by linking domestic prices to international price benchmarks.

    To enact some of the agenda, Sanders may have to court Republicans.

    According to recent reports, sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., mentioned last week that he plans to serve as the top Republican on the HELP committee next year. Sanders said Wednesday that his likely GOP counterpart “has shown an enormous amount of courage in taking on Republican leadership year after year.”.

    Sanders added that although Paul may have a different viewpoint from himself on committee concerns, he looks forward to finding common ground.

    Tech Report: In The Air & On The Ground: How Premium Demand Has Rewritten Airline Operations

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1413 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Surging demand for premium airfare has forced global airlines to rewrite how they operate both inside the cabin and at the airport terminal.
    • According to recent reports, that universal push to capture big spenders collided directly with global supply chain bottlenecks, rising oil costs, and certification delays.
    • Industry observers note that every carrier has chosen a unique strategy to balance luxury inflight with terminal perks as passenger spending shifts.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Surging demand for premium airfare has forced global airlines to rewrite how they operate both inside the cabin and at the airport terminal. Customer demand passed a decisive juncture when Delta Air Lines reported that it made more 2025 Q4 revenue from premium-cabin sales than from main cabin fares for the first time. The landmark shift came as North America and Asia were already tearing out their economy rows while pouring billions into new business suites, satellite WiFi, exclusive lounges, and more perks.

    According to recent reports, that universal push to capture big spenders collided directly with global supply chain bottlenecks, rising oil costs, and certification delays. United Airlines introduced its Elevated Boeing 787-9 with Polaris suite doors locked open pending federal sign-off, while Delta installed 44 domestic first class recliners aboard fresh Airbus A321neos after planned lie-flat pods missed testing. Overseas, Boeing's delayed 777-9 forced Emirates, Singapore Airlines, and Air Canada to spend billions rebuilding older widebodies to keep premium capacity expanding.

    Industry observers note that every carrier has chosen a unique strategy to balance luxury inflight with terminal perks as passenger spending shifts. In another landmark change, United and American Airlines retired international first class while rolling out oversized business cabins and co-branded credit card clubs, while Emirates and Singapore kept enclosed first class suites alive alongside expanded hub lounges. Even US low-cost carriers scheduled domestic first class seats and airport clubs for 2027, leaving basic economy fliers with tighter legroom and fewer perks.

    Delta Chief Executive Officer Ed Bastian explained that the second-quarter milestone by confirming nearly all latest seat growth now targets business class and premium economy fliers. American CEO Robert Isom echoed that shift on September 16, admitting his carrier sold too much Basic Economy when just 30% of seats generate half its revenue. Isom told View From The Wing: "Those 30% of seats, they're only going to grow in our fleet. That's demand that's more likely to hold up through economic uncertainty.".

    According to recent reports, delta saw immediate proof of that appetite aboard its accidental 44-seat first class A321neo subfleet flying between Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta, Los Angeles, and Seattle. Even with undersized galleys and a single forward lavatory, paying passengers filled 80% of those recliners by August. As Delta Chief Commercial Officer Joe Esposito put it to From The Tray Table: "It's a really nice surprise that we've got such high demand for our premium products. We're experimenting with how massive a domestic premium cabin can be.".

    Recent findings suggest that american backed Isom's words by removing elite upgrades and frequent-flyer miles from Basic Economy tickets purchased after mid-May, and by using its cheapest fare to direct passengers into more expensive rows. Executives also unveiled Flagship First's retirement on March 28, 2027, bringing narrowbody premium seating to 40%. Air Canada targeted those same corporate travelers by relocating Boeing 737 MAX 8 jets to Rouge's leisure arm, while reinstating Airbus A320-200 and A321-200 aircraft to regular service.

    Sources indicate that air Canada introduced lie-flat beds to single-aisle transatlantic flights in June, when it launched its first Airbus A321XLR between Montreal and Toronto before deploying the jet to Toulouse. Alaska and Hawaiian Airlines joined the narrowbody luxury drive later in the year, beginning in 2028 with lie-flat suites on upcoming Boeing 737 MAX 10 aircraft and upgraded Airbus A330-200s. Putting long-haul comfort on smaller jets allows carriers to serve narrower foreign markets profitably while avoiding widebody fuel use.

    Airlines used different strategies to rearrange their cabins to accommodate large spenders on widebody fleets. In September, American rolled out its 'Project Olympus' Boeing 777-300ER between Newly introduced York-JFK and Buenos Aires, eliminating international first class in favor of crammed Flagship Suites. In a similar vein, United expanded Polaris business class and Premium Plus capacity by eliminating dozens of regular economy seats on its Elevated Boeing 787-9.

    Even as they rebuilt their fleets, foreign competitors refused to give up on the very front of the aircraft. In July, Emirates launched the 100th aircraft from its $5 billion interior makeover in Dubai. It preserved the enclosed first class suites on all of its Airbus A380-800 and 777-300ER planes while making room for premium economy. With the addition of private first class suites to its ultra-long-range Airbus A350-900ULR aircraft operating marathon runs to Latest York-JFK, Singapore pushed its own widebody rebuild budget to more than $1.56 billion.

    Sources indicate that every square inch added to the front of these widebodies forced uncomfortable compromises behind the curtain. Singapore ran into sharp flier pushback after revealing that its retrofitted A350-900s keep older 2017 economy seats without 4K screens or Bluetooth audio. On incoming Boeing 777-9 deliveries, Singapore is also tightening standard economy from nine to 10 abreast in the upcoming 777X, trading away long-praised coach comfort to fund upfront luxury.

    Recent findings suggest that as jetliners evolve, airport clubs are becoming increasingly congested as US airlines aggressively entice frequent travelers with co-branded credit cards. In September, Southwest Airlines and Chase revealed that their first-ever Icon Lounges would debut in Austin, Baltimore, Honolulu, and Nashville in late 2027. The newly merged Alaska and Hawaiian also announced aims to open latest flagship clubs in Honolulu and Seattle in 2028, directly challenging bank-run establishments such as the Chase Sapphire Lounge at Phoenix Sky Harbor.

    Alaska Chief Executive Officer Ben Minicucci pitched those ground investments as a core part of the travel experience, saying: "We believe premium is more than a seat. It's how guests feel from the moment they book their trip to the moment they arrive at the airport to when they're in the air with us." On the same thread, to keep top international ticket holders out of packed credit card queues, Air Canada opened a seventh grab-and-go café in Québec City in June while offering apron Porsche transfers from its Signature Suites.

    In a recent development, singapore took a similar approach at its home hub, spending $34.1 million to expand its Changi Terminal 2 SilverKris lounges by 50% and give paid premium fliers dedicated space away from partner cardholders. Singapore Chief Executive Officer Goh Choon Phong said: "Our customers experience Singapore as one seamless journey, and this significant investment is designed to deliver greater comfort, choice, and convenience at every stage.".

    Sources indicate that as construction continues, high-speed satellite internet has become just as essential to winning premium bookings as private terminal clubs. United raced ahead fleet-wide, passing 640 SpaceX Starlink-equipped aircraft in October to lead US carriers in total connected jets. Emirates prioritized raw long-haul bandwidth instead, mounting twin fuselage antennas on every Boeing 777-300ER and three atop each Airbus A380-800, so hundreds of passengers can stream simultaneously above 2 gigabits per second.

    It has been revealed that in February, Capital One stopped offering free guest and authorized user access on its Venture X card. Instead, it now charges $45 per adult guest unless the member spends $75,000 annually. Even though over 70 latest lounges started construction this year, banks and airlines tightened admission requirements due to persistent overcrowding. A few days after restricting access, Capital A's 12,500-square-foot (1,161 sqm) facility was opened, arriving at LaGuardia Airport with faster table turnover and custom-made tapas.

    Alaska and Hawaiian separated their terminal spaces between domestic crowds and long-haul flyers. Hawaiian broke ground in October on a 13,000-square-foot (1,208 sq m) Honolulu lounge for 200 guests as part of a $600 million overhaul. Alaska simultaneously advanced a 41,000-square-foot (3,809 sq m) Seattle complex for late 2027, splitting a 500-seat standard club from a 200-seat Aurora Lounge for international business-class fliers.

    United and American answered bank-run clubs with giant hub expansions and quick bypass lanes. United pushed ahead on the 40,000-square-foot (3,716 sq m), 650-seat United Club in Washington Dulles Concourse E after finishing near the bottom of the recent J.D. Power satisfaction rankings. American countered at New York's JFK Terminal 8 with a quick-service coffee and snack counter while reopening its Los Angeles Flagship First Dining room.

    It has been revealed that found an error? Send it info@simpleflying.com so it can be corrected.

    Sources indicate that the next major test for airline ground operations arrives between late 2027 and 2028, when Southwest's Icon Lounges, Alaska's two-tier Seattle complex, and Hawaiian's Honolulu flagship open their doors. Adding thousands of square feet of terminal space will only ease congestion if airlines and credit card issuers keep tightening guest rules. Tracking those openings will grant a glimpse into the next stage of competition in the terminal.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Aeromexico is planning some major upgrades to its wide body fleet, which consists exclusively of Boeing 787s.
    • Sources indicate that I first covered this several days ago, when this was quietly declared at an industry conference, as flagged by Seth Miller at PaxEx.Aero.
    • To start, let me provide the context that Aeromexico’s Boeing 787 fleet currently consists of 25 planes, including:.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Aeromexico is planning some major upgrades to its wide body fleet, which consists exclusively of Boeing 787s. This is interesting on many levels — we’ll see the larger Dreamliners get all-latest business class cabins plus premium economy for the first time, we’ll see the smaller Dreamliners get the old business class cabins of the bigger Dreamliners, and we’ll see the airline adopt some Delta-style branding.

    Sources indicate that I first covered this several days ago, when this was quietly declared at an industry conference, as flagged by Seth Miller at PaxEx.Aero. However, the airline has now released a video on social media with additional details, so I’d like to publish an enhancement to reflect that.

    To start, let me provide the context that Aeromexico’s Boeing 787 fleet currently consists of 25 planes, including:.

    Aeromexico is planning on fully overhauling the premium cabins on these planes, as was revealed by the manufacturer’s CEO at last week’s APEX FTE EXPO 2026.

    Sources indicate that the plan is for the 787-9s to get all-fresh cabins, and in the process, the 787-8s will get the old business class seats from the 787-9s. That means the 787-8s will get reverse herringbone seats, which are still competitive, but of course not cutting edge (though still a huge improvement over the pairs of seats presently on the planes).

    Sources indicate that the 787-9s will really become the next-generation flagship planes for the airline, though some patience will be required. The expectation is that the cabins will be updated between 2029 and 2031, so that’s between three and five years from now (and that assumes no additional delays).

    We’ll talk more about the newly introduced business class product as such in a bit, but the idea is that the 787-9s will get business class suites, including a front row “business class plus” product. On top of that, the 787-9s will be getting a premium economy cabin for the first time.

    The plane will also have 69% more premium seats than before. Currently, Aeromexico’s 787-9s have 36 business class seats, while the retrofitted planes will have a total of 61 premium seats, between business class and premium economy. So I suspect the business class cabin won’t actually get that much bigger, but instead, most of that premium addition will come in the form of the fresh premium economy cabin.

    It’s also worth mentioning that Aeromexico is adopting some Delta-style branding, as Delta owns a 20% stake in Aeromexico, and the two airlines have a close partnership.

    It has been revealed that aeromexico’s fresh premium products will be known as Premier One Suites Plus (the “business class plus” product), Premier One Suites (business class), and Premier (premium economy). It seems the 787-8 business class will just be branded as Premier One, given the lack of suites with doors. That all sure seems to be inspired by the Delta One branding that’s used by the carrier’s partner.

    Aeromexico has published the below video about its all-latest cabins, which gives you a sense of what we can expect.

    There are all kinds of rewards these days — for travel, dining, retail, or even your local coffee shop.

    But there's one currency built specifically for sports fans that rewards you with all the things that drive your fandom — tickets, gear, collectibles and even unique experiences.

    And thanks to the upcoming Fanatics American Express® Card, there are now even more opportunities to earn it.

    Here’s everything you need to know about FanCash, Fanatics' loyalty currency.

    FanCash is the one currency built for sports fans. It takes everything we love about a loyalty program — great earning rates and a variety of redemption options — and merges it with the passion so many of us feel for our favorite sports teams. The end result? The best way to turn your fandom into real rewards.

    Sources indicate that but now, there are even more ways to earn FanCash, thanks to the launch of the new Fanatics American Express Card. This card takes your fandom to the next level by rewarding you with unlimited 5% FanCash on purchases across the full Fanatics ecosystem. Plus, you can earn 5% FanCash on ticket purchases and select streaming partners.*.

    Recent findings suggest that any FanCash you earn will expire one year from the date of purchase. However, any subsequent eligible Fanatics purchase will automatically extend the expiration date for qualifying FanCash in your account.

    But with the Fanatics American Express Card, the FanCash earned on the card will never expire, as long as you remain an active cardmember.

    You can start earning rewards by signing up for a free Fanatics ONE account.

    Industry observers note that the best way to earn FanCash is with the fresh Fanatics American Express Card. For starters, you'll earn unlimited 5% FanCash across the entire Fanatics ecosystem — including Fanatics.com, Lids, Mitchell & Ness, Fanatics Collect, Topps.com, League stores and more. You'll also earn 5% FanCash on tickets from other vendors and select streaming partners, plus 2% FanCash on all other purchases.* And when you stack on the Fanatics App, you can earn 8% or more.

    In a recent development, in addition, fresh cardholders earn $100 FanCash after spending $1,000 on purchases in the first 90 days. Plus, earn an additional $100 FanCash for spending $500 a month for 12 consecutive months.**.

    The Fanatics American Express Card has no annual fee*** and no foreign transaction fees — allowing you to earn a ton of FanCash every year, whether you’re close to home or cheering for your favorite team from abroad.

    Finally, eligible U.S. Membership Rewards cardmembers with American Express-issued cards can now transfer Membership Rewards points into FanCash — at a rate of 1,000 points for $10 in FanCash — giving you even more opportunities to spend on gear, collectibles, tickets and more.

    Sources indicate that once you’ve earned FanCash, there are a variety of ways to use it across the Fanatics ecosystem. $1 in FanCash gets you $1 in rewards toward your purchase. It’s that simple. No complicated redemption math. That $100 NFL or NBA jersey you've been eyeing? It can be yours for $100 in FanCash.

    Industry observers note that but perhaps the most powerful aspect of this loyalty currency is that there’s no minimum redemption amount. Unlike other cash-back rewards, you don’t need to wait until you’ve accumulated a certain amount to begin saving — though the more FanCash you have, the more redemption options you unlock.

    But it’s the other features of the Fanatics American Express Card that are potentially even more exciting for sports fans.

    It has been revealed that for starters, cardholders receive 2,500 Fanatics ONE Tier Points upon approval, immediately unlocking Member Pro status and even more rewards and benefits. Plus, you'll receive an additional 2,500 Tier Points every year you have the card.^ This unlocks even more rewards and benefits through the Fanatics ONE program.

    Plus, you can select from one of over 500 players for your card design, turning the card itself into a collectible — and a badge of your fandom in your wallet.

    According to recent reports, finally, starting in 2027, you’ll have access to the Championship Challenge as a cardholder. If you correctly predict all four champions across the NFL, NBA, NHL, and MLB, you’ll get up to $100,000 of your annual spending back.

    According to recent reports, eligibility requirements apply for the Championship Challenge. Program details, including timing and structure, are subject to change. Terms and conditions apply. Full details to be announced prior to launch.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that new York Kennedy Airport (JFK) is currently undergoing a $19 billion modernization.
    • As you’d expect, the opening of both terminals has been delayed, since airport construction rarely runs on time.
    • Along those lines, it’s looking like we might just be days away from the opening of Terminal 6, so I’d like to cover all the details we know.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that new York Kennedy Airport (JFK) is currently undergoing a $19 billion modernization. While this includes all kinds of updates, the two biggest developments are the opening of two new terminals — we’re talking about Terminal 6 and Terminal One (not to be confused with Terminal 1).

    As you’d expect, the opening of both terminals has been delayed, since airport construction rarely runs on time. Per the latest updates, the expectation is that Terminal 6 will open before the end of 2026, while Terminal One will open in the first quarter of 2027.

    Along those lines, it’s looking like we might just be days away from the opening of Terminal 6, so I’d like to cover all the details we know.

    JFK Terminal 6 is expected to open with a phased approach as of December 2026. To cover the very basics:.

    The below video of the terminal should give you a good sense of what to expect in terms of the passenger experience, so I’d recommend checking that out.

    Sources indicate that all things considered, this new terminal moving is awesome, given the quality of terminals at JFK otherwise. For those originating or terminating in New York, this should be ideal. For those connecting to or from JetBlue in Terminal 5, this will also make connections much easier. Meanwhile for a limited number of other passengers, this might make connections a bit more complicated, for cases where airlines are moving away from their partners (like Cathay Pacific moving from American’s Terminal 8 to Terminal 6).

    Sources indicate that roughly 17 airlines are expected to eventually operate out of JFK Terminal 6, though that will happen in two phases. Broadly speaking, we’ll see some JetBlue operations move there (since the airline is a core tenant), and on top of that, we’ll largely see airlines move from Terminal 1, Terminal 7, and Terminal 8.

    So the expectation is that the following airlines will eventually operate from JFK Terminal 6:.

    There is still a bit of a mystery as to the order in which airlines will move to JFK Terminal 6. For one, there’s the two phases of the terminal opening, but even within each phase, it won’t fully be overnight.

    We know that All Nippon Airways, Cathay Pacific, Condor, Frontier, Lufthansa Group carriers, and TAP Air Portugal, will move in the first phase. Meanwhile we know that Air India will move in the second phase. But for the remainder of the airlines, there’s a lack of certainty on that front.

    According to recent reports, now, we’ll see if this sticks, and how accurate it is, but current schedule filings suggest that Condor will start operating out of Terminal 6 as of December 3, while Cathay Pacific will start operating out of Terminal 6 as of December 15 (thanks to Peter_ for flagging this). So it sounds like we could potentially be just over a week from the first airline moving, which would be awesome!

    Sources indicate that in terms of lounges, we have confirmation that Terminal 6 will have outposts from Cathay Pacific, Lufthansa, Aer Lingus, and Air India. Hopefully the new lounges are ready to go as airlines make the move, but I wouldn’t consider that to be a sure thing, given the complexity of airport operations.

    The Air India lounge definitely won’t open anytime soon, since the airline is only moving in the second phase. Meanwhile the Cathay Pacific, Lufthansa, and Aer Lingus lounges, will hopefully open soon(ish). Of course I’m most excited to see what Cathay Pacific has in store, given its amazing lounge quality.

    JFK Terminal 6 is expected to open before the end of 2026, and if current filings are to be believed, the move could happen as soon as early December. It appears that Condor and Cathay Pacific might be among the first airlines to move, so hopefully Cathay Pacific’s fresh lounge isn’t too far behind. So we’ll mark this as “developing,” but the completion of the first exciting phase of this $19 billion project is imminent.

    #123603. Restored to Calder’s blueprint, the clouds are spinning again

    📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1154 w)
    📖 Baca
    General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Rollcall ↗ Open Full Page

    Restored to Calder’s blueprint, the clouds are spinning again

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1154 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Alex Padilla, D-Calif., speaks during a ceremony marking the restoration of Alexander Calder’s Mountains and Clouds sculpture in the Hart Senate Office Building atrium on Wednesday.
    • The day after Alexander Calder presented his initiative for a public art display in the Hart Building’s nine-story atrium to the Architect of the Capitol, he died.
    • It has been revealed that fifty years later, Alexander S.C.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sen. Alex Padilla, D-Calif., speaks during a ceremony marking the restoration of Alexander Calder’s Mountains and Clouds sculpture in the Hart Senate Office Building atrium on Wednesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

    The day after Alexander Calder presented his initiative for a public art display in the Hart Building’s nine-story atrium to the Architect of the Capitol, he died.

    It has been revealed that fifty years later, Alexander S.C. Rower felt a sense of awe as he stared up at his grandfather’s work, finally restored to what he had envisioned.

    Sources indicate that “It’s totally phenomenal,” he said, pointing up at the now-moving clouds as he spoke, spinning his finger around. “It’s not entertainment, but it’s trying to emulate naturalness, trying to emulate what nature would do.”.

    It was a long time coming for Rower, who remembers traveling to the Capitol in his 20s for the original dedication of the Mountains and Clouds sculpture in 1987. The mobile portion stopped rotating as Calder intended in the 1990s, and it was ultimately removed in 2014 after being deemed unsafe by the Architect of the Capitol. Millions of dollars in private philanthropy later, Calder’s clouds are spinning again.

    Industry observers note that rower was back on the Hill on Wednesday for an event celebrating the restoration, joining Architect of the Capitol Thomas Austin, Sens. Alex Padilla, D-Calif., Angus King, I-Maine, and James Lankford, R-Okla., and the project’s donors. As the speakers addressed the crowd, the clouds began to speed up slightly. Onlookers gathered on the balconies overlooking the atrium and peeked through office windows. Attendees left with tote bags emblazoned with images of Calder’s art.

    According to Rower, who leads the Calder Foundation dedicated to preserving and interpreting his grandfather’s art, the mobile is rotating on a 15-hour cycle that is “totally variable.”.

    Recent findings suggest that “It can go a little faster; it can go a little slower,” he said. “I told the team today that during lunchtime, I want it to speed up just a little bit because everyone’s going to lunch. There’ll be … a lot of activity passing through, and then right at 2:30, well, let’s make it go quieter.”.

    It was a labor of love for those involved, and not an inexpensive one. Jon and Kim Shirley funded the $12 million restoration. Because the pieces were so large, they were transported on an extra-wide load truck and driven at a speed of 35 miles per hour from Michigan.

    Sources indicate that “We had to call every senator or governor that we knew on that route, which went through seven states, to get permissions,” he noted. “That was a huge thing to overcome, and it all happened over a weekend. So my wife was actually on the phone with a governor’s wife on Saturday evening. The next day, he called up his Department of Transportation and got a permit.”.

    Christian Quilici, who helped manage the project on behalf of the Shirleys and said he serves as a liaison between the foundation and Congress, said the hardest part of the project was the size of it.

    Sources indicate that “We had to tear the wall down on C Street, which nobody really thought of in the beginning,” he said. “Nobody got how major this was until it revealed up on their doorstep.”.

    Sources indicate that quilici stated he spent years educating at least 30 different senators about the quest to reunite the mobile with the stationary mountains left behind. Some of the biggest champions were seated in the front row at Wednesday’s event, including Senate Democratic Whip Richard J. Durbin. Absent was Sen. Christopher S. Murphy, D-Conn., who has been away from the Capitol while recovering from a stroke but has been a supporter of the sculpture’s restoration for years, pressing former acting Architect of the Capitol Joseph DiPietro on it at a 2024 Senate Legislative Branch Appropriations budget hearing.

    “Is there any chance that before I leave the Senate, or at least before I die, we can get the clouds back up there?” Murphy remarked at the time.

    Padilla read a letter on Wednesday from Murphy, whose state was Calder’s home for much of his life.

    “This statue is actually a statement on our democracy, that we have significant pieces of monumental art right in the middle of our most key and most iconic government buildings. To get this piece of art restored to how it was designed by the artist, well, that’s good for Connecticut. But I also like to think … it’s good for democracy too,” Murphy’s statement remarked.

    The restoration was funded entirely by donations from the Shirleys, who are prominent Calder collectors, according to Rower.

    “It’s very emotional to see the work completed after 10 years of us working so hard with the Architect of the Capitol and Calder Foundation. It’s a very overpowering, overwhelming emotion,” mentioned Kim Shirley.

    In addition to helping fund the project, she’s a former Senate staffer who worked in Hart before Calder’s work was installed. Years after her time in the Senate was over, her husband Jon wanted to show her the sculpture, now filling the space she used to walk through every day.

    But when the two arrived, the clouds weren’t hanging from the ceiling like they were supposed to be. He called up Rower, who was a friend of his, and said he wanted to get them back to how Calder intended. On Wednesday, the three of them stood together in Hart, looking up.

    Technological and engineering advancements allowed for newer, lighter clouds to be built and be safe to hang from the ceiling.

    “Before it was like a bulb, it looked like a hoagie sandwich, and now it looks just really sharp, like a razor cutting through space, which was Calder’s intention,” Rower said.

    According to Rower, it involved laser-measuring the original model of Mountains and Clouds sitting in a glass case nearby in the Hart atrium. The newly introduced clouds, he mentioned, are made of carbon fiber.

    “These are giant things up in the air, and they’re just so gentle and subtle,” he said.

    According to recent reports, younger Hill staffers don’t know a time with clouds. But for those who have spent decades in the building, it was a special moment to see them spin, as Lankford told the crowd.

    “I can’t tell you how many tour groups that I’ve walked through this building and I pointed to this, and I said it’s only half there, and would take them over to the little model that’s right over here, and say this is what it’s supposed to look like,” said the senator, a former Hill staffer himself.

    Standing under his grandfather’s sculpture, Rower found himself quoting the man responsible for it all.

    “I find that everything I do, if it is made for a particular spot, is more successful,” he stated, gazing up at it.

    Emirates Axes 14 Airbus A350 Routes From Dubai: See Full List Now

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (713 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Emirates is one of approximately 45 operators of the Airbus A350.
    • It has been revealed that all of Emirates' A350s have one of two configurations.
    • According to recent reports, the UAE carrier's A350 network was examined using Cirium Diio data.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Emirates is one of approximately 45 operators of the Airbus A350. Registered A6-EXA, the Gulf giant's first A350-900 was delivered on November 25, 2024, two years to the day before this article was written. Ch-aviation shows that the airline now has 31 examples of the Airbus twinjet.

    It has been revealed that all of Emirates' A350s have one of two configurations. Some have 298 seats, with 32 in business, 28 in premium economy, and 238 in economy. This is the airline's second lowest-capacity equipment after the Boeing 777-200LR. Other A350s have 312 seats, with 32 in business, 21 in premium economy, and 259 in economy.

    According to recent reports, the UAE carrier's A350 network was examined using Cirium Diio data. This process analyzed where the type was deployed from Dubai between January and October 2026, which was then compared to where's scheduled to see the equipment from November 2026 onwards. Based on a minimum of five departures, the following 11 routes have stopped seeing it. This reflects what is known as of November 25, and certainly could change.

    In a recent development, the ongoing war in Iran inevitably played an crucial role in why some of the destinations saw the A350. The type's lower capacity helped to right-size capacity with demand during a period of lower demand. This resulted from the reduced confidence in visiting the usually very popular Gulf destination or connecting to another flight there.

    A350 Departures (January 2026 To End Month Only).

    Nothing; the specific flights on which it was used no longer run in 2026. When they return in 2027, the 777-200LR is presently down to be used.

    5 (July, September, October only).

    Recent findings suggest that 777-300ER. More on this route later in the article.

    Emirates flew the A350-900 to Brussels in July 2026 and is doing so again from October through November 30. Milan Malpensa first saw the A350 in August this year, with the final departure also on November 30. As predictable as it is, the 777-300ER will then return. Emirates has three daily flights to Malpensa: two on the A380 (one continues to Latest York JFK) and one on the A350 and soon the 777-300ER.

    Then there is Cairo, which is usually considered the most populous city in Africa. The A350-900 was deployed between March and May, with up to two daily services, before returning in November. The variant operated on November 3, 16, 19, 20, 21, and 22. There is no prize for guessing what equipment has replaced it. Cairo has five daily Emirates flights: three on the A380 and two on the 777-300ER.

    In a recent development, emirates deployed the A350 to Newcastle, in Northeast England, between March 16 and October 31. The less-premium, higher-capacity, 312-seat configuration was used on 159 of the 203 departures, while the higher-premium 298-seat layout was on 44 flights, mainly in May and June.

    Due to the ongoing war in Iran, Emirates occasionally had a lower frequency than usual to Newcastle. For example, the airline flew five times a week in April and June, down from the usual daily offering, with the A350 deployed instead of the typical 421-seat 777-300ER.

    Fewer flights (at times) and fewer seats for sale were both designed to better match capacity with demand and, therefore, to improve yields, the load factor, and overall performance. Between March and October, 30% fewer seats were available compared to last year.

    It has been revealed that while capacity fell by 48% in April and June, that considerable drop was not always enough. UK Civil Aviation Authority data for April demonstrates that Emirates transported 7,211 passengers to/from Newcastle, down from 21,752 in the same month last year. That was a substantial reduction of 67%, far outstripping the 48% fewer seats. The situation had improved by June as confidence grew, with traffic 'only' 50% lower than for the previous year, not far off the capacity reduction.

    Recent findings suggest that as you'd expect, things kept developing, with the reintroduction of a daily service in July. In September, for example, 15,917 passengers flew, 26% fewer than the prior year, with the same proportion of seats removed from operating the A350 instead of the 777-300ER. The equilibrium had returned. The Triple Seven was back on November 1.

    The Capital One Venture Card is currently offering a limited time, lucrative, two-part welcome offer, whereby you can earn 75,000 Capital One bonus miles, plus a $300 Capital One Travel stays credit, after spending $4,000 within the first three months.

In other words, you could use it to pay virtually nothing for a $300 hotel stay. All-in-all, I’d say the Capital One Venture bonus is worth up to $1,575.

    By my valuation, the current Capital One Venture Card bonus is the best publicly available offer that we’ve seen in over five years, so that makes this the ideal time to apply, and I absolutely wouldn’t wait for a better offer.     Delta Plans Seattle To Singapore A350 Flights, Carrier’s Third Longest Route

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1240 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, we know that Delta has huge growth aspirations across the Pacific, particularly to Asia.
    • A few months ago, Delta executives publicly confirmed plans to return to Singapore, a destination that hasn’t been served by the airline since 2019, when that was an intra-Asia tag flight from Japan.
    • According to recent reports, as Delta executives view it, the airline is pretty maxed out in terms of its European potential, and in the long run, they see the most long haul growth potential in Asia, the Middle East, and Africa.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, we know that Delta has huge growth aspirations across the Pacific, particularly to Asia. It’s an area where Delta has increasingly fallen behind United in recent years, but Delta now hopes to not only catch up, but even beat United. We’ll see what comes of that, and in particular, find out just how costly that growth is.

    A few months ago, Delta executives publicly confirmed plans to return to Singapore, a destination that hasn’t been served by the airline since 2019, when that was an intra-Asia tag flight from Japan. Executives also confirmed out of which airport the service would operate. There’s now an additional patch, as an announcement about the newly introduced route is imminent, which almost certainly points to a fall 2027 launch for the service.

    According to recent reports, as Delta executives view it, the airline is pretty maxed out in terms of its European potential, and in the long run, they see the most long haul growth potential in Asia, the Middle East, and Africa. So, what kind of expansion should we expect?

    Sources indicate that back in August 2026, Delta Chief Commercial Officer Joe Esposito explicitly confirmed that the airline would return to Singapore. What was perhaps most interesting is that he also indirectly confirmed the hub out of which the service would operate — Esposito ruled out that the service could operate out of Los Angeles, so it’s pretty clear that the airline will operate this service out of Seattle (SEA).

    That’s also what JonNYC reported in the past, and now we can take that a step further — Delta is holding an event in Seattle in early December 2026, and that’s when the airline is expected to announce the service.

    Sources indicate that my guess is that we’re looking at a fall 2027 service start, at best. At 8,070 miles, this will be Delta’s third longest flight, after its routes to South Africa, which are from Atlanta (ATL) to Cape Town (CPT) and Johannesburg (JNB).

    According to recent reports, one certainly wonders if this Singapore route could be operated by Delta’s newly introduced Airbus A350-1000s, which will feature an all-new passenger experience. While the plane has great range and per seat economics, the only thing I’d say is that it’s “a lot of plane” for a new market, in terms of the overall capacity (even with the very premium layout).

    It has been revealed that in both the Seattle and Los Angeles to Singapore market, Singapore Airlines is the only other carrier operating. So competitively there’s not a huge difference in that regard, though Los Angeles is a significantly larger market in terms of demand for Singapore, and for that matter, Singapore Airlines also has more service out of the airport. But perhaps Delta is also looking to beat Alaska to the punch in the Seattle market.

    It’s fantastic to see Delta looking to grow its presence in Asia. Point-to-point flying to Asia is a market that United has basically had cornered in recent years, and competition is good for consumers.

    Sources indicate that it’s amazing to think for how many years Delta basically squandered its Asia advantage. Keep in mind that back in the day, Northwest had a robust Asia network, and after the merger with Delta, we saw that network decreased slowly but steadily, as Delta instead focused on routing everything through Seoul Incheon, and into the Korean Air network. So I’m happy to see a reversal of that strategy.

    I also have to say that given Delta’s hubris, it’s kind of fun to see the airline having to increasingly play “catch up,” rather than coming in as the dominant carrier. And I think that very much sums up what’s going on in Asia.

    Industry observers note that the most basic structural disadvantage that Delta has is that United has a fortress hub in San Francisco (SFO), which is where a large part of its Asia network flies from. That’s fantastic for connectivity, not to mention San Francisco is a very strong market for Asia traffic.

    Sources indicate that delta, meanwhile, is taking a split hub approach, flying out of both Los Angeles and Seattle. Obviously Delta is trying to make the best of its situation, but there’s no denying that this is an uphill battle:.

    Industry observers note that it also has to be emphasized that in terms of actually transporting passengers profitably (or at less of a loss), United does a better job at that than Delta, despite its lower overall profitability. Comparing passenger revenue per air seat mile to cost per air seat mile, United is at 16.18 cents vs. 16.46 cents, while Delta is at 17.37 cents vs. 19.31 cents.

    Recent findings suggest that delta is growing quite a bit in Asia at the moment. The airline has already launched flights to Hong Kong, with flights now on sale to Manila and Tokyo Narita. On top of that, Delta is expected to announce a fresh Seattle to Singapore route within the next two weeks, with a launch likely planned for the fall of 2027.

    In a recent development, it’s great for passengers to see more competition across the Pacific, as Delta sure is making up for a lack of effort for years. However, the airline will also have quite the disadvantage compared to United for a long time….

    What do you make of Delta’s prepares to fly to Singapore?

    Norse Atlantic Notes Financial Situation ‘Critical’

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • After close to a year of dire financial warnings, Norway’s Norse Atlantic Airways said Wednesday that its situation is “critical” and that it must obtain short-term financing to continue operations.
    • The Arendal-based carrier has struggled with higher jet fuel prices brought on by the war in Iran and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.
    • “[The company’s financial condition is] dependent on securing financing to meet its short term liquidity needs and to continue its operations,” officials said in a statement.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    After close to a year of dire financial warnings, Norway’s Norse Atlantic Airways said Wednesday that its situation is “critical” and that it must obtain short-term financing to continue operations.

    The Arendal-based carrier has struggled with higher jet fuel prices brought on by the war in Iran and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. In the months since the war started, the airline has cut staff, furloughed some crew members, suspended unprofitable routes, and instituted temporary pay reductions for some non-flying crew, but these steps have apparently not put Norse Atlantic back on solid ground.

    “[The company’s financial condition is] dependent on securing financing to meet its short term liquidity needs and to continue its operations,” officials said in a statement. “Norse, supported by its advisors, has explored various strategic alternatives and entertains discussions for a potential takeover.”.

    “Norse is also engaged in discussions with selected parties on short term financing, however, there can be no assurances that such discussions will result in a viable solution,” the message continued. “Norse will provide further information as and when appropriate.”.

    Rising fuel costs have set back airlines around the world, but the squeeze is arguably worst in Europe, since the continent depends mainly on Gulf oil and has little domestic refining capacity. The crisis has forced Latvia’s airBaltic into bankruptcy, teed up EasyJet’s sale to Apollo Global Management, and inflicted considerable damage on Lufthansa’s core brand.

    It was not immediately clear if Norse Atlantic has any candidates in mind for a potential merger. The carrier is not part of any global airline alliance, though it partners with operators such as EasyJet, Norwegian Air Shuttle, and Pegasus through its Norse Connections program.

    Bloomberg reported in 2023 and 2024 that the carrier was weighing alliances with larger airlines, possibly through an equity stake, but none were named.

    Sources indicate that norse Atlantic operates only long-haul flights. Its network has been adjusted multiple times over the last year in an effort to reduce costs.

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rollcall ↗ Open Full Page

    Progressive advocates call on House Democrats to force Cuba vote

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (865 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Velázquez, D-N.Y., is the sponsor of a Cuba war powers resolution filed in May.
    • Progressive advocates are urging House Democrats to force a vote during the lame-duck session on a resolution aimed at preventing war against Cuba, arguing the glitch is too urgent to wait until Democrats control the chamber next year.
    • Recent findings suggest that “The Cuban people are suffering and dying, and cannot afford further months of inaction,” 50 progressive groups wrote to Democratic House leaders in a letter dated Wednesday.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Rep. Nydia M. Velázquez, D-N.Y., is the sponsor of a Cuba war powers resolution filed in May. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    Progressive advocates are urging House Democrats to force a vote during the lame-duck session on a resolution aimed at preventing war against Cuba, arguing the glitch is too urgent to wait until Democrats control the chamber next year.

    Recent findings suggest that “The Cuban people are suffering and dying, and cannot afford further months of inaction,” 50 progressive groups wrote to Democratic House leaders in a letter dated Wednesday. “In the midterm elections, U.S. voters resoundingly rejected a foreign policy of war and domination, and made clear their desire for Congress to act forcefully to rein in the Trump administration.

    Holding a vote would demonstrate that Democrats recognize the urgency facing the Cuban people, and would help set the tone for an assertive agenda of peace, diplomacy and respect for international law in the 120th Congress, the letter added.

    Recent findings suggest that at issue is a war powers resolution introduced in May by Rep. Nydia M. Velázquez, D-N.Y., and House Foreign Affairs Committee ranking member Rep. Gregory W. Meeks, D-N.Y., that would call on the president “to remove the United States Armed Forces from hostilities within or against Cuba, unless explicitly authorized by a declaration of war or a specific authorization for use of military force.”.

    Sources indicate that the letter was sent to House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries of Newly introduced York, Meeks and House Rules Committee ranking member Jim McGovern, D-Mass. It was signed by prominent anti-war groups such as Win Without War, Just Foreign Policy, the Friends Committee on National Legislation, Indivisible and Code Pink.

    Recent findings suggest that advocates are frustrated that House Democrats have not forced a vote on a Cuba war powers resolution even as they have forced multiple war powers votes on Iran and see it as an example of leadership that is at odds with the progressive wing of the party. One advocate who requested anonymity to speak candidly noted it’s their understanding Democratic leaders are hesitant to make potentially vulnerable Florida members of the caucus vote on the glitch.

    Spokespeople for Jeffries and Meeks did not respond to requests for comment Wednesday on whether Democrats will force a vote before the end of the year, what their reasoning is if they don’t and whether they plan to bring up a vote next year.

    Recent findings suggest that senate Democrats sought to force a vote on a similar resolution earlier this year, but Republicans in that chamber successfully derailed the effort. Senate Republicans raised a point of order that the resolution was not entitled to privileged status under the War Powers Resolution since U.S. troops aren't actively engaged in combat against Cuba. The point of order was sustained in a mostly party-line vote of 51-47.

    Senate Democrats later introduced another Cuba war powers resolution, which they have not tried to force a vote on and have not signaled they will do so before the end of the year.

    The resolutions have come amid several veiled threats from President Donald Trump suggesting eventual military action against Cuba.

    “I want to get Cuba done before I leave,” Trump told conservative radio host Hugh Hewitt last week when asked if he would order the use of military force against Cuba.

    “Frankly, I’d love to be able to do it for the people, for the Cubans that came and were treated really badly, and they came to America,” Trump remarked, adding he would “certainly consider” taking military action.

    Trump’s comments are on top of a pressure campaign his administration has been waging against Cuba. Since January, the United States has imposed a blockade of oil shipments to the island, causing fuel shortages that have led to lengthy blackouts and aggravated an economic crisis.

    While the Senate vote in April did not go Democrats’ way, advocates still saw it as sending a strong message.

    “Despite falling short of the majority, this was among the strongest votes in congressional history against the use of blockades, and one of the most crucial stands Congress has taken against U.S. economic sanctions toward Cuba in over six decades,” the letter from progressive organizations said. “The House should take a similarly forceful action at this crucial moment.”.

    The House vote, even if successful, would be largely symbolic since the measure Democrats can force a vote on is a concurrent resolution. Concurrent resolutions are widely considered to be nonbinding even if cleared by both chambers of Congress since they do not get a presidential signature, though anti-war advocates dispute that applies to war powers.

    The progressive groups in their letter called for “decisive leadership” in forcing a vote on the problem.

    “Across the political spectrum,” the letter said, “Americans do not want another regime change war, nor an open-ended, nation-building project abroad based on false pretenses — especially not when escalation risks exposing the United States to upcoming national security risks, placing US servicemembers in harm’s way, stoking regional instability, and becoming the latest chapter in a long history of harmful U.S. regional policies that have fueled mass migration to U.S. shores.”.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The concept of mileage running is making headlines in Japan, and not in a good way.
    • News On Japan has the story of how mileage running has caused challenges for locals on some of Okinawa’s remote islands, as they’ve struggled to purchase Japan Airlines tickets due to a flood of mileage runners.
    • It has been revealed that while the story has been published in recent days, it seems to date back to February 2026 (best I can tell), when Japan Airlines’ Mileage Bank program was offering double Life Status Points for flights.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The concept of mileage running is making headlines in Japan, and not in a good way. A lucrative promotion from Japan Airlines reportedly caused passengers to take up to 12 flights per day in remote markets, in some cases making it difficult for locals to book flights. What a story this is!

    News On Japan has the story of how mileage running has caused challenges for locals on some of Okinawa’s remote islands, as they’ve struggled to purchase Japan Airlines tickets due to a flood of mileage runners.

    It has been revealed that while the story has been published in recent days, it seems to date back to February 2026 (best I can tell), when Japan Airlines’ Mileage Bank program was offering double Life Status Points for flights. This promotion incentivized all domestic flights equally, so some savvy frequent flyers decided to seek out the shortest flights, so that they could cram in as many flights in a day as possible.

    Sources indicate that this ended up bringing them to Okinawa, where you’ll find some of the shortest flights in Japan Airlines’ system. These include flights between Ishigaki (ISG), Miyako (MMY), Naha (OKA), and Tarama (TRA). According to reports, some mileage runners booked up to a staggering 12 flights per day, leaving few empty seats on some essential flights.

    Sources indicate that at Miyako Airport, some passengers were observed arriving with just small handbags, and then immediately heading to the departures area to board their next flight. As a few travelers explained:.

    It has been revealed that the concern is that this mileage running reportedly created serious difficulties for locals, who depend on the island flights for medical appointments, shopping, and other essential travel. There were some successive days in February where flights between Miyako and Tarama were booked out in advance, leaving locals unable to book seats. Here’s what some locals had to say:.

    Tarama Mayor Mitsuo Iranami even called on mileage runners to consider the impact their activities were having on the island community, commenting “I would like those doing mileage runs to understand the situation on remote islands and exercise some consideration, taking into account the number of people participating.”.

    In a recent development, japan Airlines reportedly even introduced measures intended to counteract this, including offering full refunds without cancellation fees, along with 500 bonus miles as an incentive. Below is a news story in Japanese about this, so you can watch that with subtitles, if you’d like.

    I think this story is a good reminder of just how well frequent flyer programs can work with the purpose of filling seats on planes… for better or worse!

    Sources indicate that while it’s fairly common to see loyalty programs offer promotions, nowadays it’s rare to see deals that are actually that lucrative. When it does happen, we sometimes see that the people behind the promotion clearly didn’t think through all possible scenarios, and this is one of those situations.

    While Japan Airlines’ double status points promotion in February is pretty standard, the airline has added a latest restriction for the offer this coming year, by capping the number of bonus points that can be earned during the promotion period, presumably to prevent something like this from happening.

    Obviously I feel bad for the locals in this situation, but it’s also hard to blame frequent flyers here for simply taking advantage of a promotion as advertised.

    Japan Airlines’ Mileage Bank frequent flyer program ran a promotion that might have just done too good of a job getting people to book flights, as a double Life Status Points offer caused some people to book up to a dozen flights per day, with some flights reportedly having up to 80% of passengers be mileage runners.

    In a recent development, ordinarily that would be considered a success in terms of filling planes, but the issue here is that mileage runners descended on island routes that are also a lifeline for residents, given the efficiency of flying there. It’s not often you hear a mayor make a plea with mileage runners, but that’s exactly what happened here.
