    Citi AAdvantage Platinum Select Review—Why American Still Wins For Credit Card Spending Toward Status

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 45 min read (8972 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Viewfromthewing

    ⏱️ ~45 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • I receive compensation for content and many links on this blog.
    • Sources indicate that american Airlines has the best overall U.S.
    • Industry observers note that the Citi® / AAdvantage® Platinum Select® World Elite Mastercard® [See rates and fees] earns one Loyalty Point per eligible dollar, without a cap.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    I receive compensation for content and many links on this blog. Be aware that websites may earn compensation when a customer clicks on a link, when an application is approved, or when an account is opened. Citibank is an advertising partner of this site, as is American Express, Chase, Capital One, and others. Any opinions expressed in this post are my own, and have not been reviewed, approved, or endorsed by my advertising partners. I do not write about all offers that are available -- instead focusing on miles, points, and cash back (and currencies that can be converted into the same). Terms apply to the offers and benefits listed on this page.

    Sources indicate that american Airlines has the best overall U.S. program for making credit card spending count toward status, and the AAdvantage Mastercard is enough – you don’t need one of its expensive premium cards to take advantage of it.

    Industry observers note that the Citi® / AAdvantage® Platinum Select® World Elite Mastercard® [See rates and fees] earns one Loyalty Point per eligible dollar, without a cap. You can combine those points with what you earn flying, shopping and through many of American’s other partners, all the way up to Executive Platinum. Meanwhile, the card’s checked bag benefit can cover its annual fee on a single family trip.

    Recent findings suggest that I recently covered the card’s refresh, which adds Walmart+, an inflight credit and travel protections while raising the annual fee. Those changes take effect January 24, 2027. They improve the card for some customers, but the reason to put spending on it remains earning status.

    American’s current offer is 50,000 bonus miles after $2,500 in purchases within the first three months. There’s no annual fee for the first 12 months then $99, increasing to $150 with renewals starting January 24, 2027. That means for fresh applications, after the introductory year, the card’s annual fee is $150. Citi’s initial bonus restriction looks back 48 months. You aren’t eligible if you’ve received a Platinum Select new account bonus during that period, or converted another Citi card on which you earned a new account bonus during that period into a Platinum Select. A bonus on a different American Airlines card doesn’t, by itself, disqualify you. The miles are worth having. I’ve written about American’s partner award sweet spots, like 70,000 miles for business class between North America and the Middle East or Indian Subcontinent. And I find the miles useful for domestic travel too, often uncovering good mileage deals when cash prices are high (my sense that American doesn’t want to discount the fare, but doesn’t expect to fill the plane without doing so). Why American Is Best Overall For Spending Toward Status The card earns one Loyalty Point per dollar of eligible purchases. There’s no annual cap on that earning and no minimum flight requirement to qualify for American’s published status levels. Here are the thresholds, and the spending that would reach them if you earned nothing from flights, partners or separate Loyalty Point bonuses: AAdvantage Status   Loyalty Points   Card Spending Alone Gold   40,000   $40,000 Platinum   75,000   $75,000 Platinum Pro   125,000   $125,000 Executive Platinum   200,000   $200,000 American’s qualification year runs March 1 through the last day of February.If flights and other activity get you to 110,000 Loyalty Points, another $15,000 in eligible card purchases gets you to Platinum Pro. You can fill the gap with expenses you were going to incur anyway. The same Loyalty Points also move you toward Loyalty Point Rewards, including opportunities to select systemwide upgrades. Compare the AAdvantage Mastercard with the UnitedSM Explorer Card (See rates and fees), which earns one Premier qualifying point per $20 and caps that earning at 1,000 points annually. That’s only part of the 6,000 points needed for United’s points-based Silver qualification path, which also requires at least four United or United Express flights. The similarly priced Platinum Select can take you all the way to American’s top published tier. Even Delta’s premium Reserve card takes $255,000 in purchases to earn Diamond through spending plus that one card’s annual head start. That’s 28,000 qualifying dollars, less the card’s 2,500-dollar head start, earned at one qualifying dollar per $10 spent. American’s $200,000 Executive Platinum threshold is available on this much less expensive card. Alaska’s Atmos™ Rewards Summit Visa Infinite® credit card ($395 annual fee) earns one status point per $2, without a cap, plus 10,000 status points annually beginning with the first anniversary. It can require less spending for particular tiers. American is my overall pick because of the combination of inexpensive cards, uncapped earning, and the ability to combine spending with so many other sources of status credit. What You Earn On Purchases The January refresh expands the bonus categories: Eligible Purchases   Today   From January 24, 2027 American Airlines, restaurants and gas stations   2 miles per dollar   2 miles per dollar AAdvantage Hotels and AAdvantage Cars bookings through their respective sites   1 mile per dollar   3 miles per dollar Electric vehicle charging, select streaming services, and eligible rides and rail purchases   1 mile per dollar   2 miles per dollar Other purchases   1 mile per dollar   1 mile per dollar Two miles per dollar on American Airlines tickets still doesn’t impress me. The Citi Strata Premier® Card (See rates and fees.) earns three points per dollar on airfare, hotels, restaurants, supermarkets, gas and electric vehicle charging. Its points transfer to American, and its annual fee is $95. If I just wanted redeemable American miles, I’d generally prefer Strata Premier for those categories. The value in spending on this card is progress towards AAdvantage status. Free Checked Bags Can Pay For The Card The primary cardmember and up to four companions on the same reservation get their first checked bag free on eligible domestic American Airlines itineraries. American currently charges $45 online or $50 at the airport for the first checked bag on a standard domestic ticket. Basic economy costs $5 more. For two people each checking one bag on a domestic roundtrip, the savings are $180 compared with paying the standard fee online. That’s already more than the coming $150 annual fee. A family of four doing the same saves $360. You don’t have to buy the tickets with this card to receive the bag benefit. Your AAdvantage number needs to be on the reservation. The whole itinerary must qualify as domestic American Airlines or American Eagle travel. The primary cardmember must travel. An authorized user doesn’t get an independent bag allowance when traveling alone. If your status or cabin already includes a free bag, holding the card doesn’t add another one. You also get Group 5 preferred boarding, including up to four companions on the same reservation. That puts you ahead of later economy groups and improves your chances of finding overhead bin space. There are no foreign transaction fees, and authorized users can be added without an additional annual fee. Their spending earns miles and Loyalty Points for the primary cardmember. Holding an eligible AAdvantage card also keeps the miles in the primary cardmember’s account from expiring. What The AAdvantage Mastercard January Refresh Adds The annual fee rises $51. Key incremental benefits are: Walmart+ annual membership. The primary cardmember gets the $98 annual plan, including delivery benefits, fuel savings and a streaming choice. Someone already paying for it can come out ahead from this benefit alone. Up to $100 in annual inflight credits. Eligible food, drinks and Wi-Fi purchases qualify; Admirals Club purchases don’t. This replaces the existing 25% food and beverage rebate. Half off an annual FOX One subscription. I’d assign this value only if it’s something you already want to buy. The inflight credit is better than the old rebate for someone making a modest amount of purchases. Spend $100 on eligible food and drinks and you’d receive $100 back instead of $25. The added travel protections may be more useful than the subscription benefits. Trip delay: Up to $500 per covered traveler for eligible expenses after a covered delay of at least six hours. Paying just the taxes on an AAdvantage award doesn’t limit reimbursement to that small cash payment. Trip cancellation and interruption: Coverage is limited to the lesser of $5,000 per trip or the covered amount paid with the card and/or AAdvantage miles. Lost baggage: Up to $3,000 per covered traveler, with a $10,000 total per trip; a lower per-bag limit applies to New York residents. Rental cars: Up to $75,000 for covered damage, for eligible rentals up to 31 days. Coverage is secondary in the U.S. and primary outside it. AAdvantage Mastercard protections begin with the refresh. Required payment methods and covered reasons differ by benefit. The card also retains up to $180 in Turo credits per calendar year, limited to $30 per eligible completed trip. You need six rentals to use the full amount, must link the card to your Turo account, and need to pay directly with it rather than through a digital wallet. There’s also 10% off eligible American Airlines Vacations packages. AAdvantage Mastercard $20,000 Spending Bonus Is Useful, But Do The Math Currently, spending $20,000 on the AAdvantage Mastercard during your cardmembership year and renewing the card earns a $125 American Airlines Flight Discount. The refresh increases that to $150. The new discount adds 0.75% of the $20,000 in spending, assuming you use its full value. The increase itself is only another 0.125%. This isn’t an automatic annual flight credit just for holding the card. Under the published terms, the certificate expires one year after concern and can’t pay award-ticket taxes. Your cardmembership year also isn’t necessarily the same as the March-to-February status year. I’d count this as an extra return if I were already putting $20,000 on the card for Loyalty Points. I’d also consider moving a little spending to finish the threshold if I were close. I wouldn’t move $20,000 away from much better earning elsewhere simply because the flight discount happens to match the annual fee. Which American Airlines Card Should You Have? Platinum Select doesn’t include Admirals Club access or a general discount on award redemptions. The higher fee and extra benefits don’t change that. For an occasional American Airlines flyer without status, I’d choose it when checked bag savings and benefits I’d actually use cover the renewal fee. The first year’s $0 annual fee and initial bonus make trying it particularly easy. For someone who already has status, or another American Airlines card, I’d compare these options: Citi® / AAdvantage® Globe™ Mastercard® [See rates and fees] The $350 annual fee buys four Admirals Club Globe passes each calendar year, among other benefits. More interesting to me, the Flight Streak Bonus earns 5,000 additional Loyalty Points after every four qualifying American Airlines flight segments, up to 15,000 per qualification year. You don’t need to put spending on Globe to earn that flight bonus. Citi® / AAdvantage® Executive World Legend Mastercard® [See rates and fees] At a $695 annual fee, this is the card for an Admirals Club membership. It also awards 10,000 bonus Loyalty Points when you reach each of 50,000, 90,000, 165,000 and 240,000 Loyalty Points in a qualification year. Those thresholds can be reached through flights, partners or spending on other American Airlines cards. Citi® / AAdvantage BusinessTM World Elite Mastercard® [See rates and fees] Business owners should compare its separate initial bonus and spending benefits. Through December 31, 2028, eligible employee-card spending earns a Loyalty Point per dollar for the employee and an additional Loyalty Point for the primary cardmember. That’s status credit for two people from the same spending, rather than two points for one person. For instance, someone holding Executive can put dining and gas purchases on Platinum Select for two miles per dollar, earn the same basic Loyalty Point per dollar, and still trigger Executive’s account-wide Loyalty Point bonuses. They’d need enough value from Platinum Select’s extra miles, benefits and flight discount to justify its separate annual fee. For two people each checking one bag on a domestic roundtrip, the savings are $180 compared with paying the standard fee online. That’s already more than the coming $150 annual fee. A family of four doing the same saves $360. You don’t have to buy the tickets with this card to receive the bag benefit. Your AAdvantage number needs to be on the reservation. The whole itinerary must qualify as domestic American Airlines or American Eagle travel. The primary cardmember must travel. An authorized user doesn’t get an independent bag allowance when traveling alone. If your status or cabin already includes a free bag, holding the card doesn’t add another one. You also get Group 5 preferred boarding, including up to four companions on the same reservation. That puts you ahead of later economy groups and improves your chances of finding overhead bin space. There are no foreign transaction fees, and authorized consumers can be added without an additional annual fee. Their spending earns miles and Loyalty Points for the primary cardmember. Holding an eligible AAdvantage card also keeps the miles in the primary cardmember’s account from expiring. What The AAdvantage Mastercard January Refresh Adds The annual fee rises $51. Key incremental benefits are: Walmart+ annual membership. The primary cardmember gets the $98 annual plan, including delivery benefits, fuel savings and a streaming choice. Someone already paying for it can come out ahead from this benefit alone. Up to $100 in annual inflight credits. Eligible food, drinks and Wi-Fi purchases qualify; Admirals Club purchases don’t. This replaces the existing 25% food and beverage rebate. Half off an annual FOX One subscription. I’d assign this value only if it’s something you already want to buy. The inflight credit is better than the old rebate for someone making a modest amount of purchases. Spend $100 on eligible food and drinks and you’d receive $100 back instead of $25. The added travel protections may be more useful than the subscription benefits. Trip delay: Up to $500 per covered traveler for eligible expenses after a covered delay of at least six hours. Paying just the taxes on an AAdvantage award doesn’t limit reimbursement to that small cash payment. Trip cancellation and interruption: Coverage is limited to the lesser of $5,000 per trip or the covered amount paid with the card and/or AAdvantage miles. Lost baggage: Up to $3,000 per covered traveler, with a $10,000 total per trip; a lower per-bag limit applies to New York residents. Rental cars: Up to $75,000 for covered damage, for eligible rentals up to 31 days. Coverage is secondary in the U.S. and primary outside it. AAdvantage Mastercard protections begin with the refresh. Required payment methods and covered reasons differ by benefit. The card also retains up to $180 in Turo credits per calendar year, limited to $30 per eligible completed trip. You need six rentals to use the full amount, must link the card to your Turo account, and need to pay directly with it rather than through a digital wallet. There’s also 10% off eligible American Airlines Vacations packages. AAdvantage Mastercard $20,000 Spending Bonus Is Useful, But Do The Math Currently, spending $20,000 on the AAdvantage Mastercard during your cardmembership year and renewing the card earns a $125 American Airlines Flight Discount. The refresh increases that to $150. The new discount adds 0.75% of the $20,000 in spending, assuming you use its full value. The increase itself is only another 0.125%. This isn’t an automatic annual flight credit just for holding the card. Under the published terms, the certificate expires one year after concern and can’t pay award-ticket taxes. Your cardmembership year also isn’t necessarily the same as the March-to-February status year. I’d count this as an extra return if I were already putting $20,000 on the card for Loyalty Points. I’d also consider moving a little spending to finish the threshold if I were close. I wouldn’t move $20,000 away from much better earning elsewhere simply because the flight discount happens to match the annual fee. Which American Airlines Card Should You Have? Platinum Select doesn’t include Admirals Club access or a general discount on award redemptions. The higher fee and extra benefits don’t change that. For an occasional American Airlines flyer without status, I’d choose it when checked bag savings and benefits I’d actually use cover the renewal fee. The first year’s $0 annual fee and initial bonus make trying it particularly easy. For someone who already has status, or another American Airlines card, I’d compare these options: Citi® / AAdvantage® Globe™ Mastercard® [See rates and fees] The $350 annual fee buys four Admirals Club Globe passes each calendar year, among other benefits. More interesting to me, the Flight Streak Bonus earns 5,000 additional Loyalty Points after every four qualifying American Airlines flight segments, up to 15,000 per qualification year. You don’t need to put spending on Globe to earn that flight bonus. Citi® / AAdvantage® Executive World Legend Mastercard® [See rates and fees] At a $695 annual fee, this is the card for an Admirals Club membership. It also awards 10,000 bonus Loyalty Points when you reach each of 50,000, 90,000, 165,000 and 240,000 Loyalty Points in a qualification year. Those thresholds can be reached through flights, partners or spending on other American Airlines cards. Citi® / AAdvantage BusinessTM World Elite Mastercard® [See rates and fees] Business owners should compare its separate initial bonus and spending benefits. Through December 31, 2028, eligible employee-card spending earns a Loyalty Point per dollar for the employee and an additional Loyalty Point for the primary cardmember. That’s status credit for two people from the same spending, rather than two points for one person. For instance, someone holding Executive can put dining and gas purchases on Platinum Select for two miles per dollar, earn the same basic Loyalty Point per dollar, and still trigger Executive’s account-wide Loyalty Point bonuses. They’d need enough value from Platinum Select’s extra miles, benefits and flight discount to justify its separate annual fee.     Sources indicate that the card earns one Loyalty Point per dollar of eligible purchases. There’s no annual cap on that earning and no minimum flight requirement to qualify for American’s published status levels.

    Here are the thresholds, and the spending that would reach them if you earned nothing from flights, partners or separate Loyalty Point bonuses:.

    Industry observers note that american’s qualification year runs March 1 through the last day of February.If flights and other activity get you to 110,000 Loyalty Points, another $15,000 in eligible card purchases gets you to Platinum Pro. You can fill the gap with expenses you were going to incur anyway.

    The same Loyalty Points also move you toward Loyalty Point Rewards, including opportunities to select systemwide upgrades.

    In a recent development, compare the AAdvantage Mastercard with the UnitedSM Explorer Card (See rates and fees), which earns one Premier qualifying point per $20 and caps that earning at 1,000 points annually. That’s only part of the 6,000 points needed for United’s points-based Silver qualification path, which also requires at least four United or United Express flights. The similarly priced Platinum Select can take you all the way to American’s top published tier.

    Industry observers note that even Delta’s premium Reserve card takes $255,000 in purchases to earn Diamond through spending plus that one card’s annual head start. That’s 28,000 qualifying dollars, less the card’s 2,500-dollar head start, earned at one qualifying dollar per $10 spent. American’s $200,000 Executive Platinum threshold is available on this much less expensive card.

    Industry observers note that alaska’s Atmos™ Rewards Summit Visa Infinite® credit card ($395 annual fee) earns one status point per $2, without a cap, plus 10,000 status points annually beginning with the first anniversary. It can require less spending for particular tiers. American is my overall pick because of the combination of inexpensive cards, uncapped earning, and the ability to combine spending with so many other sources of status credit.

The Citi Strata Premier® Card (See rates and fees.) earns three points per dollar on airfare, hotels, restaurants, supermarkets, gas and electric vehicle charging. Its points transfer to American, and its annual fee is $95. If I just wanted redeemable American miles, I’d generally prefer Strata Premier for those categories. The value in spending on this card is progress towards AAdvantage status.     Presently, spending $20,000 on the AAdvantage Mastercard during your cardmembership year and renewing the card earns a $125 American Airlines Flight Discount. The refresh increases that to $150.

    Industry observers note that the newly introduced discount adds 0.75% of the $20,000 in spending, assuming you use its full value. The increase itself is only another 0.125%. This isn’t an automatic annual flight credit just for holding the card. Under the published terms, the certificate expires one year after issue and can’t pay award-ticket taxes. Your cardmembership year also isn’t necessarily the same as the March-to-February status year.

    I’d count this as an extra return if I were already putting $20,000 on the card for Loyalty Points. I’d also consider moving a little spending to finish the threshold if I were close. I wouldn’t move $20,000 away from much better earning elsewhere simply because the flight discount happens to match the annual fee.

    Platinum Select doesn’t include Admirals Club access or a general discount on award redemptions. The higher fee and extra benefits don’t change that. For an occasional American Airlines flyer without status, I’d choose it when checked bag savings and benefits I’d actually use cover the renewal fee. The first year’s $0 annual fee and initial bonus make trying it particularly easy. More interesting to me, the Flight Streak Bonus earns 5,000 additional Loyalty Points after every four qualifying American Airlines flight segments, up to 15,000 per qualification year. You don’t need to put spending on Globe to earn that flight bonus. Citi® / AAdvantage® Executive World Legend Mastercard® [See rates and fees] At a $695 annual fee, this is the card for an Admirals Club membership. It also awards 10,000 bonus Loyalty Points when you reach each of 50,000, 90,000, 165,000 and 240,000 Loyalty Points in a qualification year. Those thresholds can be reached through flights, partners or spending on other American Airlines cards. Citi® / AAdvantage BusinessTM World Elite Mastercard® [See rates and fees] Business owners should compare its separate initial bonus and spending benefits. Through December 31, 2028, eligible employee-card spending earns a Loyalty Point per dollar for the employee and an additional Loyalty Point for the primary cardmember. That’s status credit for two people from the same spending, rather than two points for one person. For instance, someone holding Executive can put dining and gas purchases on Platinum Select for two miles per dollar, earn the same basic Loyalty Point per dollar, and still trigger Executive’s account-wide Loyalty Point bonuses. They’d need enough value from Platinum Select’s extra miles, benefits and flight discount to justify its separate annual fee.     #123558. Appeals court stands by LaMonica McIver ruling

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (629 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rollcall ↗ Open Full Page

    Appeals court stands by LaMonica McIver ruling

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (629 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • LaMonica McIver, D-N.J., is seen on Capitol Hill last December.
    • LaMonica McIver, D-N.J., faced a setback Thursday in her effort to ditch charges tied to a scuffle during an oversight visit at an immigration detention facility last year, as a federal appeals court declined to reconsider its decision to let the case move forward.
    • According to recent reports, the decision by the U.S.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Rep. LaMonica McIver, D-N.J., is seen on Capitol Hill last December. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    In a recent development, rep. LaMonica McIver, D-N.J., faced a setback Thursday in her effort to ditch charges tied to a scuffle during an oversight visit at an immigration detention facility last year, as a federal appeals court declined to reconsider its decision to let the case move forward.

    According to recent reports, the decision by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 3rd Circuit leaves in place a 2-1 opinion from August which held that McIver was not immune from the charges, which stemmed from a confrontation between visiting members of Congress and federal agents while at the Delaney Hall facility in Newark. McIver has challenged the charges, arguing that her visit fell under the “speech or debate” immunity she has as a member of Congress because she was there to inspect detention conditions.

    Industry observers note that in a statement McIver remarked she and her attorneys were looking at “every possible option” in response to the appeals court ruling. Her statement invoked the Trump administration’s threats to treat oversight efforts as criminal conduct and said “we are all one step closer to a world in which the president of the United States can try to imprison people simply because he does not like what they stand for.”.

    Industry observers note that “Donald Trump continues to send warning shots to Democrats in Congress and in all levels of power — but their case against me right now, in broad daylight, goes well beyond a warning. Because of a weaponized Department of Justice and because I dared to do my job and conduct oversight of ICE, I am facing 17 years in prison,” McIver remarked in her statement.

    Following Thursday’s decision on rehearing, McIver could next ask the Supreme Court to weigh in on the case.

    The August majority opinion from Judge Cindy Chung, which Thursday’s decision leaves in place, said that two of the three charges against McIver did not fall under the immunity, which is limited to legislative acts. The majority sent the third charge back to the lower court for another ruling.

    “We have considered the ‘nature’ of the charged conduct and concluded it is unambiguously non-legislative,” the judge wrote.

    According to recent reports, separately, Judge Thomas Ambro partially dissented to offer a different approach to the case. Ambro would have required the trial judge to more closely examine the exact conduct McIver was charged with, as well as to examine whether the Trump administration targeted her because of her political views.

    “I would allow her discovery into the truth of the matter — not only for her own sake but to safeguard the independence of our legislative bodies,” Ambro wrote.

    Ambro did not vote on whether the full 3rd Circuit should rehear the case. Three judges voted to have the full 3rd Circuit hear McIver’s case, and Judge Emil Bove, a former Trump administration official and former personal attorney for the president, did not participate in the vote.

    The criminal case started shortly after the Delaney Hall visit in May 2025, as prosecutors alleged that McIver assaulted federal agents during a scuffle around Newark Mayor Ras Baraka. Officials arrested Baraka that day and charged him with trespassing, but later dropped those charges.

    In a recent development, court filings in the case alleged that McIver struck agents during the confrontation. McIver has argued that she was effectively being charged for doing her job and federal agents were interfering with her attempts to inspect the facility.

    It has been revealed that earlier this year, Judge Jamel K. Semper of the U.S. District Court for the District of Fresh Jersey disagreed and ruled that the case could move forward.

    First Look Inside American Airlines’ New Austin Lounge—Twice The Space, An Outdoor Terrace And Skyline Views

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3188 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Viewfromthewing

    ⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that I finally got inside American Airlines’ new Austin airport lounge this week.
    • American Airlines should be opening its New York JFK ‘Provisions’ grab ‘n go lounge for Admirals Club members in the next month, complete with barista bar.
    • According to recent reports, by the end of next year we should also see the newly introduced Austin Admiral’s Club as well.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that I finally got inside American Airlines’ new Austin airport lounge this week. It’s still a shell, but the covered outdoor terrace is already there, and you can see the downtown skyline from the west end of the lounge. The new Admirals Club will have more than twice the space of the current one, and Austin is just one of the places where American is building bigger lounges. American Airlines should be opening its New York JFK ‘Provisions’ grab ‘n go lounge for Admirals Club members in the next month, complete with barista bar. And we’ll see both the renovated Washington National D concourse and replacement Chicago O’Hare L concourse clubs next year. By the end of next year we should also see the new Austin Admiral’s Club as well. The core and shell space is about to be turned over to American by the airport, allowing them to begin construction work. The current club is small. It was perfect-sized when I moved to Austin, but Austin has grown and overall American Airlines lounge visits have increased 80% over the past decade. Expectations for food have increased, too, and the kitchen facilities are inadequate. American is replacing its current club with a new one at the west end of the airport’s main concourse. In March, American Airlines announced the details of the plan for the new club above gate 35. More than 12,000 square feet (more than double the size of the current club) With an outdoor terrace and views of both downtown and airport operations. Supporting a gate allocation that’s expected to nearly double when the new terminal opens in the early 2030s. I keep looking at the space, waiting for progress, each time I fly out of the airport. I’m anxious for the new lounge! So far there are two renderings of the space that have been made available: Credit: American Airlines Credit: American Airlines This week I had a chance to peek inside the space, see the actual views from the space and the outdoor terrace. When you come up the elevator or walk up the stairs you’ll see the entrance – they’ll be taking down a preexisting wall there, and will install e-gates which are a new club standard (like at the Philadelphia A-West club – that location also has e-gates for the Flagship business class lounge, but that won’t be a standard). The kitchen will be at the far left, back of the lounge when you enter. The full kitchen facilities will allow in-house preparation for upgraded food. Closer, also to the left but nearer the windows will be the bar. At the opposite (west) end of the lounge, you can see out towards the downtown skyline. It gives some perspective on how small Austin’s downtown really is, though it’s far more dense than it was when I first moved here. The lounge’s outdoor deck has covering and shade, and American tells me it will have misters and fans – making it much more usable throughout the year. Living in Austin we eat outdoors much of the year, though the summers can get very hot and there will be days you don’t want to be outdoors between November and February. The former Chase Terrace on the opposite end of the airport lacked covering and climate assistance. Taking photos from the lounge is a bit challenging, because of the screens that the airport installs on the window meant for birds to be able to identify the glass and not fly into the building. Nonetheless, angle the lens just right and zoom past it and your photos can come closer to what you see out the windows (you really don’t see these screens except when you’re up close to the glass). American’s Austin gate allocation goes from 4 to 9 — a 125% increase – when the new concourse opens in the early 2030s. American can use common use gates in addition today. All nine of their dedicated gates will be on the current concourse, near this new lounge. Austin is part of a larger investment American is now making in its clubs. After several years where there wasn’t any growth in its network, and they even closed some lounges, here’s the American Airlines lounge pipeline: Airport Project Timing / status Austin New Admirals Club above the west gate expansion: more than 12,000 square feet, roughly double the current club, with an outdoor terrace. Permits issued, but American hasn’t announced an opening date. Expected at the end of 2027. Charlotte New Admirals Club above the airport atrium: more than 40,000 square feet, with showers, multiple bars and food stations. 2028 anticipated. Charlotte First Flagship Lounge, separately announced from the new Admirals Club. Size and opening date haven’t been disclosed. Chicago O’Hare Replacement Concourse L Admirals Club exceeding 10,000 square feet, with more seating and airfield views. Construction underway. Existing L club stays open during the work. No opening date announced. Dallas–Fort Worth New Terminal C Admirals Club: 37,000 square feet near the Skylink station. No opening date disclosed. Dallas–Fort Worth Terminal F Provisions by Admirals Club, the initial lounge offering in a broader premium-space program for the new terminal. Planned for Terminal F’s first phase. Later premium spaces and individual opening dates haven’t been shared. Miami New Flagship Lounge and expanded D30 Admirals Club. The current Flagship space becomes Admirals Club space, nearly doubling American’s total lounge footprint at the airport. No opening date disclosed. Nashville Replacement Admirals Club in the new Concourse A: about 17,400 square feet including outdoor terraces and an interior balcony, replacing the current roughly 7,000 square foot club. Construction expected to begin in 2027. No firm opening date announced. New York JFK Provisions by Admirals Club in Terminal 8: 3,700 square feet near gates 12–14, with hot and cold food, a dedicated barista bar and customer assistance. Targeted for December 2026. Phoenix Expansion and refresh of all three Terminal 4 Admirals Clubs. Near term work at A19–A21 improves food service. The B5–B7 club gets 20% more seats. Longer term, the two A clubs nearly triple their combined space and add approximately 150% more seats. Announced November 2026. No completion dates disclosed. San Antonio First Admirals Club in new Terminal C. Airport aims specify a 10,000 square foot American Airlines lounge. Documented by the airport, no formal American lounge announcement yet. Terminal C targets mid-2028, but no separate lounge opening date. Washington National Rebuilt Concourse D Admirals Club: more than 10,000 square feet and approximately 50% more seats. Expected to deliver in 2027. The real treat in Austin, though, isn’t the design or that there will be an outdoor deck – it’s the staff in the Austin club who are the absolute best in the system. They know the names of all regulars on sight and welcome you into the lounge. They work magic with itineraries – and they keep working that magic even once you’ve left, frequently bird dogging inventory and improving connections even after you’ve left the lounge. When I’ve had flights cancelled and could only get a long connection in Dallas or Charlotte, I’ve found myself landing to notes saying they’ve gotten me on an earlier flight because space opened up. They do this for everyone. It’s a small city, personal customer service feel even in a growing market. And that makes Admirals Club membership (and Citi® / AAdvantage® Executive World Legend Mastercard® [See rates and fees] cardmembership) worth it. The Austin club space will finally match the service once this lounge opens. I genuinely cannot wait for the lounge to open because it’ll make flying American Airlines out of my home airport that much better.     #123556. Industry News: KLM Offloaded A Passenger Rather Than Use The Blocked Seat We Offered

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (697 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Onemileatatime ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: KLM Offloaded A Passenger Rather Than Use The Blocked Seat We Offered

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (697 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • I recently flew KLM from Amsterdam to Barcelona, and a passenger was taken off our full flight even though my wife and I offered him the empty seat between us.
    • Business class inside Europe is basically a regular economy seat with the middle seat blocked.
    • I was on KL1519 on 2 September, in row 2 with my wife, with that empty middle seat between us.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    I recently flew KLM from Amsterdam to Barcelona, and a passenger was taken off our full flight even though my wife and I offered him the empty seat between us. The crew followed a rule exactly, and as far as I can tell, nobody got anything out of it.

    Business class inside Europe is basically a regular economy seat with the middle seat blocked. On some planes the middle seat is physically blocked with a small table. On this flight it was just empty, blocked online so nobody could book it, but technically a regular seat anyone could sit in.

    I was on KL1519 on 2 September, in row 2 with my wife, with that empty middle seat between us.

    It has been revealed that after the doors closed, it turned out that two passengers had boarding passes for the same seat. Whoever got there first sat down. The other one was a fairly young guy, and now he had nowhere to sit. The flight was completely full, there wasn’t a single free seat in economy.

    I heard the crew apologizing to him and saying they would have to take him off the plane and put him on the next flight.

    According to recent reports, I knew this would take a while, because the doors were already closed and he had boarded. Getting him off meant opening the doors again, and maybe taking his bag off too. Once on another flight someone got off and everyone had to hold up their bags.

    In a recent development, and I felt sorry for the guy. Maybe he was in a hurry to get somewhere, and none of this was his fault. The airline gave two people boarding passes for one seat, and he was already on board.

    So I asked my wife if she minded giving up the empty seat between us. The flight is only about two hours. She was fine with it, so I went to the crew and offered it.

    The crew was very grateful, but said seating someone there was against the rules and they couldn’t decide it themselves, they had to check with someone.

    That took about 10 minutes. Then they came back, thanked me again, and said that unfortunately it wasn’t possible under the rules.

    Industry observers note that so they opened the doors and offloaded the guy, I hope they rebooked him on the next one. In the end we pushed back about 40 minutes late and landed in Barcelona about half an hour late. After landing I think even the captain came over, shook my hand and thanked me.

    According to recent reports, as I understand it, the middle seat is blocked to give the business class passengers more space. In this case that was us, and we were the ones offering to give that space up.

    We didn’t need the space, and we’d have put up with one more person in the row for two hours.

    It has been revealed that on a completely full KLM flight, two passengers got boarding passes for the same seat. My wife and I offered the empty blocked seat between us in business, so he wouldn’t have to get off. The crew checked with someone, the answer was no, and he was offloaded anyway, and we left about 40 minutes late.

    I get that the crew couldn’t make this call themselves. Still, we didn’t need that seat at all.

    Is there a good reason for this rule that I’m missing?

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that malaysia Airlines has just placed a upcoming aircraft order, as the airline will be adding a new wide body aircraft type to its fleet.
    • Industry observers note that malaysia Airlines has placed its first-ever Dreamliner order, as the airline will be taking delivery of up to 16 Boeing 787-10s.
    • According to recent reports, for context, the 787-10 is the largest variant of the Dreamliner.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that malaysia Airlines has just placed a upcoming aircraft order, as the airline will be adding a new wide body aircraft type to its fleet. This seems logical enough, even if the carrier’s long haul fleet seems rather diversified at this point.

    Industry observers note that malaysia Airlines has placed its first-ever Dreamliner order, as the airline will be taking delivery of up to 16 Boeing 787-10s. This includes a firm order for 10 jets, plus options for six more, with deliveries expected between 2032 and 2035.

    According to recent reports, for context, the 787-10 is the largest variant of the Dreamliner. While it has the least range of any 787 variant, the per-seat economics are great, given how it’s “stretched.” While some airlines have started to use the 787-10 for high capacity regional routes, Malaysia Airlines is taking a different approach.

    In a recent development, the oneworld carrier intends to use these planes to support its long haul fleet modernization and international expansion, including routes to Europe, along with destinations throughout Asia-Pacific. The airline points out how long haul demand to and from Southeast Asia has increased by more than 50% over the past decade.

    Here’s how Malaysia Airlines Group CEO Nasaruddin Bakar describes this:.

    “The acquisition of the 787 Dreamliner represents a strategic investment in the future of Malaysia Aviation Group. As we look ahead to the next phase of growth, these aircraft will strengthen our ability to serve key international markets with greater capacity, efficiency and flexibility, while delivering the elevated travel experience our customers expect. Beyond fleet renewal, this investment reinforces our commitment to maintaining a modern, competitive airline that supports Malaysia’s connectivity and global aspirations.”.

    It has been revealed that for context, Malaysia Airlines at the moment has a fleet of just over 90 aircraft, with another 75 aircraft on firm order. As it stands, Malaysia Airlines has:.

    Now the airline has the following planes on firm order:.

    A few things stand out here. First of all, it’s cool to see Malaysia Airlines growing again, after a rather rough… what, nearly 15 years? At this point the airline has enough planes on order to both replace its previous generation fleet, and expand. I’d expect the 16 A330ceos will be retired at some point in the coming years, and more than replaced by the A330neos that remain on order. Furthermore, the 737-800s will all be replaced by the 737 MAXs.

    The 787-10 is an incredible plane in terms of economics, especially as Boeing has been able to make incremental range improvements, turning it into a true long haul aircraft.

    At the same time, I can’t help but feel like it’s unusual how the airline has just seven A350s, with no more on order, and is now switching to the 787 for fleet renewal. Admittedly the A350 was ordered back in the day under a completely different management team, which also at one point thought the A380 was a good fit for the airline.

    So I am curious how the carrier’s fleet evolves. Will the seven A350s stick around, or will they eventually just be replaced by 787-10s? Even with airspace restrictions and headwinds, it seems like all of Malaysia Airlines’ routes should be within range for the 787-10, though admittedly London (LHR) might be on the cusp, depending on how airspace closures evolve, how dense of a configuration the airline selects, etc.

    According to recent reports, the big challenge with the airline industry is that it’s never static, and decisions aren’t made in a vacuum. One management team makes one decision, and then a management team later on can’t just undo what the other management team did, without it being costly. So I get that they’re doing what they can….

    In a recent development, malaysia Airlines is the newest customer for the Boeing 787, as the airline has ordered up to 16 787-10s, including 10 firm orders and six options. The airline looks to use this for a long haul expansion to Europe, as well as for flights in Asia-Pacific.

    It’s cool to see Malaysia Airlines continuing to grow, as the carrier has quite the order book at this point. I am curious if the airline keeps around the seven A350s in the long run, or how the airline manages its three wide body aircraft types.

    What do you make of Malaysia Airlines’ Boeing 787-10 order?

    #123553. Maine senators at odds over credit for earmarks

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (940 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rollcall ↗ Open Full Page

    Maine senators at odds over credit for earmarks

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (940 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Collins took sole responsibility for a larger share of Maine earmarks.
    • After a bruising reelection defeat, Senate Appropriations Chair Susan Collins, R-Maine, is ready to play hardball.
    • Eager to show how much she's delivered for her constituents, Collins took the lion's share of credit in her committee's fiscal 2027 spending bills for Maine earmarks — at the expense of her delegation colleague, independent Angus King, who caucuses with Democrats.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Collins took sole responsibility for a larger share of Maine earmarks. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    After a bruising reelection defeat, Senate Appropriations Chair Susan Collins, R-Maine, is ready to play hardball.

    Eager to show how much she's delivered for her constituents, Collins took the lion's share of credit in her committee's fiscal 2027 spending bills for Maine earmarks — at the expense of her delegation colleague, independent Angus King, who caucuses with Democrats.

    The amount of earmarks King secured fell dramatically compared to his previous year's total in Senate Appropriations Committee bills, as Collins took sole credit for most earmarks both senators had requested.

    It has been revealed that the power play has instigated a dispute over how to award credit for "congressionally directed spending," better known as earmarks. It has also raised questions about a Senate rule that requires committee leaders to disclose the name of each senator who requested projects to be included in a spending bill before it can move on the floor.

    It’s undeniable that as the chair of the spending panel, Collins has more influence over which projects reach the final bills than her delegation mate. Collins spokesperson Phoebe Keller said that since available earmark funding is split into separate pots for the majority and minority to dole out, the bills reflect which of those funding sources was tapped to provide money to the relevant projects.

    Keller said that Collins deserves sole credit for the contested projects, as listed in the reports accompanying the bills.

    "When only Collins is listed, it reflects only she chose to fund the project,” Keller noted.

    A Democratic committee aide contested that characterization, saying that traditionally all requesters are named regardless of which party’s funding allocation is tapped for a project.

    “The handling of these particular projects is a clear departure from the norm and will need to be rectified in conference negotiations,” the aide remarked.

    King is credited with approximately $54 million in fiscal 2027 earmarks in the bills Collins released this month, including joint projects with Collins. That's down from around $231 million in the Senate's fiscal 2026 bills, according to a CQ Roll Call analysis.

    Last year, King and Collins were both listed on 75 of the 77 projects that both requested that were included in the Senate bills, with just two carrying only Collins’ name. This year, Collins claimed sole responsibility for over $125 million in projects that both she and King requested, approximately two-thirds of the joint requests.

    While King’s overall requests fell by more than $200 million this year versus last, his success in securing requested funds plummeted at a far greater rate with less credit for overlapping projects.

    The joint requests for which Collins claimed sole credit include five for the Maine Department of Transportation in the Transportation-HUD bill, including $10.7 million for northern freight rail improvements; $9.6 million for Route 26 reconstruction in Oxford; and $7.2 million for improvements in Rockport, among others.

    In the Labor-HHS-Education bill, projects Collins took sole credit for include $4 million for the University of Maine for biology laboratory equipment and just over $4 million for the creation of a modern emergency helipad at Lincoln Hospital.

    And the Interior-Environment bill features $4 million each for wastewater improvements in Limestone and Kennebec that both Collins and King asked for but are only attributed to Collins, among others.

    Similarly, the Agriculture, Commerce-Justice-Science and Homeland Security bills all include a project requested by both senators that only Collins is listed as securing in the bill.

    The outgoing Appropriations chair’s ability to fuel billions of dollars in federal funding for her state during her career was the centerpiece of her ultimately unsuccessful campaign for reelection, which she lost to Democrat Troy Jackson.

    As written, the draft bills appear to risk running afoul of a Senate rule that requires the committee’s chair to identify each senator who requested projects in a bill online at least 48 hours before a vote to advance the legislation on the floor.

    Industry observers note that the relevant rule, Senate Rule 44, states that it is out of order to vote on a motion to proceed to consider a bill unless the chairman of the committee certifies that “each congressionally directed spending item . . . has been identified through lists, charts, or other similar means including the name of each Senator who submitted a request to the committee for each item so identified.”.

    That information must be “available on a publicly accessible congressional website in a searchable format at least 48 hours before such vote.”.

    A King spokesman called on the spending panel to add his name to the relevant requests.

    “We believe this must have been an oversight and assume the committee will update the requests —per Senate rules — once it’s called to their attention,” King spokesman Matthew Felling said.

    According to recent reports, the bills released by Collins are drafts, and no floor action on final fiscal 2027 spending bills is expected this Congress. There’s limited time left before the Dec. 11 spending deadline, when all current funding is set to expire, and Democrats want to wait to negotiate final bills until they retake majorities in both chambers next year.

    But to comply with the rule, before the bills reach the floor the reports accompanying the bills, that includes the earmark tables, may have to be rewritten to list King on the contested projects, or the committee may need to disclose the information elsewhere online.

    Both chambers unveiled stricter ethics guidelines surrounding earmarks in 2021 when the practice returned after a decade-long ban.

    Peter Cohn contributed to this report.

    #123551. Ryanair Flew 208 Million Passengers At An Average Fare Of $56—Now Its Rivals Want It Grounded For Not Being European Enough

    📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2597 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Viewfromthewing ↗ Open Full Page

    Ryanair Flew 208 Million Passengers At An Average Fare Of $56—Now Its Rivals Want It Grounded For Not Being European Enough

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2597 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Viewfromthewing

    ⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, A trade group representing Lufthansa, Air France and KLM has gone to court in Ireland to challenge Ryanair’s right to fly.
    • European investors hold just 30% of Ryanair’s shares.
    • The European Network Airlines Association says it asked the European Commission and national regulators to check Ryanair’s ownership after the airline loosened its share purchase rules.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, A trade group representing Lufthansa, Air France and KLM has gone to court in Ireland to challenge Ryanair’s right to fly. Their objection is to who owns the airline that carried 208 million passengers at an average fare of just €51 in the year ended March 31. European investors hold just 30% of Ryanair’s shares. Competitors say they run afoul of foreign ownership rules, but those European investors exercise 100% voting control of the ariline. I don’t see Europe grounding Ryanair. I do see why its competitors might like want to pick this fight. The European Network Airlines Association says it asked the European Commission and national regulators to check Ryanair’s ownership after the airline loosened its share purchase rules. That didn’t get them what they wanted so they sued the Irish Aviation Authority. On November 16, the judge declined to add Lufthansa, Air France and KLM as parties to the case, though they can submit affidavits. A hearing is scheduled for December 16. Who Owns Ryanair, And Who Gets Control? Brexit turned British shareholders into foreign investors without anybody having to sell a share. Since January 2021, nonqualifying shareholders haven’t been allowed to attend, speak or vote at Ryanair shareholder meetings. On March 7, 2025, Ryanair let them buy ordinary shares in Dublin again. It kept the voting ban, including for any votes the chairman might otherwise cast on their behalf. Ryanair says the change opened the door to inclusion in stock indexes. Its board said it would restrict purchases again if European ownership fell to 20%. . At both March 31 and September 30 this year, Ryanair put qualifying European ownership at 30%. That includes investors from Norway, Iceland, Liechtenstein and Switzerland. Shares held through its U.S. depositary are generally non-qualifying. Here’s who shows up in Ryanair’s March 31 shareholder disclosure. Reported holder    Share of Ryanair Capital Group 14.6% MFS 4.7% Artisan Partners 4.5% Michael O’Leary 4.0% BlackRock 4.0% Fidelity 3.3% By October, Capital Group reported 15.70% for client accounts, and T. Rowe Price reported 3.00%. O’Leary’s 4% economic stake translates to 13% voting control. Does It Matter More Who Owns The Shares Or Who Controls The Airline? European law requires both. Qualifying states or their nationals have to own more than half the airline and effectively control it. Giving Europeans every vote solves the legal concern of control. The key legal question here is whether shares that carry no voting rights count as equity for the ownership test. European regulators have allowed this in the past. Wizz Air says British and Hungarian regulators approved its plan to suspend some foreign shareholders’ votes after Brexit so Wizz Air Hungary could keep its European license. easyJet just did this in a takeover vote. When shareholders approved an Apollo deal on November 11, qualifying Europeans owned 35.07% of easyJet. It suspended voting rights on 233,921,894 shares. Those shareholders keep their dividend rights. The proposed deal itself caps Apollo’s ordinary equity at 49.9%. But this is complicated. A 1995 Swissair–Sabena decision found that Swissair held 49.5% of the Belgian airline’s voting shares, plus special certificates that the European Commission agreed to leave out of the ownership calculation. Those certificates had no votes, generally paid at least 5% and gave Swissair no share of the assets left over in liquidation. That looked like debt. In contrast, a Ryanair shareholder who can’t vote still collects dividends (which aren’t fixed) and gains or loses money on fluctuations of the stock. What Happens If Ryanair Loses? If all the ordinary shares count, Ryanair has to get qualifying ownership above 50%. That’s 207 million existing shares moving from non-European to European owners (assuming they don’t issue newly introduced shares). The airline’s articles of incorporation allow it to direct restricted holders to sell to qualifying investors. This is being framed in some quarters as Ryanair having to shut down. That doesn’t seem likely. I’ve been writing about foreign airline ownership since 2003. If someone abroad is willing to put up the money for more planes and cheaper flights, what does the passenger gain by turning them away? If Europe needs aircraft and crews available for defense, it can pay airlines to provide them. Forcing a British retiree to sell Ryanair stock to a Frenchman doesn’t add aircraft that Europe can use for its defense. It does, however, give Lufthansa and Air France a way to raise a competitor’s cost of capital. So it’s decent return on trade association dues.     #123550. Industry News: House Democrats eye stock trading ban as early priority next Congress

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1328 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rollcall ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: House Democrats eye stock trading ban as early priority next Congress

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1328 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, here at a news conference on Capitol Hill last week, claims banning stock trading in Congress is a “high priority.” Now Democrats must decide what form their push will take.
    • After stock trading became a major talking point on the campaign trail this fall, Democrats are feeling pressure to push through a bill in the latest year.
    • But banning trading by members of Congress may not be easy, and some worry the matter could get bogged down in larger debates over the party’s anti-corruption agenda.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, here at a news conference on Capitol Hill last week, claims banning stock trading in Congress is a “high priority.” Now Democrats must decide what form their push will take. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    After stock trading became a major talking point on the campaign trail this fall, Democrats are feeling pressure to push through a bill in the latest year.

    But banning trading by members of Congress may not be easy, and some worry the matter could get bogged down in larger debates over the party’s anti-corruption agenda.

    Sources indicate that “I’d rather have it be a clean bill focused on stock trading, and not muddy it by adding other topics, even if they’re good policies,” said Rep. Seth Magaziner, D-R.I.

    The incoming majority could plant a flag on government accountability with a broad package ranging from insider trading to campaign finance and more. Or they could zoom in on the stocks issue with a standalone bill.

    Magaziner noted he hasn’t received any assurances from House Democratic leaders, instead describing a “collaborative conversation” about what form the legislation could take.

    “I worry that it would get weighed down under its own weight if you try to load it up with too many things,” Magaziner said, while stressing he would support whatever expected incoming Speaker Hakeem Jeffries decides.

    Meanwhile, more than half of the Democrats in the incoming freshman class are calling for action on Day One of the new Congress, sending a letter to Jeffries last week suggesting they make a “down payment on much-needed reform” by changing House rules to curb stock trading.

    In a recent development, “Democrats may have won the election, but we have a long way to go to earn back the trust of voters across the country,” reads the letter, led by Reps.-elect Sarah Trone Garriott of Iowa and Jamie Ager of North Carolina. “A stock trading ban alone will not fix Washington, but it is the fastest way to show voters we heard them.”.

    In a recent development, folding new language into the House’s internal rules would be a relatively easy path, requiring just a majority vote on the House floor, instead of passage in both chambers and the president’s signature. But such internal limits wouldn’t have the force of law, and some believe it would cool the urgency around the concern while doing little to crack down on insider trading.

    Colorado Rep. Jason Crow said moving forward quickly with a rule change wouldn’t preclude passing a bill, suggesting his fellow Democrats do both.

    Recent findings suggest that “I want to pursue a parallel track,” mentioned Crow, who co-chairs the End Corruption Caucus. “We want to move via rule and just prohibit it right out of the gate, or as much as we can.”.

    Jeffries has repeatedly mentioned the topic is high on his to-do list as he looks to deliver on the accountability the “American people are demanding.”.

    “We’re committed to making sure we pass legislation that bans members of Congress from trading stocks. That will be a high priority,” he remarked at a news conference this week.

    But with more than two dozen different bills on the topic introduced over the past few years alone, lawmakers will have to decide exactly what a “ban” means to them.

    According to recent reports, some want to force members of Congress to fully offload their stocks with the exception of widely held mutual funds. Other proposals would block lawmakers from buying upcoming stocks but allow them to keep the ones they already own, like a Republican-led bill that passed the House earlier this year but stalled in the Senate.

    Democrats resisted that push, which was led by outgoing House Administration Chair Bryan Steil, R-Wis., partly because it included an unrelated voter ID provision they called a “poison pill.” Many also complained the measure didn’t go far enough, extending to members’ spouses and dependent children but leaving out key figures in other branches of government, such as the president.

    Recent findings suggest that rep. Pramila Jayapal, D-Wash., said she wants to stay close to the text of a consensus bill she hammered out last year with a small bipartisan group that included Magaziner and Reps. Chip Roy, R-Texas, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., Tim Burchett, R-Tenn., and Brian Fitzpatrick, R-Pa.

    “That is the most comprehensive, thorough, thoughtful proposal and bipartisan proposal that we have,” she stated of the bill, dubbed the Restore Trust in Congress Act.

    Sources indicate that that measure would not apply to President Donald Trump, as many Democrats have urged as they seek to draw attention to his ballooning wealth while in office. Still, Jayapal suggested a presidential stock trading ban could be moved separately.

    “There is discussion about the president, vice president, Cabinet, Supreme Court. I know we’re working on some language around enforcement, around those pieces, but I actually think that can be a separate bill,” Jayapal said. “We want to hold everyone accountable — but at minimum, we have to do ourselves.”.

    Sources indicate that it’s not clear how much appetite will exist next year for a bipartisan compromise that could realistically clear a 60-vote cloture threshold in the Senate. Notably, key Republicans who worked on the consensus bill will be leaving Congress, with Roy losing a primary bid for Texas attorney general and Fitzpatrick unseated by a Democratic challenger.

    While lawmakers could in theory advance a new stock-trading bill even sooner, before Democrats take control of both chambers, time and patience is short in the lame-duck session.

    At a news conference at the Capitol earlier this week with Crow and Jayapal, a group of freshman and returning Democrats took matters into their own hands, promising not to hold or trade individual stocks as part of a broader pledge backed by the Political Integrity Project.

    “My district, New York 10, happens to include Wall Street, but I don’t represent Wall Street. I represent the people of Brooklyn and Manhattan who deserve someone who goes to work every single day and shows right up front, ‘I work for you.’ And what better way to prove that than by day one showing we will ban members of Congress from enriching themselves, from trading stocks?” Rep.-elect Brad Lander remarked.

    In a recent development, while momentum has grown in recent years as key senior lawmakers softened their resistance to a stock trading bill, not everyone is on board. Some members still argue, whether publicly or privately, that they should be able to trade on the stock market just like other citizens or that existing disclosure requirements established by a 2012 law are already enough to discourage dubious trades.

    According to recent reports, as they iron out the legislative text of any new bill, members will have to decide how to handle emerging topics such as prediction markets and crypto, along with sticky questions such as whether to allow blind trusts. And extending restrictions to the president could be a nonstarter for many Republicans.

    Sources indicate that sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., said Democrats in the next Congress should look to a bipartisan bill that advanced out of the Senate Homeland and Governmental Affairs Committee in July 2025 as a model.

    Recent findings suggest that “The legislation we passed out of the committee applied to the executive branch,” he mentioned. “But it didn’t take effect for anybody until their next terms, which was a compromise.”.

    Sources indicate that that proposal would apply to future presidents but not the current one, potentially freeing up more Republicans to vote for it without angering Trump. Still, it hasn’t seen action on the Senate floor.

    Hawley mentioned that while he’d like to see a “full ban on trading and holding” in Congress, he would be open to a weaker proposal in the interest of getting something done.

    “I’ll take anything that’s an incremental improvement over what we have now, which is nothing,” he said.

    Aris Folley contributed to this report.

    #123549. Delta Flight Attendants May Get Their First Union Vote Since 2010 — But Saying Yes Could Mean Smaller Paychecks

    📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 33m • 📚 Deep Dive (6521 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Viewfromthewing ↗ Open Full Page

    Delta Flight Attendants May Get Their First Union Vote Since 2010 — But Saying Yes Could Mean Smaller Paychecks

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 33 min read (6521 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Viewfromthewing

    ⏱️ ~33 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that delta Air Lines flight attendants could be on the cusp of unionizing, but creating a union may be a card best kept in reserve – rather than one they should actually play.
    • It has been revealed that AFA-CWA union head Sara Nelson claims she’s close to the card count her union wants before asking for a vote at Delta Air Lines.
    • Nelson told Sumers she’s close to the union’s private target, which is above 50%.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that delta Air Lines flight attendants could be on the cusp of unionizing, but creating a union may be a card best kept in reserve – rather than one they should actually play. It can be a useful stalking horse, where the airline pays up generously to keep its crew from unionizing. But once they actually pull the trigger, there’s little reason – or ability – to continue paying above industry wages. AFA-CWA union head Sara Nelson says she’s close to the card count her union wants before asking for a vote at Delta Air Lines. Brian Sumers came away from their November 12 interview at the Skift Aviation Forum thinking she’ll get an election and win it. A vote in 2027 is a real possibility. If I were Delta crew I’d vote no. The union would get about 30,000 flight attendants to represent. Crews who already get better than what other airline unions bargain for could wind up taking home less. Nelson told Sumers she’s close to the union’s private target, which is above 50%. The National Mediation Board needs valid cards from at least half the eligible flight attendants, and a card more than a year old won’t count. Delta organizers put the minimum at roughly 15,000 signatures. Once there’s an election, a majority of valid votes cast decides it. Nelson also mentioned she was months away in 2024. Later that November organizers said they were weeks from having the cards. Delta flight attendants have rejected representation three times, but the vote after the Northwest merger was close. In 2010, 9,544 voted against representation and 9,216 voted for it. Sumers says he hears more confidence from Nelson this time. She can pick when to file, and a loss would normally mean waiting a year to try again while cards expire. If Nelson files with a comfortable cushion above the threshold, that would give her the edge in an election. Delta’s Pay Advantage Is Profit Sharing American Airlines and United Airlines now pay slightly higher hourly rates at the top of the flight pay scale. It’s $86.32 per flight hour at Delta, $87.04 at American and $87.47 at United. At 80 flight hours a month, United’s $1.15 advantage is about $1,100 a year in base pay.For newer hires, Delta starts a little higher than both. But Delta flight attendants actually make quite a bit more. Delta paid out $1.3 billion in February for 2025, or 8.9% of eligible earnings. United recorded $704 million for profit sharing and associated payroll taxes for the same year. Delta calculates that a flight attendant working 80 flight hours a month makes $5,100 more than United for a new hire and $6,200 at the top of the scale, including United’s retro pay attributable to 2026. United got boarding pay in its new deal. It kept a its inferior profit sharing formula. Delta puts 10% of the first $2.5 billion of eligible pretax profit into the pool and 20% above that. At United, the 20% rate kicks in only on earnings above the previous year’s. American negotiated the Delta thresholds and still has much smaller checks because American Airlines doesn’t make money. . The Delta campaign’s website still lists $50 a month in dues and says they’d start after flight attendants ratify a first contract. The union’s board raised the standard rate to $65.36 in June so Delta’s cabin crew are being sold a lower cost than they’d actually face. That’s $784 a year, or about $23.5 million in gross annual dues from 30,000 flight attendants. Union Flight Attendants Go A Long Time Between Raises Delta gave its flight attendants a 4% raise in June, its fifth annual increase in a row (there was a pause for the depths of the pandemic, when Delta didn’t furlough anyone while unionized American and United furloughed tens of thousands). United’s old wage table last went up in 2020. The contract became amendable in August 2021, and the next general raise took effect May 31, 2026 with the new contract. Consumer prices went up about 29% between September 2020 and May 2026. A senior United flight attendant was still on $67.11 per flight hour just before the new deal. It took more than $86 by then just to buy what $67.11 did in 2020. Airline labor contracts become amendable and the old terms generally stay in force while the parties bargain. The National Mediation Board can release the parties from mediation, normally starting a 30 day cooling off period before the union can strike or the airline can impose new terms. In practice that hasn’t happened for flight attendants since 1993. Nelson said at Skift that she wants more frequent bargaining to deliver smaller, more regular raises. Why It Took So Long To Pay For Boarding Delta started paying for scheduled boarding time in 2022 at half the flight hourly rate. I wrote then that the organizing drive probably helped get it done. American added boarding pay in 2024 and United now uses the same half-rate approach as Delta. At Hawaiian Airlines, the same union asked for boarding pay and came away without it in its 2025 extension. AFA-CWA hadn’t gotten it at Spirit, either. There’s a reason boarding pay is a bigger deal to junior crew. Fly three short flights and you board three airplanes. Fly one long trip with the same flight hours and you board once. If the airline’s putting a limited amount of money on the table, the senior flight attendant who can bid the long trips generally does better with a higher flight rate. A junior flight attendant gets more out of a separate boarding premium. Both have to live with what the bargaining committee prioritizes. Boarding pay didn’t happen until non-union Delta did it because unions are often about dividing a fixed pie of spoils between members, rather than getting more from the airline. Senior crew preferred higher hourly rates, redistributing income up to them from more junior crew. Once Delta did it, though, that changed the dynamic and flight attendant unions had to re-prioritize their bargaining. What Delta And Its Crews Have To Lose I generally find Delta’s crew a little friendlier and more interested in getting the service right. Southwest Airlines has some of the friendliest flight attendants in the business and they’re unionized. Southwest has always hired for the right attitude. At Delta, part of the advantage comes from being able to change how the cabin runs and reward the people doing the work. The union’s first contract policy calls for writing existing work rules into a contract. If new rules make it harder to run the operation or deliver service that passengers pay extra for, Delta has less money and profit sharing falls. Bear in mind also that while the union says they protect workers from management, sometimes it’s the union that a flight attendant needs protection from. I covered United firing two union representatives after the airline concluded they’d solicited false complaints against a flight attendant who raised a safety concern. The union sued over United’s investigation of the reps and a federal judge dismissed its suit. At Southwest, four flight attendants faced internal charges for allegedly trying to replace their union. Another flight attendant won $1 million after the union got the airline to fire her. Alaska Airlines flight attendants, meanwhile, have been suing saying that the union pushed htem out over their Christianity and views on LGBT rights. If Delta flight attendants vote down a first contract, they’re still stuck with the union. If union leaders don’t follow the wishes of flight attendants, they’re still stuck with the union (and they don’t actually have direct say in how the parent union is governed). To go back to representing themselves, they’d normally have to wait two years from certification, get valid cards from at least half the workgroup and then win another election. Union organizers at Delta pitch that they’d take current pay, benefits and work rules and negotiate up from there. That’s not how any of this works. The current union status and bundle they receive today is all bundled together. A union deal would be ex nihilo and more like other airlines. There are tradeoffs between their pay and work rules. Someone working at Delta might prefer a different arrangement (though they should remember why they chose Delta over others in the first place). But it’s a different arrangement. At some airlines I’d take that deal. At Delta, flight attendants already have it better than at their peers. They have better pay and a product they’re proud of. Sara Nelson wants them to give her union their money – and possibly wind up taking home less. Since it’s virtually an irreversible decision, that’s not a button I’d push. It seems like a decision to make only when things are dire, not when they’re going well relative to peers.
