    Industry observers note that but Delta flight attendants actually make quite a bit more. Delta paid out $1.3 billion in February for 2025, or 8.9% of eligible earnings. United recorded $704 million for profit sharing and associated payroll taxes for the same year.

    Delta calculates that a flight attendant working 80 flight hours a month makes $5,100 more than United for a new hire and $6,200 at the top of the scale, including United’s retro pay attributable to 2026.

    United got boarding pay in its fresh deal. It kept a its inferior profit sharing formula. Delta puts 10% of the first $2.5 billion of eligible pretax profit into the pool and 20% above that. At United, the 20% rate kicks in only on earnings above the previous year’s. American negotiated the Delta thresholds and still has much smaller checks because American Airlines doesn’t make money. .

    Recent findings suggest that the Delta campaign’s website still lists $50 a month in dues and says they’d start after flight attendants ratify a first contract. The union’s board raised the standard rate to $65.36 in June so Delta’s cabin crew are being sold a lower cost than they’d actually face. That’s $784 a year, or about $23.5 million in gross annual dues from 30,000 flight attendants.

    Delta gave its flight attendants a 4% raise in June, its fifth annual increase in a row (there was a pause for the depths of the pandemic, when Delta didn’t furlough anyone while unionized American and United furloughed tens of thousands). United’s old wage table last went up in 2020. The contract became amendable in August 2021, and the next general raise took effect May 31, 2026 with the fresh contract. Consumer prices went up about 29% between September 2020 and May 2026. A senior United flight attendant was still on $67.11 per flight hour just before the new deal. It took more than $86 by then just to buy what $67.11 did in 2020. Airline labor contracts become amendable and the old terms generally stay in force while the parties bargain. The National Mediation Board can release the parties from mediation, normally starting a 30 day cooling off period before the union can strike or the airline can impose new terms. In practice that hasn’t happened for flight attendants since 1993. Nelson said at Skift that she wants more frequent bargaining to deliver smaller, more regular raises. Why It Took So Long To Pay For Boarding Delta started paying for scheduled boarding time in 2022 at half the flight hourly rate. I wrote then that the organizing drive probably helped get it done. American added boarding pay in 2024 and United now uses the same half-rate approach as Delta. At Hawaiian Airlines, the same union asked for boarding pay and came away without it in its 2025 extension. AFA-CWA hadn’t gotten it at Spirit, either. There’s a reason boarding pay is a bigger deal to junior crew. Fly three short flights and you board three airplanes. Fly one long trip with the same flight hours and you board once. If the airline’s putting a limited amount of money on the table, the senior flight attendant who can bid the long trips generally does better with a higher flight rate. A junior flight attendant gets more out of a separate boarding premium. Both have to live with what the bargaining committee prioritizes. Boarding pay didn’t happen until non-union Delta did it because unions are often about dividing a fixed pie of spoils between members, rather than getting more from the airline. Senior crew preferred higher hourly rates, redistributing income up to them from more junior crew. Once Delta did it, though, that changed the dynamic and flight attendant unions had to re-prioritize their bargaining. What Delta And Its Crews Have To Lose I generally find Delta’s crew a little friendlier and more interested in getting the service right. Southwest Airlines has some of the friendliest flight attendants in the business and they’re unionized. Southwest has always hired for the right attitude. At Delta, part of the advantage comes from being able to change how the cabin runs and reward the people doing the work. The union’s first contract policy calls for writing existing work rules into a contract. If new rules make it harder to run the operation or deliver service that passengers pay extra for, Delta has less money and profit sharing falls. Bear in mind also that while the union says they protect workers from management, sometimes it’s the union that a flight attendant needs protection from. I covered United firing two union representatives after the airline concluded they’d solicited false complaints against a flight attendant who raised a safety concern. The union sued over United’s investigation of the reps and a federal judge dismissed its suit. At Southwest, four flight attendants faced internal charges for allegedly trying to replace their union. Another flight attendant won $1 million after the union got the airline to fire her. Alaska Airlines flight attendants, meanwhile, have been suing saying that the union pushed htem out over their Christianity and views on LGBT rights. If Delta flight attendants vote down a first contract, they’re still stuck with the union. If union leaders don’t follow the wishes of flight attendants, they’re still stuck with the union (and they don’t actually have direct say in how the parent union is governed). To go back to representing themselves, they’d normally have to wait two years from certification, get valid cards from at least half the workgroup and then win another election. Union organizers at Delta pitch that they’d take current pay, benefits and work rules and negotiate up from there. That’s not how any of this works. The current union status and bundle they receive today is all bundled together. A union deal would be ex nihilo and more like other airlines. There are tradeoffs between their pay and work rules. Someone working at Delta might prefer a different arrangement (though they should remember why they chose Delta over others in the first place). But it’s a different arrangement. At some airlines I’d take that deal. At Delta, flight attendants already have it better than at their peers. They have better pay and a product they’re proud of. Sara Nelson wants them to give her union their money – and possibly wind up taking home less. Since it’s virtually an irreversible decision, that’s not a button I’d push. It seems like a decision to make only when things are dire, not when they’re going well relative to peers.     According to recent reports, last week, South African President Cyril Ramaphosa arrived in Silicon Valley seeking investment. He also had a message for Elon Musk: Remember your South African roots and “give back.”.

    Sources indicate that it is an extraordinary appeal from the leader of a country crippled by unemployment, corruption, and economic stagnation. His African National Congress bears most of the responsibility. Yet Ramaphosa came to America, begging bowl in hand, asking successful entrepreneurs to help repair the damage. His government, meanwhile, obstructs one of the most obvious ways Musk could help — allowing Starlink to operate in South Africa.

    Marian L. Tupy is the founder and editor of HumanProgress.org and a senior fellow at the Cato Institute’s Center for Global Liberty and Prosperity.

    On “Elon Musk Owes South Africa Nothing”.

    Photo Credit: An American Airlines Boeing 777-200 aircraft. Vincenzo Pace.

    American has spent much of the year building back its Chicago presence, even earning another gate at O’Hare just from increasing capacity at the airport, which has been the backdrop of an intense turf war with United.

    American Airlines dropped its lawsuit challenging Chicago’s 2025 decision to shift O’Hare International Airport gate space from American to United Airlines, days after losing an appeal in the case.

    Sources indicate that the reallocation, which took effect October 1, 2025, cost American more than 500 feet of gate space, about four narrow-body gates. American stated it would operate out of seven fewer. United gained about four and a half.

    American has since added three gates at O’Hare: two acquired from Spirit and one earned by growing at the airport.

    Woman Faced A Felony Charge For Stealing A Rental Car—Then Won A Seat In Congress And Prosecutors Dropped The Case

    ⏱️ ~31 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, this year was such a wave election that in some cases candidate quality didn’t matter at all.
    • Industry observers note that shortly before the election, Democratic congressional candidate LaKesha Womack pulled into a high school parking lot in North Carolina for a Sunday rally.
    • According to recent reports, the incumbent congressman she was running against turned the rental into a television ad.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, this year was such a wave election that in some cases candidate quality didn’t matter at all. It was enough to win just not to be a Republican. Shortly before the election, Democratic congressional candidate LaKesha Womack pulled into a high school parking lot in North Carolina for a Sunday rally. A sheriff’s deputy pulled up behind her. He handed her a felony summons for stealing a Toyota Corolla she’d rented from Budget nearly seven years earlier. The incumbent congressman she was running against turned the rental into a television ad. She won anyway. And on Tuesday, after Budget got paid for the six weeks its car was overdue, the district attorney dropped the charge for good. It’s good to get elected to Congress. Budget Car Rental Got The Corolla Back In 2019 Womack picked up the car in Charlotte on August 27, 2019, and renewed the rental twice. Her last extension began October 7, 2019. According to the police report the vehicle was due back at noon on October 23. On November 26 an officer reported that police couldn’t find her and put out an all points bulletin. Police recovered the Corolla and returned it to Budget on December 4, 42 days late. Budget sold the vehicle the following year. Womack has a number of excuses for never returning the car. She states a diabetic seizure and long hospitalization had wiped her out financially. (It’s not clear why that kept her from returning it.) Her son went into foster care while she was in the hospital (again, unclear why that kept her from returning it) and the two of them wound up living in a hotel (hotels have parking, but the hotel didn’t force her to keep the car). She’d expected the firm to come get the car. She says she had nowhere reliable to receive mail (when you rent a car you know you’re supposed to give it back, even without a mailed notice) and she thought the matter was settled (exactly how it would have been is unclear). On January 14, 2020, a court issued a summons for felony failure to return the car. Under North Carolina law, willfully keeping a rental vehicle past its deadline is a felony if the vehicle is worth more than $4,000. The car was valued at $20,000. Womack says she first heard about the case on Friday, October 9, 2026. A local reporter posted the records. She responded, “I do owe them people some money, obviously.” BREAKING: Documents pulled from the NC Courts government website show District 14 congressional candidate Lakesha Womack has a “pending” felony warrant for failure to return a rental car in 2019. Pics and links attached. https://t.co/4WZRvweFxM — Brett Jensen WBT News (@Brett_Jensen) October 9, 2026 Two days later, on October 11, the summons was reissued. A Polk County deputy’s body camera caught the handoff outside the county Democratic rally. Republican Congressman Tim Moore ran an ad on this. Watch Tim Moore’s campaign ad, “Keep Your Money.” He Helped Draw The District. She Didn’t Even Live In It. Moore spent ten years as speaker of the North Carolina House, helped gerrymander the district to favor Republicans and won it in 2024 by nearly 65,000 votes. Womack, an ordained minister making her first run for public office, lived in a neighboring district and stated she had no prepares to move. A House member only has to live in the state. Through October 14, Moore had spent $1,921,880 to Womack’s $55,626. He spent nearly $1 million on ads. She had no paid full-time staff and didn’t buy a TV spot. Three days after the deputy served her she was handing out T-shirts to striking workers at Charlotte Douglas airport. Moore won five of the six counties. He even won the Election Day vote by 21,246. But early in-person voting, which started four days after the deputy indicated up, gave Womack a 24,700 vote lead. With the felony case still pending, she posted, “#HatersGonnaHate I’m still Congresswoman-Elect.” On November 16 prosecutors learned she’d reached a deal with Budget. She paid the assessed rental cost for the overdue period. Budget told prosecutors it was satisfied. Campaign donations may not have mattered in the race, but that’s an unusually inexpensive way to buy goodwill with a member of the U.S. House of Representatives. On November 24 the state dismissed the charge with prejudice. This Wasn’t Hertz When I first wrote about Womack on October 11, my entire comment was “Ruh roh – it wasn’t Hertz.” A reader guessed Budget had lost track of a car it already had back. A father and his 13-year-old daughter were held at gunpoint outside Savannah in a car they’d just rented from Hertz’s Thrifty brand. When police let the father show them his rental agreement, it was 36 minutes old. The car had been reported stolen before Thrifty handed him the keys. A Hertz President’s Circle member wound up in jail over a Salt Lake City rental he’d extended, returned and paid $3,900 for. Those arrest stories seemed to dry up after Hertz brought in Palantir to help track its fleet in 2022 and agreed to pay $168 million to settle 364 claims. At Least Womack Was Still Campaigning North Carolina Republicans drew a map they expected would give them 11 of the state’s 14 U.S. House seats. Democrats won 11. Elsewhere the wave carried a couple of candidates who’d actually stopped campaigning. In Iowa, Eric Armstrong suspended his state House campaign on September 7 for health reasons. He beat a county supervisor and retired police lieutenant by about ten points. In Texas, Ericka Lomick suspended her campaign when a federal mortgage fraud conviction raised questions about whether she could serve. Her name stayed on the ballot for both the rest of the outgoing state representative’s term and the next one. She beat the same Republican in both elections. He’s asked the Texas Supreme Court to block certification of the special election. In California, Womack’s $55,626 would’ve looked like a fortune to Hipolito Cerros. The 28-year-old former mayor raised no campaign money, hired no staff and bought no ads. He unseated the Republican leader of the state Assembly. Tennessee tech support worker Victoria Broderick lost to Congressman Scott DesJarlais in 2024. He took 70% of the vote. After Republicans redrew the district, she ran again. She was still working full time and had to message her boss the morning after the election. The race was called for her the same day Womack’s charge was dropped. My personal favorite this cycle is Maricopa County, Arizona’s Sebastian Matta – a 19-year-old Arizona State philosophy sophomore – who beat a former state senator to become clerk of the Superior Court. He’d filed his campaign finance paperwork late and blamed his accountant for going quiet on him. He’ll run an office that processes 15,000 documents a day. To rent a Corolla from Budget at the Phoenix airport, he’s still two years short of the usual minimum age. That race was featured in season two, episode eight of The Newsroom. (HT: Paul H.)     Industry observers note that shortly before the election, Democratic congressional candidate LaKesha Womack pulled into a high school parking lot in North Carolina for a Sunday rally. A sheriff’s deputy pulled up behind her. He handed her a felony summons for stealing a Toyota Corolla she’d rented from Budget nearly seven years earlier.

    According to recent reports, the incumbent congressman she was running against turned the rental into a television ad. She won anyway. And on Tuesday, after Budget got paid for the six weeks its car was overdue, the district attorney dropped the charge for good. It’s good to get elected to Congress.

    Industry observers note that womack picked up the car in Charlotte on August 27, 2019, and renewed the rental twice. Her last extension began October 7, 2019. According to the police report the vehicle was due back at noon on October 23. On November 26 an officer reported that police couldn’t find her and put out an all points bulletin. Police recovered the Corolla and returned it to Budget on December 4, 42 days late. Budget sold the vehicle the following year. Womack has a number of excuses for never returning the car. She states a diabetic seizure and long hospitalization had wiped her out financially. (It’s not clear why that kept her from returning it.) Her son went into foster care while she was in the hospital (again, unclear why that kept her from returning it) and the two of them wound up living in a hotel (hotels have parking, but the hotel didn’t force her to keep the car). She’d expected the tech giant to come get the car. She says she had nowhere reliable to receive mail (when you rent a car you know you’re supposed to give it back, even without a mailed notice) and she thought the matter was settled (exactly how it would have been is unclear). On January 14, 2020, a court issued a summons for felony failure to return the car. Under North Carolina law, willfully keeping a rental vehicle past its deadline is a felony if the vehicle is worth more than $4,000. The car was valued at $20,000. Womack says she first heard about the case on Friday, October 9, 2026. A local reporter posted the records.     Latest Update: At the Races: The fresh Trump Democrats

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Editor’s note: At the Races will not publish next week on Thanksgiving Day.
    • By Niels Lesniewski, Mary Ellen McIntire and Daniela Altimari.
    • Senate Democrats powered their way to a majority by flipping nine seats – their biggest gain in nearly 70 years.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Editor’s note: At the Races will not publish next week on Thanksgiving Day. We’ll be back the following week.

    By Niels Lesniewski, Mary Ellen McIntire and Daniela Altimari.

    Senate Democrats powered their way to a majority by flipping nine seats – their biggest gain in nearly 70 years.

    Eight of those wins were in states that Donald Trump has carried every time he’s run so it’s no surprise that some of the incoming senators are talking up the prospect of working with him over the next two years.

    “We don't have time to wait until we have a different administration in the White House,” South Carolina Sen.-elect Annie Andrews told reporters this week. “We have two years ahead of us. We have very real problems that we need to address.”.

    Andrews is the first Democrat elected to the Senate from South Carolina since 1998. A pediatrician, she cited reducing prescription drug costs as a potential area of common ground with Trump.

    Recent findings suggest that “I support the president's attempts to stop taxes on tips and taxes on Social Security,” Andrews noted, citing two selling points of last year’s GOP reconciliation law. During the campaign, she issued a policy paper expressing support for making those provisions of the tax code permanent.

    James Talarico, the incoming senator from Texas, told fellow Democrats gathered in Denver last week that if Trump wanted “the same plaques and portraits and busts as LBJ, we can help make that a reality.”.

    “We should make the final two years of his presidency the most productive of any presidency in American history,” said Talarico, the first Democrat in nearly 40 years to win a Senate race in the Lone Star State.

    The idea of Trump and congressional Democrats working together might seem far-fetched, but with the incoming Democrats hailing from places such as Alaska, the Carolinas, Mississippi, Kansas and Texas, there’s a political incentive to appeal to Republican-leaning voters back home.

    But intentionally or not, Talarico and other newly elected Democrats might be borrowing from the playbook of New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who has welcomed Trump when goals align, including on an effort to redevelop the Sunnyside rail yard in the president’s native Queens.

    Trump has stressed that he will veto legislation he opposes from the incoming Democratic Congress, but, at least for the moment, he seems open to deals.

    “I have a feeling that this is going to be an unbelievably productive two years,” Trump told Fox News early Thursday morning in Shenzhen, China, adding that  he would invite Democrats to the White House.

    “I respect them,” he stated. “Politics is a nasty game, and they won.”.

    Sources indicate that peltola prevails: Former Rep. Mary Peltola’s victory over Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska brings the Senate Democratic Caucus to 56 seats in the 120th Congress. Peltola finished with just over 50 percent of the vote, negating the need to use the state’s ranked choice voting system. The race for the state’s at-large House district was decided by a ranked choice tally, with Republican Rep. Nick Begich defeating independent Bill Hill 51 percent to 49 percent in the final round. Alaska voters also rejected an attempt to eliminate ranked choice voting in the state by a vote of 54 percent to 46 percent.

    In a recent development, leadership elections: House Democrats nominated Hakeem Jeffries to serve as the next speaker in a 251-11 closed-door Wednesday vote, Roll Call’s Lauren Green reports. That puts Jeffries in prime position to become the first Black speaker when the full chamber votes in January. Meanwhile, Senate Democrats are scheduled to pick the next majority leader on Dec. 1, as our colleague Savannah Behrmann reports. Charles E. Schumer, who’s being challenged by Maryland’s Chris Van Hollen, maintains he has the votes to win.

    According to recent reports, A victory lap and a warning: Even as the Congressional Hispanic Caucus celebrates its largest roster ever, the group’s leaders had a warning for their fellow Democrats: “Latino voters gave Democrats a two-year lease, but it expires in 2028 unless the party changes its playbook for good,” stated California Rep. Linda T. Sánchez, who leads the group’s campaign arm.

    Recent findings suggest that #KYGOV: Republican Rep. James R. Comer, who was just elected to a sixth full term, released his much-anticipated run for Kentucky governor this week. The Bluegrass State is one of three states holding statewide executive  elections in 2027, along with Louisiana and Mississippi.

    Recent findings suggest that rocky Mountain roundup: Rep. Lauren Boebert, an outspoken Republican with a national reputation as a Second Amendment provocateur, lost her bid for reelection in Colorado’s 4th District to Democrat Eileen Laubacher, a retired Navy rear admiral. Meanwhile, Republican Gabe Evans, who fell short in his bid for a second term in the neighboring 8th District, declared he intends to challenge Laubacher in two years, Roll Call’s Samantha Freeman reports.

    They’re back: Our colleague Nina Heller tracked down former congressional staffers who are back on the Hill as newly elected members. “I never thought this would be the path, but I’m honored to do it,” remarked Rep.-elect Sydney Gruters, who worked for fellow Florida Republicans Greg Steube and Vern Buchanan, her soon-to-be House predecessor.

    RIP: Former Rep. Jim McDermott, a longtime advocate for universal health care, died last week at the age of 89. The Washington Democrat, who retired to a small town in southwestern France after 28 years in the House, was hailed by his home state’s senior senator, Patty Murray, “as one of the first and most powerful voices fighting to fix our broken health care system in Congress.”.

    Recent findings suggest that where the House stands: As of 3 p.m. Eastern time, House Democrats have flipped 46 seats to three for the Republicans and are on track to hold at least 257 seats in the next Congress. Six races remain uncalled by The Associated Press, including two in Louisiana that will be decided by December runoffs. The AP is also yet to call Tennessee’s 4th District, where Republican Rep. Scott DesJarlais has conceded to Democrat Victoria Broderick, who leads by 272 votes out of nearly 200,000 cast.

    Recent findings suggest that thompson loses: California Rep. Mike Thompson lost his bid for a 15th term to former venture capitalist Eric Jones, a political newcomer who poured millions into his campaign. Thompson is the second California member to lose to a fellow Democrat this year, after Rep. Jimmy Gomez. But Rep. Doris Matsui held off an intraparty challenge from democratic socialist Mai Vang.

    2028 draft: Supporters of former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg released Team Pete PAC on Thursday, an effort to urge him to launch a second presidential bid.

    Recent findings suggest that battleground rep: Michigan Rep. Kristen McDonald Rivet will be House Democrats' battleground leadership representative in the next Congress, acting as a bridge between members in competitive districts and party leadership. McDonald Rivet, who ran unopposed for the position, will succeed Nevada Rep. Susie Lee.

    In a recent development, #INGOV: Indiana Gov. Mike Braun debuted his 2028 reelection campaign as speculation swirls that state Attorney General Todd Rokita could challenge him for the Republican nomination. Rokita, a former congressman, has criticized Braun for not disciplining state educators who posted controversial comments after Charlie Kirk’s assassination but said last week that he wanted Braun to “run for governor” and “be successful.” The two previously faced off in a 2018 Republican Senate primary, with Braun going on to serve one term in the Senate.

    Latest leader for New Dems: Illinois Rep. Nikki Budzinski will chair the New Democrat Coalition next year, taking over from fellow Illinois Rep. Brad Schneider. New Mexico’s Gabe Vasquez, Ohio’s Greg Landsman and Washington’s Kim Schrier and Marilyn Strickland will serve as co-chairs of the center-left group, the largest ideological entity in the Democratic Caucus.

    Remembering Holden: Former Pennsylvania Rep. Tim Holden, who served 10 terms in the House before losing a Democratic primary to Matt Cartwright in 2012, died Sunday at the age of 69. House members held a moment of silence for Holden on the floor Thursday. Republican Rep. Dan Meuser, whose district includes territory Holden once represented, described him as “well-liked and widely respected, including by those on both sides of the political aisle.”.

    Sources indicate that investigated: Ohio Rep.-elect Brian Poindexter is under investigation for alleged sexual harassment after the Democrat’s campaign hired a human resources firm to investigate the complaint. Both the Blue Dog PAC and the Congressional Progressive Caucus, which had endorsed Poindexter’s candidacy, dropped their support in the closing days of the campaign after learning of the allegation.

    Tennessee two-step: Tennessee Democrat Jeri Green, who narrowly lost the open governor’s race to Republican Sen. Marsha Blackburn, confirmed a bid for the state Senate seat GOP Rep.-elect Brent Taylor is expected to vacate. Taylor narrowly defeated Democratic state Rep. Justin Pearson in the redrawn 9th District, though both men were simultaneously reelected to their legislative seats.

    The  historic “blue tsunami” that swept Democrats into commanding Senate and House majorities has some pundits questioning whether Republicans will ever be in charge again, observes Roll Call elections analyst Nathan L. Gonzales of Inside Elections.

    But you just have to look at the election results from two years ago to realize that when it comes to winning party coalitions, nothing is permanent anymore, Nathan writes.

    Only the young: Latest York magazine catches up with young Republicans in South Carolina and finds that immigration policy and the war in Iran have turned many of the MAGA faithful against the GOP.

    From satirist to senator: The Washington Post traces South Carolina Democrat Annie Andrews’ journey from an online agitator who made relentless fun of Republicans to a newly elected senator who says she’s eager to work with her GOP colleagues.

    Bad blood: The Boston Globe explores the long-standing rivalry between Maine’s two newest members of Congress: Democratic Sen.-elect Troy Jackson and Republican Rep.-elect Paul LePage.

    Schumer’s choice: Uncertainty around whether Schumer will seek another term in 2028 has risen as the Fresh York Democrat seeks to become Senate majority leader next year, Politico reports.

    That's how long it's been since the Senate Democratic Caucus last saw a contested race for its top leadership position, with Maryland’s Van Hollen now challenging Schumer for the job.

    After Democrats lost eight Senate seats (and their majority) in the 1994 Republican Revolution, 42-year old South Dakota Sen. Tom Daschle edged out Connecticut's Christopher J. Dodd by a single vote, 24-23, to succeed outgoing leader George Mitchell of Maine.

    The last time a sitting Democratic Senate leader faced a formal challenge was a decade earlier, in 1984.

    Recent findings suggest that west Virginia's Robert C. Byrd, who’d been leading his party in the chamber since 1977, easily fended off a bid by Florida’s Lawton Chiles.

    The last time either party experienced a contested race for the position was four years ago, when Florida Sen. Rick Scott challenged Republican leader Mitch McConnell of Kentucky.

    As Byrd did before him, McConnell handily defeated his challenger in the secret-ballot vote.

    Machine recounts in a pair of House races in North Carolina are expected to be completed Monday. Republican Rep. Virginia Foxx trails Democrat Chuck Hubbard by 331 votes, while GOP Rep. Pat Harrigan leads Democratic challenger Ashley Bell by just over 2,500 votes. The trailing candidate could then request a partial hand recount.

    Recent findings suggest that monday is also the deadline for Republican Rep. Brad Finstad to formally request a recount in his razor-thin race against Democrat Jake Johnson in Minnesota’s 1st District. Finstad, who reportedly said he’ll seek one, trails Johnson by 321 votes.

    Lufthansa Group has spent years bringing its airlines closer together behind the scenes. This latest move suggests Frankfurt increasingly wants to own the customer relationship, too.

    Lufthansa Group is taking another step toward becoming a consumer brand in its own right with the launch of a fresh app that brings together six of its airlines under a single digital identity.

    Unveiled on Monday, the app combines the digital services of Lufthansa, Swiss, Austrian Airlines, Brussels Airlines, ITA Airways, and Discover Airlines, alongside elements of the group’s Miles & More loyalty program. Passengers can book flights, purchase additional services, check in, access boarding passes, and track their baggage.

    While much of the functionality will be familiar to people of the existing airline apps, Lufthansa Group chief commercial officer Dieter Vranckx described it as a logical step in developing the parent firm’s brand and “making it more tangible” to passengers.

    His comments this week echo an earlier observation that the firm “is evolving from a group of airlines into an integrated airline group.”.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Rove is offering up to 55% more miles when you transfer to five airline and hotel programs, along with 10 miles per dollar on hotel bookings that still earn hotel points, elite night credit and status benefits. For the hotel offer there’s no stay deadline, so you can book future travel on Black Friday and collect the higher earning rate. Rove is a standalone rewards program. You earn its miles through travel bookings, shopping, dining and gift cards, then redeem them for travel or transfer them to airline and hotel programs. There’s no particular credit card you need to carry. Most of these offers last just one day. Here’s the schedule Rove gave me: November 26–30: transfer bonuses and double referral bonuses, ending at 11:59 p.m. Eastern on Monday, November 30. Black Friday, November 27: the 10x Loyalty Eligible hotel offer, boosted shopping and gift card earnings, first hotel booking bonus and double qualifying miles. These end at 11:59 p.m. Eastern that night. 40%–55% Transfer Bonuses To Five Programs The same percentage bonus applies to Japan Airlines Mileage Bank, Air France KLM Flying Blue, Finnair Plus, Copa ConnectMiles and ALL Accor. Your Rove status determines the percentage. The four airlines normally transfer 1:1. Accor’s normal ratio is 1.5 Rove miles to 1 Accor point. Here’s what transferring 15,000 Rove miles gets you: Rove Status Bonus Airline Miles Or Avios Accor Points Member or Gold 40% 21,000 14,000 Platinum 50% 22,500 15,000 Diamond 55% 23,250 15,500 Those percentages already include the extra transfer bonus for Platinum and Diamond. Japan Airlines is worth looking at for its own flights and partner awards, including American Airlines and Alaska Airlines itineraries with three free stopovers. Rove offered everyone a 50% Japan Airlines transfer bonus in October, though. The 40% offer for most members is lower than that, while Diamond’s 55% is higher. Japan Airlines miles expire after 36 months, so a bonus doesn’t make them a good place to park miles indefinitely. Finnair is useful even if you don’t strategy to fly Finnair. You can move Avios to British Airways at 1:1. Your Finnair account needs to be at least 30 days old before you can link it to another Avios program. Accor points are generally worth 2 euro cents each toward eligible hotel stays. The 15,000 Rove miles in the table therefore produce €280, €300 or €310 in hotel value, depending on status. Platinum effectively gets a 1:1 transfer to Accor during this promotion, and Diamond does slightly better. 10x Hotel Miles While Keeping Hotel Points And Benefits On November 27, new Loyalty Eligible hotel bookings earn 10 Rove miles per dollar. Rove notes there are no property or rate exclusions within that category, and no promotional deadline to complete the stay. I’ve liked this feature since it released. You can earn Rove miles while retaining hotel program points, qualifying nights and applicable elite benefits, along with the rewards from the card you use to pay. A $1,000 qualifying room subtotal earns 10,000 Rove miles. At 1.5 cents per mile, that’s $150 in additional travel value, before the hotel and credit card rewards. 5,000 Miles On A First Hotel Booking Has Different Rules Promo code BF500 adds 5,000 Rove miles to an eligible first Rove Rate hotel booking of $500 or more made on Black Friday. Join if you aren’t already a member and then take advantage of this. Rove clarified that you must never have booked a hotel through them before. Someone who’s already made a Loyalty Eligible reservation doesn’t qualify merely because this would be their first Rove Rate booking. An existing Rove account can qualify if it hasn’t booked a hotel. The code can combine with an eligible Rove elite hotel discount. However, Rove Rate bookings don’t earn hotel points or elite night credit, or guarantee hotel elite benefits. At exactly $500, the bonus adds 10 Rove miles per dollar to the booking’s standard earnings. I’ve covered a 5,000 mile first booking offer at the same spending threshold before. Double Qualifying Miles Includes Purchased Miles Boost Black Friday transactions that ordinarily earn qualifying miles will earn twice as many toward Rove status. Rove confirms that includes purchased Miles Boost and elevated earnings for elite members. For example, $1,000 in qualifying hotel spending at the promotional 10x rate generates 10,000 redeemable miles and 20,000 qualifying miles. The extra status credit doesn’t double the redeemable miles you can transfer or spend. Rove’s annual requirements remain: Gold: 50,000 qualifying miles and 5 qualifying transactions. Platinum: 125,000 qualifying miles and 10 qualifying transactions. Diamond: 250,000 qualifying miles and 20 qualifying transactions. Flat bonuses such as BF500’s 5,000 miles don’t ordinarily qualify, so they aren’t part of the doubling. Status earned for 2026 lasts through December 31, 2027. Travel counts toward the year it’s completed, while shopping and gift card purchases count by purchase date. A hotel stay ending in 2027 won’t be 2026 qualifying activity because it was booked in 2026. Higher Gift Card Earnings And The Full Shopping List Rove is offering up to 30% more miles on nearly all gift cards on Black Friday. A 30% increase would turn a 5x rate into 6.5x, for instance. (The actual rate depends on the gift card.) Rove sells gift cards marked for instant mileage earning which can help with this weekend’s transfer bonuses.     #123538. IndiGo Adds Southeast Asia Flights as Westbound Costs Climb

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (228 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Skift ↗ Open Full Page

    IndiGo Adds Southeast Asia Flights as Westbound Costs Climb

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (228 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Skift

    ⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Photo Credit: An Indigo A320neo aircraft.
    • IndiGo calls it "disciplined growth." It's also a retreat to safer ground: Southeast Asia suits its narrowbodies while fuel is expensive and Pakistan's airspace is closed.
    • IndiGo is adding more flights to Southeast Asia at a time when rising fuel costs and geopolitical tensions are making some of its westbound operations more expensive.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Photo Credit: An Indigo A320neo aircraft. Airbus / Airbus.

    IndiGo calls it "disciplined growth." It's also a retreat to safer ground: Southeast Asia suits its narrowbodies while fuel is expensive and Pakistan's airspace is closed. But it's the same region where IndiGo cut six routes this summer, so the real test comes after the holiday peak.

    IndiGo is adding more flights to Southeast Asia at a time when rising fuel costs and geopolitical tensions are making some of its westbound operations more expensive.

    India’s largest airline will launch daily flights between Delhi and Kuala Lumpur, as well as Bengaluru and Hanoi, from Dec. 20. It will also increase Delhi–Singapore services to twice daily from the same date and Delhi–Bangkok flights to 19 a week from Dec. 28.

    The additions give IndiGo more capacity in a region that has long been popular with Indian travelers. They also come as the airline is becoming more careful about where it deploys aircraft internationally, with higher fuel bills and airspace restrictions making some routes harder to operate profitably.

    Recent findings suggest that for the quarter ended Sept. 30, international capacity, measured in available seat kilometers, fell 3% from a year earlier, while domestic capacity remained broadly flat.

    #123537. Cathay Pacific Asia Miles Confirms Partner Award Devaluation, Starting January 5

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2554 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Viewfromthewing ↗ Open Full Page

    Cathay Pacific Asia Miles Confirms Partner Award Devaluation, Starting January 5

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2554 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Viewfromthewing

    ⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that starting in January, it’ll take more Cathay Pacific miles to fly British Airways first class from Los Angeles to London than to fly Cathay first class all the way from Latest York to Hong Kong.
    • In a recent development, A week after Chase added 1:1 transfers to Cathay Pacific, Cathay tells me its partner airlines are charging it more for award seats.
    • These are the nine examples Cathay shared, in Asia Miles per passenger each way.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that starting in January, it’ll take more Cathay Pacific miles to fly British Airways first class from Los Angeles to London than to fly Cathay first class all the way from Latest York to Hong Kong. The London flight goes from 135,000 to 162,000 Asia Miles each way. Hong Kong stays at 160,000. For two people booking London, that’s an extra 54,000 miles one way. A week after Chase added 1:1 transfers to Cathay Pacific, Cathay tells me its partner airlines are charging it more for award seats. It’s raising the mileage price of selected partner awards and dropping Companion Ticket Awards. The new rates kick in at midnight in Hong Kong on January 5, 2027. In the U.S., get your ticket issued before 11 a.m. Eastern on Monday, January 4 (10 a.m. Central, 8 a.m. in Los Angeles) for future travel to book at the old rates. Partner Award Prices Starting January 5 These are the nine examples Cathay shared, in Asia Miles per passenger each way. The airline notes its flight award search will show prices for every route and cabin starting January 5. They aren’t revealing all the changes in advance. Miles flown · Cabin Current Jan. 5 Increase Up to 750 · Economy 10,000 12,000 20% 751–2,750, Type 2 · Economy 17,500 21,000 20% 751–2,750, Type 2 · Business 37,000 44,000 18.9% 751–2,750, Type 2 · First 60,000 66,000 10% 2,751–5,000 · First 100,000 110,000 10% 5,001–7,500 · Business 93,000 100,000 7.5% 5,001–7,500 · First 135,000 162,000 20% 7,501+ · Business 120,000 130,000 8.3% 7,501+ · First 170,000 204,000 20% Hong Kong–Tokyo falls in the short “Type 2” band. Japan Airlines business class on that route goes from 37,000 to 44,000 miles. Pick the Cathay Pacific flight and it’s still 33,000 miles for the same trip. What Happens To The British Airways Surcharge Deal? One reason to use Asia Miles has been to pay less in British Airways fuel surcharges. It’s a way to save ~ $500 each way on taxes and fees between the U.S. and Europe. However, Japan Airlines generally charges fewer miles for the same award and offers equally low surcharges. JAL is a Bilt, Rove, Citibank, and Capital One transfer partner. Flying New York–London is a distance of under 5,000 miles. Cathay gave us a new first class price for that band, but hasn’t noted what happens to business class. Los Angeles–London falls in the next band up. Business class there cost 89,000 miles before last May’s increase, costs 93,000 today and goes to 100,000 in January. That 100,000-mile award will take 100,000 Chase points or 125,000 American Express points. American Express gives you 800 Asia Miles per 1,000 points. Bilt, Capital One, Wells Fargo, Rove Miles and eligible Citi ThankYou cards all offer 1:1 transfers. When An American Airlines Connection Changes The Price The biggest reason I’d transfer points to Cathay is access to first and business class seats that American AAdvantage and Alaska Airlines Atmos Rewards often can’t book. Last year I flagged two first class award seats at a time between New York and Hong Kong, available only with Asia Miles. I’d still check American before transferring points. Just last week Seattle and Toronto to Hong Kong opened up in business class for 70,000 American miles each way. Cathay is keeping its Standard Award prices in place. Changes are only to partner awards. New York–Hong Kong is still 119,000 miles in business class. The oneworld Multi-Carrier Award chart which covers two oneworld airlines without Cathay, or Cathay plus at least two other oneworld airlines, isn’t changing either. Cathay says very few members used its Companion Ticket Award. If work bought you a qualifying Cathay business or first class roundtrip, you could use fewer miles to bring someone along on the same flights in the same cabin. Cathay will stop issuing companion awards in January as well. If you find the partner flights you want but might need to move the trip a day, I’d ticket before the cutoff. Changes to date only preserves the ticketed mileage price, subject to award availability and any change fee. Change the route, cabin or anything else after the cutoff and the new award prices apply.     A George Floyd Musical: What Could Go Wrong?

    ⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Playbill, a site for all things theater-related, posted a job listing seeking “comedic singers and musical theater vocal talent” to record George Floyd: The Musical, a latest project by the Busted Broadway group based in New Jersey that “exists to shake the snow globe and remind audiences that laughing at dark humor is not only allowed but necessary.” On its website, the group’s tagline for the show is “The $20 Bill That Changed the World!”.
    • It has been revealed that playbill has since released an apology claiming it “incorrectly approved” the job posting for its site, and is now reviewing its internal processes.
    • Abigail Anthony is a staff writer at National Review.

    Playbill, a site for all things theater-related, posted a job listing seeking “comedic singers and musical theater vocal talent” to record George Floyd: The Musical, a latest project by the Busted Broadway group based in New Jersey that “exists to shake the snow globe and remind audiences that laughing at dark humor is not only allowed but necessary.” On its website, the group’s tagline for the show is “The $20 Bill That Changed the World!”.

    It has been revealed that playbill has since released an apology claiming it “incorrectly approved” the job posting for its site, and is now reviewing its internal processes. “We know this listing has upset and offended many, and the fact that it made it onto our site has disappointed those who trust us as an outlet. For that, we are sorry, and are committed to regaining your trust,” the statement reads. In response to the post, some people have demanded that Playbill take more accountability by explaining exactly how such a thing was approved for the site, expose who is behind the musical (though that was already public), hire more minorities to prevent similar wrongdoing in the future, and matter apologies to the Floyd family and the black community. Others have more firmly called for barring the musical’s creative leader from the platform entirely.

    Abigail Anthony is a staff writer at National Review.

    On “A George Floyd Musical: What Could Go Wrong?”.

    #123534. House Ethics panel adopts changes aimed at speeding up investigations

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rollcall ↗ Open Full Page

    House Ethics panel adopts changes aimed at speeding up investigations

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (653 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Ethics Chairman Michael Guest, left, and ranking member Mark DeSaulnier arrive for a committee meeting on Capitol Hill in April.
    • In a year roiled by sexual misconduct allegations in the House, the Ethics Committee approved a series of changes Thursday that its members say are intended to improve how the panel handles its investigations.
    • In a rare public meeting lasting less than 10 minutes, the committee discussed proposed tweaks aimed at speeding up its processes, after some observers have criticized its pace.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Ethics Chairman Michael Guest, left, and ranking member Mark DeSaulnier arrive for a committee meeting on Capitol Hill in April. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    In a year roiled by sexual misconduct allegations in the House, the Ethics Committee approved a series of changes Thursday that its members say are intended to improve how the panel handles its investigations.

    In a rare public meeting lasting less than 10 minutes, the committee discussed proposed tweaks aimed at speeding up its processes, after some observers have criticized its pace.

    Recent findings suggest that “My problem with the Ethics Committee is it just takes too damn long,” Rep. Madeleine Dean, D-Pa., noted earlier this year.

    The internal rule changes were adopted in a voice vote by the committee, which is evenly divided between Republicans and Democrats.

    “We believe that these rule changes will provide more transparency. They will expedite our investigative process while maintaining protections for witnesses and victims, while also making sure that … due process is protected,” Chair Michael Guest, R-Miss., said during the meeting.

    When former Reps. Eric Swalwell, D-Calif., and Tony Gonzales, R-Texas, resigned earlier this year amid misconduct allegations, it sparked outrage as some called to rethink how the House polices bad behavior. Both men were on the radar of the Ethics Committee at the time, but such investigations have tended to move slowly.

    “I want the Ethics Committee to move faster,” said panel member Rep. Suhas Subramanyam, D-Va., back in April.

    The committee did not immediately make available the exact text of the changes it adopted Thursday. But a summary sent in a news release earlier this week included one proposal aimed at “consolidating deadlines” for a member to respond to an investigative subcommittee’s findings. Another tweak aimed at speeding things up would give the chair and ranking member subpoena power on behalf of the committee, rather than requiring a full committee vote.

    The summary described “codifying the Committee’s policy of publicly disclosing any findings that a Member engaged in sexual harassment or other sexual misconduct” while “prohibiting publication of the identity of any victim.”.

    Also on the list: “Expanding the circumstances under which fines and denials of privileges are considered an appropriate sanction to include any abuses of position.”.

    Sources indicate that it comes as women on both sides of the aisle have formed a partnership aimed at reviewing how Congress deals with sexual misconduct and suggesting concrete ideas for an overhaul. Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández, D-N.M., has been co-leading that effort as the chair of the Democratic Women’s Caucus alongside Republican Women’s Caucus head Kat Cammack, R-Fla.

    According to Leger Fernández, the Ethics Committee has “consulted” with her group as it weighed the changes to its internal rules.

    “The Ethics Committee was clearly listening to women staffers, and has been a great partner in our work. We appreciate how they’ve consulted DWC and that these proposals will improve transparency and help protect the identities of those who report alleged misconduct. Together with RWC, we will continue to work on additional legislation in our sexual misconduct reform agenda,” she said in a statement earlier this week.

    Cammack remarked that, while “the entire system on Capitol Hill has been designed to create a chilling effect for victims,” the Ethics committee rule changes would help.

    According to recent reports, “Putting public disclosure of misconduct findings in writing, while protecting every victim’s identity, gives staffers a commitment they can count on. Faster investigations mean they get answers in time to matter,” Cammack mentioned in a statement. “This is exactly the kind of change our bipartisan task force has been pushing for.”.

    Ethics ranking member Mark DeSaulnier, D-Calif., noted everyone in the House should have “zero tolerance” for sexual harassment.

    “We’ve worked very hard to look at ways that we could make the committee’s process fair, transparent and accountable, and I think we’ve done that,” he mentioned at Thursday’s meeting.

    #123533. Industry News: DSA Is Right: Congressman-Elect Mocked For Refusing TSA Facial Scan—But He Brought A Passport Card, And The Photo Is Optional

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 30m • 📚 Deep Dive (6016 w)

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Viewfromthewing ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: DSA Is Right: Congressman-Elect Mocked For Refusing TSA Facial Scan—But He Brought A Passport Card, And The Photo Is Optional

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 30 min read (6016 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Viewfromthewing

    ⏱️ ~30 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • A newly elected congressman is getting mocked for refusing a TSA face scan, with commenters telling him to take the bus or train instead.
    • The democratic socialist gets some of the explanation wrong.
    • Rabb, a Pennsylvania state representative, was elected to represent Philadelphia in Congress and takes office in January.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A newly elected congressman is getting mocked for refusing a TSA face scan, with commenters telling him to take the bus or train instead. The post sharing his video accuses him of refusing to have identification. But Chris Rabb claims he brought a U.S. passport card, which is accepted ID. And the checkpoint photograph he declined is optional. The democratic socialist gets some of the explanation wrong. However, the people demanding his arrest appear to have a bigger problem with the rules than he does. Rabb, a Pennsylvania state representative, was elected to represent Philadelphia in Congress and takes office in January. In the video, he says he’s returning to Philadelphia from Boston. He says he doesn’t have a REAL ID card. He got a passport card so he wouldn’t need to carry his actual passport. He says TSA’s equipment wouldn’t process his identification, employees asked for another ID, and he didn’t have one with him. He also says he’d told them he didn’t consent to the photograph. DSA Congressman Chris Rabb already working for the people by refusing to let TSA take his photo and also refusing to have an ID card. So brave. https://t.co/DnZSKeKZ7e — Lee Kuan Yimby (@LeeKuanYimby) November 23, 2026 He Brought A Type Of ID TSA Accepts The State Department says a U.S. passport card can be used for domestic air travel instead of a REAL ID driver’s license. It fits in a wallet. It doesn’t work for international air travel, but Boston to Philadelphia isn’t international. REAL ID enforcement doesn’t mean every passenger needs a state license with a star. A passport, passport card, and other documents on TSA’s accepted identification list are acceptable. Ye replies include “Arrest his ass,” “poor Comrade,” “Bro just ride the train,” and sarcastic declarations of bravery. I have plenty of disagreements with democratic socialists. I’ve criticized Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez’s intervention in American Airlines’ maintenance dispute and Bernie Sanders getting airline taxes wrong. That doesn’t make a socialist’s privacy objection wrong. And disliking someone’s glasses isn’t a reason to demand he surrender a choice even the government says he has. You Can Decline The Photo. You Still Have To Complete Screening. Rabb’s most useful advice is simple: Just say, “I don’t consent to being photographed.” That’s TSA’s published policy. Travelers can decline facial recognition and use the standard ID verification process instead. Rabb Wants To Avoid Being Put In A Database Rabb says he’s trying to avoid being put into another database. Too late! The standard checkpoint camera compares your face to the photograph on the ID you present. TSA says the image isn’t saved after a positive match, apart from limited testing used to evaluate the technology. You don’t necessarily have to believe them. Touchless programs can work differently. Identifying an enrolled traveler using a gallery of existing government photographs doesn’t add you to the database, you’re already there. Opting out doesn’t remove your travel records. The government already receives passenger information for Secure Flight screening. And obtaining a passport card already means you supplied a photograph. There are cameras everywhere, but for the most part there’s so much data that at least we benefit from security through obscurity. At least we did before AI made it all so much more easily searchable. I’ve covered passenger information collected for aviation security being used to help immigration agents intercept travelers. Law enforcement has access to passenger data even without this additional photo. Positive ID Matches Don’t Contribute Much To Security Positive identification is supposed to make sure you can’t simply fly under somebody else’s name. That’s necessary for the government’s database of people they want to bar from flying or ensure receiving extra screenig works. Of course, the database itself is corrupted. The terrorist screening database has over two million people in it. I’ve written about the sprawling watchlist system and agents using the no fly list to retaliate against people who wouldn’t become informants. Identity checks also serve a separate economic purpose for airlines. Matching the traveler to the name on a nontransferable ticket helps enforce price discrimination. If you could buy a cheap ticket months ahead and freely sell it to someone traveling tomorrow, you’d compete with the airline’s expensive last-minute fare. Preventing that resale helps airlines separate passengers willing to strategy ahead from those willing to pay more. It doesn’t create a real aviation security benefit. I Made My Own Compromise Long Ago I’m an old line civil libertarian on this. I was late signing up for Global Entry in 2013 because I didn’t like volunteering fingerprints and a photograph to the government in exchange for easier travel. When I finally joined, before the Edward Snowden revelations, I was already writing about government collection of cellphone geolocation data, license plate readers, and other surveillance. The government already had the information, so I might as well get the benefits. At the same time, I think we’ve largely lost this argument in practice. I’ve written about the spread of checkpoint photography and biometric boarding gates becoming normal. The surveillance state has won. Rabb himself concedes that his refusal won’t make much practical difference. He sees value in reminding people they can object and in resisting normalization. I have sympathy for this. What To Do If You Want To Opt Out Bring an accepted physical ID and make the request before the camera takes your picture. “I’m opting out of the facial photograph. Please use the standard ID check.” Hand over the document and cooperate with that check. Separate a camera objection from a document problem. If the reader won’t process a passport card, ask for a supervisor and an alternative document check. Carrying a second accepted ID can save time if something fails. With millions of passengers processed per day small failure rates mean actual failures happen regularly. Escalate a refusal of the opt out calmly. TSA says you can request a supervisor or passenger support specialist. Record the airport, checkpoint, date, time, and what was said, and submit a complaint. They’ll go ahead and ignore or dismiss it. Don’t confuse any of this with arriving without allowable identification. Since February, TSA’s ConfirmID requirement costs $45. The payment covers a ten day travel period and doesn’t guarantee identity verification. Meanwhile, at the border, U.S. citizens can request an alternative inspection. Noncitizens, including permanent residents, generally cannot claim the same photo opt-out. Rabb will shortly have a better tool than an argument at a document podium: a seat in Congress. He can press for enforceable limits on retention and sharing, a meaningful manual alternative, and a way to challenge bad database entries. It won’t matter, because the security state is far more powerful than he is. But I’d be happy to see a democratic socialist spend some of his time constraining government power over travelers. Identifying an enrolled traveler using a gallery of existing government photographs doesn’t add you to the database, you’re already there. Opting out doesn’t remove your travel records. The government already receives passenger information for Secure Flight screening. And obtaining a passport card already means you supplied a photograph. There are cameras everywhere, but for the most part there’s so much data that at least we benefit from security through obscurity. Positive ID Matches Don’t Contribute Much To Security Positive identification is supposed to make sure you can’t simply fly under somebody else’s name. That’s necessary for the government’s database of people they want to bar from flying or ensure receiving extra screenig works. Of course, the database itself is corrupted. Preventing that resale helps airlines separate passengers willing to initiative ahead from those willing to pay more. It doesn’t create a real aviation security benefit.     Your complete guide to the ALL Accor hotel loyalty program

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (190 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Thepointsguy

    ⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
  • ALL Accor is the loyalty program for Accor Group, covering over 5,800 hotels across more than 45 brands worldwide, with a strong presence outside North America.
  • Reward points in this program have a fixed value in euros toward eligible hotel stays, making redemptions straightforward but limiting opportunities for outsized value.
  • Elite status can be earned through nights or eligible spending, with higher tiers offering perks such as lounge access, suite upgrades and complimentary breakfast in certain regions.
  • Paid ALL Accor+ memberships provide discounts, status nights and other benefits, potentially offsetting their cost for frequent guests.
  • Not all Accor brands or properties participate fully in the program, and some benefits are region-specific or subject to availability.
  • Points earned and elite status qualification are based on brand, status tier and eligible pre-tax spending, with annual resets for status each calendar year.
  • Transfers from U.S.-accessible partners generally occur at less than a 1:1 ratio, and there is no U.S.-issued cobranded card for this program.

    • What you'll miss from the article

  • A detailed breakdown of elite status tiers, earning and redemption options, and tips for maximizing value with ALL Accor.

    Thieves Are Stealing Used Cooking Oil From Hotels—It May Be Fueling Your Next Flight

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1270 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Viewfromthewing

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that thieves stole 350 gallons of cooking oil from an airport hotel in Pennsylvania.
    • Pennsylvania State Police responded on November 18 to the theft at 3400 Airport Road, the Days Hotel by Wyndham Allentown Airport / Lehigh Valley.
    • The listed victim was Buffalo Biodiesel, which deals in used cooking oil, which it processes and sends to biodiesel refineries.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that thieves stole 350 gallons of cooking oil from an airport hotel in Pennsylvania. The haul was valued at $2,100, and the victim named by state police was a biofuel organization. Hotel kitchen grease has become valuable enough to steal. Used grease can fetch more than new! And it can eventually wind up fueling an airline flight and helping a carrier meet its environmental goals. Pennsylvania State Police responded on November 18 to the theft at 3400 Airport Road, the Days Hotel by Wyndham Allentown Airport / Lehigh Valley. The hotel has a restaurant and banquet facilities, so there’s a kitchen generating oil to collect. The loss works out to $6 per gallon.     Latest Update: Iran resolution blocked in first war powers vote since midterms

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Tim Kaine, D-Va., seen here at the Capitol on June 17, stated additional war powers votes are under discussion for when Democrats control both chambers in the 120th Congress.
    • The Senate rejected a resolution Thursday meant to rebuke President Donald Trump over the Iran war weeks after the midterm elections demonstrated the depth of public anger about the war and its effects on the U.S.
    • Senators voted 48-51 against adopting the Iran war powers resolution that the House previously adopted in mid-September that would direct the president to withdraw U.S.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., seen here at the Capitol on June 17, stated additional war powers votes are under discussion for when Democrats control both chambers in the 120th Congress. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

    The Senate rejected a resolution Thursday meant to rebuke President Donald Trump over the Iran war weeks after the midterm elections demonstrated the depth of public anger about the war and its effects on the U.S. economy.

    Senators voted 48-51 against adopting the Iran war powers resolution that the House previously adopted in mid-September that would direct the president to withdraw U.S. forces from the war.

    Recent findings suggest that as they have previously with similar measures, GOP Sens. Susan Collins of Maine, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska and Rand Paul of Kentucky broke with their party to support the resolution, while Democratic Sen. John Fetterman of Pennsylvania broke with his party to oppose it. Departing GOP Sens. Thom Tillis of North Carolina and Bill Cassidy of Louisiana, who have at times voted in support of similar measures, this time voted against the resolution.

    Even if the resolution was adopted in both chambers of Congress, it would be largely symbolic since, as a concurrent resolution, it would not go to the president for his signature.

    But the vote afforded senators the opportunity to register their complaints about the war for the first time since Democrats routed Republicans in the midterm elections.

    It also comes amid a larger debate within the Democratic Party on how best to fulfill their campaign promise of ending the war as they prepare to take control of Congress next year.

    Industry observers note that democrats have become increasingly interested in trying to cut off funding for the war rather than continuing to hold war powers votes. But they are divided on whether to demand an immediate end to funding in the next government funding bill in December or to wait until they take power in January.

    According to recent reports, “When we have the gavels, we are contemplating other things, and we're actually contemplating things in connection with the CR discussion,” Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., told reporters Thursday in an apparent reference to the debate among Democrats.

    As of Nov. 13, the war has cost at least $48.3 billion, up from $47 billion last month, the nominee to be Navy comptroller, Arthur Miller, told the Senate Armed Services Committee at his confirmation hearing Thursday.

    As with previous estimates, the number Miller cited Thursday includes munitions, equipment replacement costs and operational costs but does not factor in the cost of damage to U.S. bases, which alone is likely to run in the billions.

    Recent findings suggest that last week, a trio of Senate Democrats unveiled legislation to prohibit funding for offensive military operations in Iran that they said they intend to introduce as an amendment to the next government funding bill, which Congress will need to pass to avoid a government shutdown after Dec. 11.

    On Thursday as the Senate voted on the war powers resolution, Sens. Tammy Duckworth, D-Ill., and Kirsten Gillibrand, D-N.Y., two of the sponsors of the proposed amendment, demanded it be included in the next funding bill.

    “We’ve already tried tool after tool to get the president to rein in this conflict. Nine months in, defunding the war is the only way to force Trump to end it,” Duckworth, who vowed to vote against any continuing resolution that doesn’t include the amendment, stated at a news conference.

    It has been revealed that sen. Michael Bennet, D-Colo., unveiled his own proposed amendment Thursday to bar any future and previous funding from being used to “support directly or indirectly combat activities by United States personnel in or over Iran, or in Iranian territorial waters” unless specifically authorized by Congress.

    His legislation is modeled off of language Congress passed in 1973 to cut off funding for the Nixon administration’s bombing campaign in Cambodia, Bennet’s office said in a news release.

    Industry observers note that “When we vote on short-term spending in the near future, we can fund the government and end this war. It is what the American people demand, and what they deserve,” Bennet noted in a statement.

    Meanwhile, the House is likely to vote again on a war powers resolution before year’s end.

    “Before the lame duck’s over, I hope to enforce a war powers resolution vote, and it’ll be a chance for Republicans to say whether they did or didn’t get the message on Nov. 3,” Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., remarked Thursday in a brief interview, referring to the date of the elections.

    It has been revealed that as with previous resolutions, Massie’s would direct the president to remove U.S. military units from hostilities against Iran unless specifically authorized by Congress or needed to defend against an imminent attack.

    In a recent development, the resolution was filed Nov. 10, and under the 1973 War Powers Resolution, Massie can force a vote 15 calendar days after its introduction.

    In a recent development, john M. Donnelly and Lauren Green contributed to this report.

    Dubai’s hotels are under pressure, but developers are still signing deals for branded residences. The main bet is on buyers, with brands delivering a healthy premium over the wider market.

    Developers in the UAE are still launching branded residences, betting on long-term demand as the U.S.-Iran war that began in late February weighs on Dubai’s hotel market.

    Branded residences are residential properties developed in partnership with an established brand, such as a luxury hotel operator.

    According to recent reports, avenew Development has rolled out The St. Regis Residences at Dubai Islands with Marriott International. Dubai South has signed UK-based Cheval Collection for Cheval South Bay. And Al Seeb Real Estate Development has started main construction on Chedi Private Residences in Dubai.

    Industry observers note that the releases come against a weakened hotel market. Dubai occupancy fell to 68.4% in October, down 16.5 points from 84.9% a year earlier, according to CoStar’s STR. Average daily rate dropped 28.1% to $181 and RevPAR fell 42% to $124. International visitors in the first 10 months of the year fell 38% to 9.7 million, according to Dubai’s Department of Economy and Tourism.

    Van Hollen: Senate rules changes a matter for caucus to decide

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (557 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., during a press conference on Thursday.
    • Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., endorsed a bipartisan plan Thursday to adopt latest rules aimed at speeding up Senate procedures but stopped short of calling for abolishing the filibuster, laying down a marker on a key internal debate for Democrats as he positions himself to challenge Senate Minority Leader Charles E.
    • Jeff Merkley, D-Ore., at a press conference Thursday to express his support for a proposal from Merkley and Sen.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sen. Jeff Merkley, D-Ore. looks on as Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., during a press conference on Thursday. (Finn Gomez/Getty Images).

    Industry observers note that sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., endorsed a bipartisan plan Thursday to adopt latest rules aimed at speeding up Senate procedures but stopped short of calling for abolishing the filibuster, laying down a marker on a key internal debate for Democrats as he positions himself to challenge Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y.

    Van Hollen joined Sen. Jeff Merkley, D-Ore., at a press conference Thursday to express his support for a proposal from Merkley and Sen. Steve Daines, R-Mont., to, among other changes, adopt a “talking filibuster,” requiring senators to continuously hold the floor if they seek to prevent a bill or nomination from moving forward.

    Van Hollen went further to say that while his personal view is that the filibuster itself is “anti-democratic,” changes beyond what Merkley and Daines are proposing are a matter for further discussion.

    Industry observers note that “I’m in favor of filibuster reform,” Van Hollen mentioned. “How and when we do that is a matter for the caucus to decide.”.

    The filibuster, a Senate tactic that effectively requires a 60-vote threshold to advance most legislation, has long been the subject of calls for change or outright abolition from members of both parties.

    Other changes Merkley and Daines unveiled in October include eliminating cloture requirements for nominations and amendments, reducing post-cloture time for legislation, and introducing a fresh suspension process modeled after the House rules to allow bills with broad support to move quickly.

    Merkley actually held two separate press conferences Thursday on his filibuster proposal, one with his Montana Republican co-sponsor and then later with Van Hollen, whose bid to become majority leader he has endorsed.

    At the earlier appearance, Daines noted that he thought the changes, if adopted, would “truly be a cultural change for the Senate” and lead to greater bipartisanship.

    “We believe these reforms are appropriate no matter who is in the majority, no matter what the election outcomes were,” Daines remarked.

    Daines also reiterated his view that implementing any rules changes would require 67 votes from the full chamber.

    But Democrats have been debating whether to use their newly introduced majority in 2027 to change the rules on the first day of the session with 51 votes, or to eventually employ the so-called “nuclear option,” a series of procedural moves leading to a simple majority vote.

    Democrats used that tool in 2013 to lower the voting threshold for advancing some presidential nominations with a simple majority, rather than 60 votes. A Republican majority followed in 2017 by extending that change to include Supreme Court nominations, and again in 2019 to reduce the number of hours between a cloture and final confirmation vote.

    A spokesperson for Schumer declined to comment on Van Hollen’s endorsement of the Merkley-Daines blueprint.

    Schumer has said he remains confident in his bid to remain party leader.

    Van Hollen reiterated Thursday that his “momentum is growing,” after several senators-elect have thrown their support behind the Maryland Democrat.

    “I think people recognize that if we're going to deliver on the substantial things that the American voters stood up for and voted for, you can't just go back to business as usual and status quo,” Van Hollen stated.

    Culture Is Driving Latest Interest in Travel for Ramadan
